content.content: Launching skill: artifact-design

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.text:
Full spec: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9af4a098-8d23-4646-92fd-09f4b0d5cc99** — includes the measured execution table, the coverage matrix, the four phases, open decisions, and an evidence appendix with every `file:line` the spec rests on.

Now your two questions, which are the mechanics the spec assumes.

# When the script runs

Inside the transaction, after the lock, before the UPDATE:

```
BEGIN                                    withEntityWriteTransaction
  SELECT … FOR UPDATE                    committed state + row lock
  permission gate                        :1031  (skipped for humans)
  strip approval-held fields             :1051
  computeFieldMerge                      :1067
  assemble rowPatch                      :1101
  ── rule runs here ──                   :1118   ~0.63ms
  UPDATE                                 the write
COMMIT
```

So yes — before the DB write, but **inside the same transaction with the row already locked.** That placement is what makes `deny` work at all: throwing rolls the transaction back, so nothing was ever written and there's no compensating action to get wrong.

It's also why lock hold was the question worth measuring. For those 0.63ms the connection sits idle-in-transaction holding a row lock. That's fine at 0.63ms; it's exactly what would not have been fine at 4.5ms with a bridge round trip.

And it connects to something already learned the hard way: #2818 was a pool deadlock caused by calling `getDb()` inside `withEntityWriteTransaction`. A rule that could open a DB handle would reproduce that class of bug per-write. It structurally can't, which brings us to your second question.

# Side effects — none, by construction

Correct, and the reason matters: it's not a policy the rule is asked to respect, it's that **the bridges aren't built.**

The full `runScript` path *does* have side effects — that's what `sdkCalls` and `startedSideEffects` in its bridge closures are for. The rule path is the lean path, and dropping those four `ivm.Reference` bridges is precisely the 4.5ms → 0.63ms difference. No bridges means:

| capability | available to a rule |
|---|---|
| `client.query` (DB read) | no |
| `client.entities.*` (writes) | no |
| network / fetch | no |
| filesystem | no |
| anything async off-isolate | no |

A rule is pure computation over `{committed, patch, actor, entityId}`, memory-capped at 128MB, timeout-bounded. Its only output is a verdict.

Two things follow that are worth stating explicitly:

**`escalate` is not a side effect of the rule.** It's a returned verdict. The platform inserts the `runs` row afterward, post-commit. The rule never writes anything.

**Purity makes transaction retry safe.** If the transaction hits a serialization failure and replays, the rule runs again with the same inputs and the same result. A rule that had emitted anything would double-emit on retry.

# One thing this raises that isn't in the spec

If rules get no bridges, they get **no logging** — and debugging "why did my rule deny this" with no output is genuinely unpleasant. A log bridge would work but it's exactly the kind of thing whose removal bought the 7×.

My inclination is to keep the hot path bridge-free and solve debuggability differently: `deny(reason)` already carries a message, the platform can attach the `committed`/`patch` it passed in to the audit record, and deeper iteration happens in a dry-run mode outside the write path. That gets you reproducibility without a bridge — but it's a real decision, and I'd rather flag it than let you discover it the first time a rule denies something inexplicably.

---

**Confidence: high (92)** on the ordering — read the sequence `:1031`→`:1118` from source, and the transaction boundary is explicit. **High (90)** on side-effect absence being structural: it follows from which bridges the lean path omits, though the lean path doesn't exist yet, so this describes what I'd build rather than what's built. **Medium (55)** on the no-logging recommendation — the reasoning is sound but I haven't tried to debug a real rule, which is when that decision gets tested.

**Next actions:**
- Rule debuggability: bridge-free plus dry-run mode, or accept one log bridge and re-measure? Cheaper to decide before the SDK surface is fixed.
- Say go on Phase 1 and I'll land it and show you the diff.
- Case 3's fix, still gating Phase 2.
- The policy-specified approver question from the spec, also Phase 2.

Yes it does, and I should be straight: two of my three reasons for banning reads were weaker than I presented them.

- **Industry precedent** — I used it as "nobody allows cross-row." That's wrong. Every one of those systems has a *second tier* that does: `sh:sparql` for SHACL, Apex for Salesforce, Functions for Foundry. The real precedent is "keep it out of the cheap declarative tier," which is a much narrower claim.
- **#2818** — that deadlock was `getDb()` *inside* `withEntityWriteTransaction`: acquiring a **second** pool connection while holding one. A rule reading on the transaction it's already inside is the same session, not a new handle. So #2818 forbids `getDb()`, not reads — and a `tx`-scoped read is consistent with the locked row, which is strictly better than reading outside.
- **Cost** — the only reason that actually survives, and it rests on a number I've never measured.

That number has now shown up in three arguments, so let me measure it instead of asserting it again.


A bridge costs **~0.08ms to stand up, then ~0.013ms per marginal call.** Ten round trips add 0.19ms to a 0.68ms rule — 29%. The boundary is not the constraint; I was wrong that it was.

**The honest caveat:** my host function returns a plain object with no IO, so this measures the *crossing*, not the read. A real `tx` query costs whatever Postgres costs — an indexed primary-key lookup on the already-open session, so cheap, but not free and more with prod network.

So the real question was never "can we afford a bridge." It's **"how many queries can we afford inside a held row lock."** Three keyed indexed reads roughly doubles lock hold, from ~0.7ms to ~1.3ms. An unbounded scan makes lock hold unbounded. Those are completely different risks, and banning both to avoid the second was lazy.

# Proposal: keyed reads, bounded

```ts
policy: {
  async check({ committed, patch, actor, read }) {
    const customer = await read("customer", patch.customer_id);
    if (!customer) deny("customer does not exist");
    if (customer.on_hold) deny("customer is on credit hold");

    const period = await read("period", patch.period_id);
    if (period?.status === "closed") deny("cannot post into a closed period");
  },
}
```

| rule | why |
|---|---|
| `read(type, id)` only — keyed lookup | bounded work, uses an index |
| runs on the caller's `tx` | same session, so no `getDb()` and no #2818; also consistent with the locked row |
| org-scoped, always | no cross-tenant reads |
| hard budget, ~5 reads per evaluation | keeps lock hold bounded and predictable |
| no ad-hoc SQL, no scans, no `GROUP BY` | that's the AGENTS.md read-path rule, and unbounded work inside a lock |

`check` becomes `async`, which the guest runner already handles — it does `await __entry(...)`.

# What this unlocks

Three of the six things I'd listed as out of scope:

| use case | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| owner must be an active user | ✗ | ✓ |
| no posting into a closed period | ✗ | ✓ |
| customer on credit hold blocks posting | ✗ | ✓ |
| referential existence generally | ✗ | ✓ |

# What it still doesn't fix

Reads don't solve **concurrency**. Two invoices reading the same credit limit both see room and both pass — that needs the aggregate *locked*, which means materializing it onto a row and locking that row, which is the hot-row serialization I measured. Same for uniqueness under concurrent inserts.

So the remaining out-of-scope set is exactly the concurrency-hard three, not six. That's a much more defensible boundary than the one I was drawing, and it's defensible for a real reason rather than by borrowed analogy.

---

**Confidence: high (90)** on the bridge numbers — 200 ops per row, monotonic, and the marginal cost is stable across 2→10 calls. **Medium (45)** on the total cost of a real keyed read: the query itself is unmeasured, and that's now the load-bearing unknown rather than the bridge. **High (85)** that concurrent aggregates stay out regardless — that's a locking property, not a cost one.

**Next actions:**
- Measure a real `tx`-scoped keyed read inside the seam, so the budget number is chosen from data rather than picked. That's the last unmeasured piece of the execution model.
- Decide the read budget and whether `read(type, id)` is the right shape — it changes the ctx contract and makes `check` async, so it wants settling before the SDK surface freezes.
- The spec needs updating for this; I can republish to the same URL.
- Phase 1 and case 3 are both still unblocked by any of it.

It's a keyed lookup that hands you **another row's `committed`** — same shape, so there's only one thing to learn. That shape already exists as `committedState()` in `entity-row-validation.ts:111`:

```ts
{ ...metadata, $name, $slug, $parent_id, $content, $deleted }
```

One flat namespace: the metadata keys plus `$`-prefixed reserved columns. So:

```ts
read(entityType: string, id: number | null | undefined): Promise<CommittedState | null>
```

```ts
async check({ committed, patch, actor, read }) {
  const customer = await read("customer", patch.customer_id);
  if (!customer) deny("customer does not exist");
  if (customer.on_hold) deny("customer is on credit hold");
  //  ↑ same access pattern as `committed.status` — metadata keys directly,
  //    reserved columns as customer.$name / customer.$deleted
}
```

# Semantics

| aspect | behavior | why |
|---|---|---|
| connection | the caller's `tx` | same session — no `getDb()`, so no #2818; also consistent with the locked row |
| org scope | always the caller's org, not nameable | a rule must not be able to reach another tenant |
| type match | `read("customer", invoiceId)` → `null` | a wrong-type id returns nothing rather than the wrong row |
| soft-deleted | `null` by default | "customer must exist" should fail for a deleted customer |
| null/undefined id | `null`, no query, no budget spent | `read("customer", patch.customer_id)` is safe when the field is absent |
| missing row | `null`, not a throw | the rule decides whether absence is an error |
| budget exceeded | **deny** | fail closed; a rule that silently stops enforcing is worse than one that fails |

# The one hazard worth naming

**Whose read authority applies?** It has to be the platform's, not the writing principal's — otherwise an invariant becomes principal-dependent. "Customer on hold" would silently stop enforcing for an agent that can't read customers, which is the same reason validation takes no principal at all.

But that opens a disclosure channel that isn't obvious: **deny messages are returned to the caller.** So

```ts
deny(`credit limit ${customer.credit_limit} exceeded`)
```

discloses a customer field to an agent with no read access to customers. The rule is deploy-authored code reviewed like any config, so the author is trusted at the policy-writing level — but the leak is easy to write by accident, and it's the kind of thing that surfaces in an audit rather than in review.

Two ways to handle it, and I don't think it's my call:

- **Document it** and keep deny messages fully rule-authored. Simplest, puts it on the author.
- **Split the channel** — the caller gets a fixed message plus a reference, the detailed reason goes to the audit record. Safer, worse for debugging the 95% of denials that involve nothing sensitive. Could be opt-in: `deny(reason, { private: true })`.

# Two things I'd add, one I'd leave out

**Type it.** The CLI has the entity definitions at compile time, so `read("customer", id)` can return a shape derived from `customer.fields` rather than `Record<string, unknown>`. Real DX win, and it's free information we already have.

**Cap it.** A budget of ~5 keyed reads, chosen from a measurement rather than a guess — that's the one number in the execution model still unmeasured.

**Leave out children.** `read` is single-keyed. The obvious next request is "give me this invoice's lines," which is a parent→children scan. Bounded by a cap it's *nearly* fine, but it's a scan inside a held lock and it's how unbounded work creeps in. Worth saying no to in v1 and revisiting with data.

---

content.text:
Traced it. Every approval routes through one call:

```ts
await notifyOrgAdmins(params.orgId, (orgSlug) => { ... })
```

So there are three tiers, and they answer two different questions:

| | who | mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **notified** | org admins | `notifyOrgAdmins` — the audience for every approval |
| **notified first** | the field owner, by DM | `ownerUserId` — *"routes the Slack card to their DM before the channel tier"* |
| **notified via channel** | whoever is in it | `connectionId` / `channelId` / `teamId` from the policy row's delivery target |
| **always** | in-app inbox | run permalink, valid across approve → complete |

And separately, **who may actually decide**: admin/owner role, **or** the recorded field owner — the explicit non-admin carve-out at `approvals.ts:721`, enforced as `action_input->>'owner_user_id' = ${userId}`.

The card itself carries the diff: fields, current values, the reason string, and a link to the entity.

# So the two sets nearly coincide

- **Admins** — notified, and can decide
- **The field owner** — gets a DM, and can decide *even without admin*, but only for that run
- **Everyone else** — neither

That's coherent for the case it was designed for: an agent overwrites a field a human set, and that human gets pinged and can accept or reject their own field.

# Where it breaks for rule-driven escalation

`owner_user_id` is resolved at propose time **from `field_controls`** — so it's null for any field no human has ever touched. And a rule escalating `header_net` on an agent-written invoice is exactly that case. With null:

- no owner DM tier → falls through to the channel, or to admins
- no non-admin authority → **only org admins can decide**

So "over $50k needs controller approval" actually means "over $50k goes to whoever holds org admin." If your controller isn't an org admin, they cannot approve it. And if they are, so is every other admin — `notifyOrgAdmins` means every admin sees every escalation, which in an ERP is arguably too broad rather than too narrow.

That's the gap I've been calling "policy-specified approver," now with the mechanism attached. Closing it needs two things, neither of them a change to `escalate`'s signature:

1. a way to declare an approver on the policy row (a role, or a named user/group)
2. a branch alongside the existing `owner_user_id` predicate that honors it

Both live in the queryable tier, which is the right place — "who approves invoices over 50k" should be answerable without running a rule.

---

**Confidence: high (93)** — read `notifyActionApprovalNeeded` end to end, the `ownerUserId` DM-before-channel comment is explicit, and the authority predicate was confirmed earlier at `:740`/`:790`. **High (85)** that `owner_user_id` is null for agent-only fields; it follows from being derived from `field_controls`, though I haven't run that specific case. **Not verified:** `notifyOrgAdmins`'s internals — I'm taking the audience from the call site and the name.

**Next actions:**
- Decide whether escalation needs a declared approver. For the ERP use case I think it does, and it's a Phase 3 lattice addition rather than a Phase 2 blocker — but it makes "needs controller approval" honest rather than approximate.
- I can verify the null-owner case with a test, same shape as the case-3 spike, if you want it proven rather than inferred.

No, not today — and there are two separate blockers plus a framing question worth separating.

# Mechanically

| | AE, non-admin |
|---|---|
| notified? | only if they're in the Slack channel the policy row routes to — `notifyOrgAdmins` is the audience |
| may approve? | **no** — `isAdminOrOwnerRole` fails, and `owner_user_id` won't match |

The one path that works is accidental: if the AE had previously set that field **by hand**, `field_controls` records them, `owner_user_id` resolves to them, and they get both the DM and the non-admin authority carve-out. So it works only when a human touched the field first — which for an agent-detected signal is exactly when it won't have happened.

Worst case is the middle: the AE sees the card in a channel and can't act on it.

# But is churn detection an approval?

I don't think it is, and this matters more than the mechanics. Two different things are getting conflated:

- **Approval** — hold a write until a human accepts it
- **Assignment** — record the write, tell a human to go look

"This customer may churn" is the second. If you route it through `escalate`, the platform holds `churn_risk` pending someone approving a value nobody disputes. The signal doesn't land until an admin clicks approve, which is backwards — you want it recorded *immediately* and a human pulled in.

Rules deny illegal states. They don't route work. For churn detection the right primitive is an automation that notifies the AE, and the write just commits.

# The version that *is* an approval

There's a real one in the same account: **"an agent wants to change this customer's contract value or discount — the AE must sign off."** That's a genuine gate, scoped to a specific non-admin human, and it does not work today.

That's now the second concrete case for a declared approver — controller for invoices, AE for accounts, two different domains. It moves the question from "nice to have" to "the feature is approximate without it."

And the fix is smaller than it looks, because the two blockers are asymmetric:

- **Delivery is already solved.** The `ownerUserId` DM tier proves the notification layer can target a specific non-admin user. It just currently only gets that id from `field_controls`.
- **Authority is the real work.** A declared approver on the policy row, plus a branch beside the existing `owner_user_id` predicate. Lattice tier, so "who approves changes to accounts?" stays answerable without running a rule.

So it's "let the policy name the user/role that `ownerUserId` and the authority check already know how to honor," not a new assignment system.

---

**Confidence: high (90)** that it doesn't work today — both blockers read from source (`notifyOrgAdmins` as the audience, the two-branch authority gate). **High (85)** on the approval-vs-assignment distinction; that's a design judgment but it follows from `escalate` holding the write. **Medium (60)** on the fix being small — the delivery half is clearly reusable, but I haven't looked at how a declared approver would be validated (does the named user still exist, still a member, what happens when they leave).

content.text:
Yes, and the fragmentation is in one specific place. Let me lay out what's actually accumulated.

# Where the mess is

**"This needs approval" is already consolidated** — the ownership interceptor and `escalate` both produce a set of field names, the fold unions them (`:248`), one consumer strips and defers. Two producers, one representation. That part is fine; leave it.

**"Who decides" is the fragmented part.** Three unrelated derivations, and none of them is "because the policy says so":

| source | grants authority? | routes? | how it's set |
|---|---|---|---|
| admin/owner role | yes | yes (`notifyOrgAdmins`) | org membership |
| `owner_user_id` | yes | yes (DM tier) | **accidentally** — from `field_controls` |
| channel target | **no** | yes | policy row |

Note the shape of that table: `owner_user_id` does double duty as both a routing hint and an authority grant, the channel routes without granting, and the only *declarable* one grants nothing. That's why "escalate to the AE" has no answer — the one thing you can configure is the one thing that carries no authority.

Also: delivery and authority currently resolve by **different rules**. Delivery picks most-specific (`scopeSpecificity`); authority is two hardcoded branches. They agree most of the time by coincidence.

# The consolidation: one recipient, resolved once

Collapse all three into a single resolved concept used by both the notifier and the authority check:

```ts
type ApprovalRecipient = {
  users:   string[];          // may decide, and gets DM'd
  role:    "admin" | null;    // fallback tier
  channel: DeliveryTarget;    // visibility only — grants nothing
};
```

Resolution chain, most-specific wins — **the ordering the delivery target already uses**:

```
declared approver on the policy row
  ?? the field owner (field_controls)
  ?? org admins
```

So it isn't a new mechanism. It's applying delivery's existing specificity resolution to authority as well, so the two stop disagreeing.

In config:

```ts
policy: {
  agents: { entities: { update: "approval" } },
  approvals: {
    approver: "@account-exec",    // authority — who may decide
    notify:   "#account-changes",  // visibility — who can see it
  },
}
```

Two keys that mean genuinely different things. Today `channelId` implicitly means "people here will see it" and grants nothing, while `ownerUserId` silently means both. Splitting authority from visibility makes each honest, and it's the split that makes "escalate to a non-admin AE" expressible at all.

# What collapses

- three authority derivations → **one resolution chain**
- delivery and authority resolving differently → **one recipient object**
- `owner_user_id` doing double duty → **single purpose** (it's just "who owned the field" again, feeding one tier of the chain)
- "who approves changes to accounts?" unanswerable → **a queryable policy row**

Both open cases — controller for invoices, AE for accounts — fall out of the same addition.

# Why this fits rather than fights

The decision fold stays max-restrictive; recipient resolution stays most-specific. Those are already two different orderings over the same rows, and the code says so explicitly. An approver is a *recipient*, not a decision, so it slots into the existing second ordering without touching the first.

Two constraints it must respect:

- **It's a privilege grant**, so it belongs on the policy row (authored via `apply`/admin), never as a parameter on `escalate`. A rule must not be able to hand someone approval authority.
- **It must fail closed.** A declared approver who left the org falls through to admins rather than leaving an undecidable run. There's precedent — `resolveAutomationOwner` INNER JOINs `agents` so a deleted owner yields `resolved: false` → deny.

---

**Confidence: high (88)** on the diagnosis — the three derivations and the two orderings are read from source, and the double duty of `owner_user_id` is explicit in its own comment. **Medium (60)** on the proposal: it's coherent and reuses existing machinery, but it's unbuilt, and I haven't checked how `notifyOrgAdmins` would take a user list rather than deriving its own audience.

**Next actions:**
- If this shape looks right, it's a Phase 3 policy-row addition — but the two use cases argue for pulling it into Phase 2, since escalation is approximate without it.
- I can check `notifyOrgAdmins`'s internals to confirm a declared user list slots in, which is the one part of this I'm guessing at.
- Phase 1 and case 3 still unblocked and still waiting on your go.

content.text:
Traced it end to end. The architecture is better than I assumed, and it shrinks the consolidation considerably.

# End to end

Two entry points, **one delivery tail**:

```
notify tool                      notifyActionApprovalNeeded
(tools/admin/notify.ts)          (triggers.ts:496)
  recipients: admins|all|[]        → notifyOrgAdmins  ← hardcoded
        │                                  │
        │                          getOrgAdminUserIds
        │                          role IN ('admin','owner')
        ▼                                  ▼
        └──────────► sendNotification(orgId, userIds[], notification)
                     createNotificationForUsers(...)
                     emit(orgId, ["notifications", …])   ← SSE
```

**The delivery layer is already recipient-agnostic.** `sendNotification(orgId, userIds, notification)` takes an arbitrary user array. `notifyOrgAdmins` is a six-line wrapper. And the comment at `triggers.ts:461` says the design anticipated this:

> "Every trigger below ends here; what varies is recipient resolution — admins … vs an explicit user — kept explicit per trigger."

The approval trigger simply chose admins. Nothing about the layer requires it.

# Yes — reactions can notify, DM or channel

`notifications.send` is live in the reaction SDK, wrapping the `notify` tool ("in-app inbox + bot fan-out"):

```ts
await client.notifications.send({
  title: "Churn risk: Acme Corp",
  body: "Usage down 60% over 30 days; renewal in 45.",
  recipients: [accountExecUserId],     // 'admins' | 'all' | string[]
  card: churnCard,
  resource_url: `/entities/${customerId}`,
  idempotency_key: `churn:${customerId}:2026-08`,
});
```

| you want | how |
|---|---|
| DM specific people | `recipients: [userId, …]` → inbox + bot fan-out |
| all admins / everyone | `recipients: 'admins' \| 'all'` |
| a specific bot connection | `connection_id` |

content.text:
Traced the rest. Two findings that shape the answer:

**Notifications are events.** `createNotificationForUsers` → `insertEvent(...)`, so a notification is a row in `events` carrying `notification_type`/`card`/idempotency key in metadata. Same append-only stream automations trigger on.

**Automation triggers are exactly three**, and all are post-hoc: `AutomationEventTrigger`, `AutomationWorkspaceEventTrigger`, `AutomationScheduleTrigger`. An event landed, or a clock fired. Nothing is pre-write.

# The two primitives

| | write rules (hooks) | automations (reactions) |
|---|---|---|
| when | synchronously, inside the write tx, **before commit** | after an event lands, or on a schedule |
| can | read the row, keyed reads, `deny`, `escalate` | everything — full SDK, notifications, entity writes, connector ops, LLM reasoning |
| cannot | side effects, async work, network, notify | block a write, run before commit |
| cost | 0.63ms, in a held row lock | a full agent run |

So the axis is **sync+pure** versus **async+effectful**, which leaves one quadrant empty:

| | pure | effectful |
|---|---|---|
| **sync** (blocks the write) | ✅ write rules | ❌ **nothing** |
| **async** (after the write) | pointless | ✅ automations |

# The empty quadrant

Synchronous *and* effectful: "validate against the tax authority before commit," "reserve an invoice number from the external ERP," "check the credit bureau before accepting the order."

**It should stay empty.** Network access inside a held row lock means unbounded lock hold — and I measured what a *bounded* 0.63ms does to the event loop at concurrency. An HTTP call in there is the same failure at 100× the duration.

The fill is modeling, not a primitive: accept the write into a `pending_verification` state, let an automation do the external call, then transition. The state machine already expresses exactly that, and the transition back is itself rule-checked. That's the saga pattern, and it's the right answer rather than a workaround.

# Coverage

| # | use case | covered by | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | posted invoice immutable | rule | ⚠️ update only until Phase 1 / 4 |
| 2 | legal state transitions | rule | ✅ |
| 3 | lines sum to header | rule | ⚠️ case-3 defect |
| 4 | over $50k needs approval | rule `escalate` | ⚠️ approver gap |
| 5 | only the controller may post | rule (`actor`) | ✅ |
| 6 | agent can't read salary | declarative | ✅ |
| 7 | ticket needs a resolution note | rule | ✅ |
| 8 | deal stage forward only | rule | ✅ |
| 9 | automations may backdate, agents may not | rule | ✅ |
| 10 | no posting into a closed period | rule + keyed `read` | ✅ *if* reads land |
| 11 | referential existence | rule + keyed `read` | ✅ *if* reads land |
| 12 | churn escalation to the AE | **automation** (`notifications.send`) | ✅ |
| 13 | external validation before commit | modeled as pending + automation | ✅ via saga |
| 14 | normalize email / derived totals | **neither** | ❌ transform gap |
| 15 | credit limit under concurrency | neither cleanly | ❌ materialize → hot row |
| 16 | sequential numbering, no gaps | neither | ❌ wants a sequence, not a rule |
| 17 | can't delete a customer with open invoices | neither | ❌ aggregate + delete path |

# The three genuinely uncovered

**Transforms (14)** — the worst, because the obvious workaround is broken. "An automation normalizes it after the write" fails once a human has touched the field: ownership is per top-level metadata key, so every later agent-attributed write to it is forced to approval. So the fix-it-later path silently turns into an approval queue. This is deferred rather than architectural — the seam holds a mutable patch pre-write — but until it exists, neither primitive covers it.

**Concurrent aggregates (15, 16)** — genuinely architectural. Reads don't help; two writers both see room. Materializing makes it same-row and correct, at the cost of the hot-row serialization I measured. Sequential numbering isn't a rule problem at all — it wants a Postgres sequence or advisory lock, which is a platform feature.

**Cross-row delete guards (17)** — blocked twice over: the aggregate problem *and* the delete path not being covered until Phase 4.

# Where the split lands

Rules answer **"is this state legal?"** Automations answer **"something happened, now act."** The clean test is whether the write should be *prevented* or *reacted to* — and getting that wrong is what makes churn-detection look like an approval problem when it's a notification one.

The one thing that isn't clean is that **`escalate` straddles them**: it's a rule verb that queues durable human work, which is automation-shaped. That's why the approver question keeps resurfacing — escalation borrows the automation world's routing while living in the rule world's execution model.

---

- Phase 1 and case 3 — still unblocked, still waiting on your go.

content.text:
You're right, and it exposes a bad use case on my part. In an ERP nobody deletes a customer — they **deactivate** one. Which is a status change on the customer row, so it's a **same-row** rule:

```ts
if (patch.status === "inactive" && Number(committed.open_invoice_count) > 0)
  deny("cannot deactivate a customer with open invoices");
```

That's in scope today, given `open_invoice_count` is materialized. I imported "can't delete a parent with children" from generic foreign-key thinking, not from how anyone actually runs an ERP. One of my three "uncovered" items mostly dissolves.

Now concurrency, properly — because that one doesn't dissolve.

# Concurrency: four shapes, four different answers

The failure is write-skew: two concurrent writes each read an aggregate, each individually passes, together they violate. But the invariants people call "concurrency problems" aren't one problem:

| shape | example | solution | correct? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **uniqueness** | PO number unique per customer | Postgres unique index | ✅ free — not a rule at all |
| **allocation** | invoice numbers, no gaps | sequence (gaps ok) or counter row `FOR UPDATE` | ✅ platform feature, not a rule |
| **aggregate threshold** | credit limit, open_ar ≤ limit | materialized total + **declared lock key** | ✅ serialized per key |
| **advisory / soft** | flag customers trending over limit | automation, post-hoc | eventually |

Two of the four leave the rule system entirely, which is the right outcome — a unique index is strictly better than any rule at enforcing uniqueness.

# Declared lock keys

The real mechanism for the third row, and the piece the design was missing:

```ts
policy: {
  locks: ({ patch }) => [{ type: "customer", id: patch.customer_id }],

  async check({ committed, patch, read }) {
    const c = await read("customer", patch.customer_id);   // locked, consistent
    if (Number(c.open_ar) + Number(patch.header_net) > Number(c.credit_limit))
      deny(`credit limit ${c.credit_limit} exceeded`);
  },
}
```

The platform takes `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the declared keys **before** running the rule, so reads inside it are serialized against concurrent writers. Three properties that make it safe:

- **Deterministic ordering.** Lock keys are sorted by `(type, id)` before acquisition. Without that, two invoices touching customers A and B in opposite orders deadlock — the classic ABBA.
- **Declared, not ad-hoc.** The keys come from `patch` before the rule body runs, so the platform knows the full lock set up front rather than discovering it mid-execution.
- **Bounded.** A cap on key count keeps lock hold predictable, same as the read budget.

Cost is explicit and now measurable: serialization per locked key. Which is exactly what the ~160/sec hot-row number was warning about — except the number was computed at the wrong 4.5ms. At 0.63ms plus a keyed read it's several hundred per second per customer. Fine for ordinary ERP traffic; the constraint bites on bulk import against one customer, and that wants a different path anyway.

Let me fold all of this into the spec properly.

content.text:
A lock is how you make concurrent writers take turns. Lobu already uses one, and the comment at `entity-management.ts:948` says why:

> "Lock the entity row, merge metadata, and write in ONE transaction: concurrent updates to the same entity serialize on the row lock, fixing the pre-existing non-transactional read-modify-write race on `entities.metadata`."

```sql
SELECT … FROM entities WHERE e.id = ${entityId} … FOR UPDATE   -- :958
```

# What `FOR UPDATE` actually does

It marks that row as claimed until your transaction ends. Another transaction that tries to `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` the same row **blocks** until you commit or roll back — then it proceeds and reads your committed result.

Two things it does *not* do: it doesn't block plain `SELECT` readers (that's MVCC — they see the old version and carry on), and it doesn't lock anything but that row.

# Why the existing lock isn't enough

It locks the row being **written**. That fixes concurrent edits to the same invoice. It does nothing for an invariant that spans rows — because two different invoices never contend.

Credit limit 10,000, customer currently at 6,000 open AR, two invoices of 3,000 arrive at once:

```
T1: SELECT customer            → open_ar = 6000
T2: SELECT customer            → open_ar = 6000     ← both read the same stale value
T1: 6000 + 3000 = 9000  ≤ 10000 → pass → commit, open_ar = 9000
T2: 6000 + 3000 = 9000  ≤ 10000 → pass → commit, open_ar = 12000   ✗ violated
```

Neither transaction did anything wrong. Each check was correct against what it saw. The invariant broke in the *interleaving* — that's write-skew, and no amount of reading fixes it. This is exactly why I said earlier that allowing `read` doesn't solve credit limits.

# What `locks` adds

Declare the rows the rule depends on, and the platform locks them **before** running it:

```
T1: SELECT customer FOR UPDATE → 6000, lock held
T2: SELECT customer FOR UPDATE → ░░ blocks ░░
T1: 9000 ≤ 10000 → pass → update open_ar = 9000 → COMMIT   (lock released)
T2: ▶ unblocks, reads 9000 → 9000 + 3000 = 12000 > 10000 → DENY   ✓
```

The mechanism is that T2 **waits**, and when it wakes it reads the committed result of T1 rather than the stale value. That's the whole trick: serialize the readers of the shared row so their checks compose.

# The hazard, and the fix

Two rules touching two customers in opposite orders:

```
T1: locks A ──wants──▶ B
T2: locks B ──wants──▶ A          → deadlock; Postgres kills one
```

Which is why the declaration is `locks: ({ patch }) => [...]` — derived from the patch *before* the rule body runs, so the platform knows the full set up front and can **sort by `(type, id)`** before acquiring. Everyone takes A then B, so T2 simply waits instead of deadlocking. Discovering locks mid-execution can't do that.

The lock is held from acquisition until COMMIT — so it covers lock acquisition, rule execution, and the write. Everything else declaring that same key queues behind it. That's the serialization I measured: at 0.63ms plus a keyed read, several hundred writes/sec per customer. Ample normally; it's the binding constraint on bulk-importing thousands of invoices against one customer.

# Convex Concurrency Control

Convex employs **optimistic concurrency control (OCC)** rather than pessimistic locking. Here's how it works:

## Core Mechanism

The system treats transactions as "declarative proposals" based on read and write sets. "At the end of the transaction, the writes all commit if every version in the read set is still the latest version of that record."

## No Locks

Convex doesn't use locks. Instead, it "assumes the transaction will succeed and doesn't worry about locking anything ahead of time."

## Conflict Detection

The database tracks which records were read and their versions. If another concurrent transaction modifies a record in your read set before your writes commit, a conflict is detected—similar to a Git push failure when not at HEAD.

## Automatic Retry

Here's the key advantage: "We know the transaction is deterministic...we can simply re-run the transaction; you never need to worry about temporary data races."

Since mutations are deterministic (no external side effects), Convex automatically retries conflicted transactions without developer intervention. "This rebase operation will always eventually succeed without developer intervention."

## Isolation Level

Convex provides true **serializability**, not just snapshot isolation. This guarantees correct results regardless of concurrent transaction combinations.

The practical benefit: "you can simply write your mutation functions as if they will always succeed, and always be guaranteed to be atomic."

I found relevant information about Salesforce record locking and Apex triggers. Here's what the search results reveal:

## Key Findings:

**FOR UPDATE Record Locking:**
Use FOR UPDATE when your logic must read a value and then write a value based on it, especially for money or counters. This approach prevents the concurrency issues that can occur when multiple processes access the same record simultaneously.

**Concurrency Problem Context:**
In order to avoid such scenarios, the execution context must be able to obtain exclusive access to the record – in other words, lock the record while reading it. The issue arises when read and write operations aren't atomic, allowing data corruption in multi-user environments.

**Trigger Design Best Practices:**
Use before triggers to prepare and validate your records before save, and after triggers for cross-object work that depends on record IDs. Keep updates bulkified, minimal, and grouped by parent to reduce lock contention.

**How Salesforce Handles Locks:**
When a transaction modifies a record, it takes a lock and holds it until the transaction ends. Another transaction that tries to update the same record waits for about 10 seconds. If the lock is not released in time, Salesforce throws UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW.

The FOR UPDATE clause in SOQL queries is particularly useful for scenarios like validating aggregate credit limits, as it ensures you're reading the most current value and holding the lock while making decisions based on that value.

I've found several relevant results about Odoo concurrency and serialization errors. Here's what the search revealed:

## Retry Mechanism

Odoo framework will detect transaction conflicts in most cases and silently retry the failed transaction. You will notice this in the logs with messages such as: "SERIALIZATION_FAILURE, retry 1/5 in 0.324 sec"

## Concurrency Issues with Invoices

When validating more than one invoice at the same time, Odoo can throw a "could not serialize access due to concurrent update" error. Odoo version 14 and above raises new concurrency issues since it locks the last journal entry to get the new number, causing problems when creating 2 or more invoices/bills at the same time or creating draft invoices/payments.

## Strategies to Mitigate

One approach involves using a savepoint context with a SELECT FOR UPDATE query to acquire row-level locks, preventing other transactions from modifying the same records.

In a real-world case, a company syncing 3,200 orders per day was hitting serialization errors on 340+ orders daily (10.6% failure rate), but after switching to Job Queue, the failure rate dropped to 0.3%.

The search results indicate this is a well-documented issue in Odoo, particularly affecting concurrent operations on invoices and accounting documents.

content.content:
# SERIALIZABLE Isolation and SSI in PostgreSQL

## Does it detect write-skew?

Yes, SERIALIZABLE detects write-skew (serialization anomalies). The documentation provides this example:

> "This monitoring does not introduce any blocking beyond that present in repeatable read, but there is some overhead to the monitoring, and detection of the conditions which could cause a _serialization anomaly_ will trigger a _serialization failure_."

The documentation illustrates write-skew with a concrete example where two concurrent transactions each read a sum from different classes and insert results into different classes. Without Serializable isolation, both would commit, but Serializable detects this is inconsistent with any serial order and rolls back one transaction.

## Requirement to Retry on Serialization Failure

The documentation explicitly requires application retry logic:

> "applications using this level must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures."

> "When relying on Serializable transactions to prevent anomalies, it is important that any data read from a permanent user table not be considered valid until the transaction which read it has successfully committed."

> "It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies."

## Performance vs. SELECT FOR UPDATE / Explicit Locking

The documentation recommends Serializable over explicit locking in many cases:

> "balanced against the cost and blocking involved in use of explicit locks and `SELECT FOR UPDATE` or `SELECT FOR SHARE`, Serializable transactions are the best performance choice for some environments."

However, it acknowledges overhead:

> "The monitoring of read/write dependencies has a cost, as does the restart of transactions which are terminated with a serialization failure"

Key optimization advice:

> "Eliminate explicit locks, `SELECT FOR UPDATE`, and `SELECT FOR SHARE` where no longer needed due to the protections automatically provided by Serializable transactions."

The tradeoff: Serializable avoids blocking but requires retry logic; explicit locking blocks but commits deterministically.

## Implementation: Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

> "The Serializable isolation level is implemented using a technique known in academic database literature as Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which builds on Snapshot Isolation by adding checks for serialization anomalies."

> "To guarantee true serializability PostgreSQL uses _predicate locking_, which means that it keeps locks which allow it to determine when a write would have had an impact on the result of a previous read from a concurrent transaction, had it run first. In PostgreSQL these locks do not cause any blocking and therefore can _not_ play any part in causing a deadlock."

content.text:
Four systems, and they split into two camps — with one finding that changes my recommendation.

# What they do

| system | approach | on conflict |
|---|---|---|
| **Convex** | OCC, **no locks** | auto-retry, invisible to the developer |
| **Postgres SSI** | predicate locks that **don't block** | `40001`, app must retry |
| **Odoo** | SERIALIZABLE + auto-retry | `SERIALIZATION_FAILURE, retry 1/5 in 0.324 sec` |
| **Salesforce** | pessimistic `FOR UPDATE` | blocks ~10s, then `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW` |

Only Salesforce does what I proposed. Three of four are optimistic.

# The finding that matters

Convex's OCC works **because mutations are deterministic**:

> "We know the transaction is deterministic… we can simply re-run the transaction; you never need to worry about temporary data races."

**Our rules are already deterministic and pure** — no side effects, no clock, no network. That was a decision made for other reasons, and it happens to unlock the retry option that isn't available to general application code.

And Postgres gives it directly. From the docs:

> "PostgreSQL uses *predicate locking*… these locks do not cause any blocking and therefore can *not* play any part in causing a deadlock."

> "balanced against the cost and blocking involved in use of explicit locks and `SELECT FOR UPDATE`… Serializable transactions are the best performance choice for some environments."

> "Eliminate explicit locks, `SELECT FOR UPDATE`… where no longer needed due to the protections automatically provided by Serializable transactions."

That's the Postgres documentation recommending against exactly what I proposed. It detects write-skew — the credit-limit interleaving — without holding anything during rule execution. Which also dissolves my main architectural worry: **no lock held while the isolate runs.**

# But Odoo is the cautionary half

Odoo runs SERIALIZABLE with automatic retry and it hurts in production. One reported sync of 3,200 orders/day hit 340+ serialization errors daily — ~10.6% — dropping to 0.3% only after moving to a job queue.

The cause is instructive though: **Odoo 14+ locks the last journal entry to allocate the invoice number**, so concurrent invoice creation collides. That's *allocation*, not validation — the row in my taxonomy I'd already said isn't a rule problem. Their horror story is evidence for keeping allocation out of the write transaction, not against OCC.

# Revised recommendation

`locks` shouldn't be the default. Match the mechanism to the contention profile:

| case | mechanism |
|---|---|
| no cross-row reads (the vast majority) | READ COMMITTED + the existing row lock — **unchanged** |
| cross-row invariant | **SERIALIZABLE for that transaction + retry** — rules are pure, so retry is safe, and nothing blocks during the isolate |
| known-hot parent (bulk import) | declared `locks` as an **opt-in** escape from retry storms |
| allocation (numbering) | out of the write transaction entirely — this is Odoo's lesson |

Postgres sets isolation per transaction, so SSI overhead is paid only where a rule declares cross-row reads. `locks` survives as the pessimistic opt-in rather than the primary mechanism.

**One honest wrinkle:** the write transaction isn't *literally* replayable in Convex's sense — `computeFieldMerge` takes `nowIso: new Date().toISOString()`, so a retry produces a slightly different timestamp. Harmless, but it means "deterministic" holds for the rule, not the whole transaction. Retry handling would need to live in `withEntityWriteTransaction`, and the app would need to tolerate `40001` on those paths.

Sources: [Convex OCC](https://docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/occ) · [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) · [Odoo concurrent invoice creation](https://github.com/odoo/odoo/issues/90465) · [Odoo serialization retries](https://www.braincuber.com/tutorial/multi-threading-odoo-handling-concurrent-requests-safely) · [Salesforce record locking](https://www.salesforceben.com/salesforce-record-locking-tips-for-developers-how-to-avoid-concurrency-issues/)

---

**Confidence: high (93)** on Postgres SSI and Convex — both from primary documentation, quoted directly. **Medium (65)** on Odoo: the GitHub issues are primary but the 10.6%→0.3% figure is from a tutorial blog, not a case study I can verify. **Medium (60)** on Salesforce — Salesforce Ben is secondary; I didn't reach the official Apex docs. **Medium (55)** on the revised recommendation: the reasoning is sound and doc-supported, but retry-under-load is exactly the thing that looks fine in design and bites in production, per Odoo.

**Next actions:**
- This is worth measuring rather than choosing on doctrine — SSI-plus-retry versus `FOR UPDATE` on the same contended-row benchmark I already have. Same harness, and it settles it with numbers instead of three vendors' opinions.
- The spec needs revising; I'd rather do that after the measurement than encode a recommendation I might reverse.
- Phase 1 and case 3 remain unblocked by all of this.

content.text:
No — and it's inverted relative to what you'd want.

| what happened | audited? |
|---|---|
| successful **update** | ✅ field-level diff — `recordChangeEvent`, `manage_entity.ts:585` |
| successful **create** | ❌ nothing |
| delete / merge / link / unlink / update_link | ❌ nothing |
| **denied write** | ❌ nothing, and structurally so |
| the audit write itself fails | ❌ dropped — `"change audit event DROPPED after retry — audit trail is missing this row"` |

`recordChangeEvent` is `void`, not awaited, with a `.catch` at `insert-event.ts:775` that logs and drops. And `handleCreate` (`:271`), `handleMerge` (`:675`), `handleDelete` (`:1365`), `handleUpdateLink` (`:1737`) don't call it at all — only `handleUpdate` does.

# Why denials are invisible, structurally

A deny throws → the transaction rolls back → anything written inside it disappears. And the audit is post-commit anyway, so it never runs. Same shape as the case-3 approval card vanishing.

So today you get a diff when nothing went wrong, and nothing when it did. **Adding rules makes this materially worse**: every `deny` becomes a silent failure. Someone's import stops, they ask why, and there is no record of which rule rejected what — while case 3 proves a denial can be *wrong* and misattributed ("frozen" when the real cause was an approval hold).

# What I'd do for creates and updates

**1. Audit the denial — a prerequisite for rules, not a follow-up.** After the rollback, write an audit event on a fresh connection: rule, reason, actor, entity, attempted patch. This is the one place `getDb()` outside the write transaction is correct, because the transaction has already ended — no #2818 risk.

**2. Audit creates.** With Phase 1 validating creates, a created row leaving no trace is a hole that only widens.

**3. Make the denial audit durable.** Fire-and-forget with an explicit DROP log is acceptable for a convenience diff. It isn't acceptable as the record of *why a write was refused* — that's the thing someone reads during an incident.

**4. Concurrency** — as the research landed: READ COMMITTED plus the existing row lock by default; SERIALIZABLE plus retry only when a rule declares cross-row reads; declared `locks` as the opt-in escape for known-hot parents; allocation stays out of the write transaction.

# One thing that already works in our favour

Retry and audit compose cleanly. `insertConnectionlessAuditEvent` already enforces idempotency via `metadata._lobu_idempotency_key` plus a unique index, and handles the unique violation at `:713-725`. So an SSI retry re-running the transaction won't duplicate audit rows. That's one integration problem that's already solved.

---

**Confidence: high (94)** on the audit coverage gaps — the `recordChangeEvent` call sites and the DROP log are read from source this session, and the four unaudited handlers are confirmed by their line numbers. **High (90)** that denials are structurally invisible; it follows from rollback plus post-commit placement. **Medium (60)** on my ordering — auditing denials before shipping rules is my judgment call, though case 3 makes it hard to argue the other way.

**Next actions:**
- Denial auditing should join Phase 2's prerequisites alongside the case-3 fix. Both are about a rule failing in a way nobody can see.
- Auditing creates is arguably Phase 1 scope, since that's when creates start being validated.
- The SSI-vs-`FOR UPDATE` measurement is still the open concurrency question, and still cheap on the harness I have.
- Phase 1 and case 3 remain waiting on your go.

content.text:
You already have that guarantee, for free — it falls out of where the seam sits.

The lock is taken at `entity-management.ts:958` (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`), and the rule runs at `:1101`, before the UPDATE and COMMIT. So a second writer to the same row **blocks at `:958`** and its isolate never starts until the first commits. Two isolates can't run against one row concurrently. No mutex needed; it's already true by construction.

# What that fully covers

Everything same-row — which is the overwhelming majority of what people actually write:

| invariant | covered by the existing lock? |
|---|---|
| posted invoice frozen | ✅ |
| legal state transitions | ✅ |
| lines sum to header | ✅ |
| required-when-status | ✅ |
| currency immutable once set | ✅ |
| deactivate blocked by `open_invoice_count` | ✅ |
| only the controller may post | ✅ |

For all of these, **no SERIALIZABLE, no declared locks, nothing new.** The read-modify-write is already serialized by the row lock the code has held since before any of this work.

# What it doesn't cover

Cross-row, and the reason is that the two writers aren't contending on the same row at all:

```
invoice#1 → locks invoice#1, reads customer.open_ar = 6000 → passes
invoice#2 → locks invoice#2, reads customer.open_ar = 6000 → passes
                    ↑ different rows, so neither ever blocks the other
```

Per-row serialization is exactly the wrong key here — the shared thing is the *customer*, and nothing locks it. That's the whole reason declared `locks` or SERIALIZABLE exists in the proposal.

# So the shape is

**Default: nothing new.** Same-row invariants are correct today on the lock that already exists.

**Opt-in, only for cross-row aggregates:** SERIALIZABLE+retry or declared `locks`. And that slice is narrower than it first looked, because uniqueness goes to a unique index and numbering goes to a sequence — neither is a rule.

That's a better framing than the one in the spec, which reads as though concurrency machinery is part of the design rather than an escape hatch for a small minority of rules. I'd rather the default path carry zero new concurrency concepts.

# One thing it isn't

Per-row serialization does **not** bound global isolate concurrency. A hundred writes to a hundred different rows means a hundred concurrent isolates, and that's the case that zeroed the event loop at ≥8. The starvation cap is keyed on the *process*, not the row — two different mechanisms solving two different problems, and it'd be easy to think the first covers the second.

---

**Confidence: high (93)** that per-row isolate serialization already holds — it follows from the lock at `:958` preceding the rule position at `:1101`, both read from source. **High (90)** on the same-row coverage list. **Medium (70)** on "the default needs nothing new" — it depends on cross-row invariants really being the minority for your users, which is a product judgment I'm inferring from the ERP cases we've walked.

**Next actions:**
- I'd restructure the spec's concurrency section around this: default is the existing lock, machinery is an opt-in escape hatch. Currently it reads too centrally.
- That also demotes the SSI-vs-`FOR UPDATE` measurement from blocking to worth-knowing, since it only affects the opt-in path.
- Phase 1, case 3, and now denial auditing are the three things actually gating progress.

name: reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial
description: "REPRODUCED — an approval hold on the state field strips the transition, making a legal write illegal; the write AND the approval card are both lost"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: d4dd595f-7813-471b-8289-6923b28b89fa
  modified: 2026-08-17T17:30:00.000Z
---

Reproduced 2026-08-17 with a passing CONTROL that isolates the cause. Test:
`packages/server/src/__tests__/integration/authz/spike-approval-hold-vs-invariant.test.ts`
(uncommitted, worth promoting to a regression test).

## The sequence

1. invoice in `draft`; spec is `issued: { to:["posted"], frozen:true,
   writableOnExit:{ posted:["einvoice_uuid"] } }`
2. a HUMAN moves `draft → issued` — legal, and claims ownership of `status`
3. an AGENT writes `{ status:"posted", einvoice_uuid:"…" }` — the legal exit plus
   the one field `writableOnExit` permits
4. the gate holds `status` (human-owned), `computeFieldMerge` STRIPS it
5. effective patch = `{ einvoice_uuid }` with NO transition → frozen state,
   non-exempt field → **DENY**

**CONTROL passes:** the identical agent write SUCCEEDS when no human owns
`status`. So the cause is the ownership hold, not the rule.

## Why it is worse than a failed write

- The error says `frozen in state "issued": cannot write einvoice_uuid`. That is
  NOT the real cause (an approval hold on a different field). Misdiagnosed.
- **The approval card is never created.** `entity-management.ts:1134` returns from
  inside the tx; the deferral is built at `:1142`–`:1147` AFTER it. The throw
  skips it. So the agent's work is denied AND dropped with no pending record.

## The general principle

Partial field commits and cross-field invariants are **logically incompatible** —
committing a subset of a consistent set can produce an inconsistent state. Any
system with both must pick. Today Lobu picks silently-lose-the-write.

**Recommended fix:** when a type has a `check`, an approval hold becomes
ALL-OR-NOTHING — defer the whole write rather than partially commit. The
alternative (pass `pending: string[]` into ctx so rules can skip held fields)
pushes platform mechanics into every multi-field rule.

**This is introduced by the validation branch, not pre-existing** — with no rules
there is nothing to deny. So it must be fixed BEFORE rules ship, not after.

Related: [[reference_entity_write_validation_seam_state]],
[[reference_entity_audit_trail_is_inverted]]

---
name: reference_entity_approval_routing_and_authority
description: "TRACED — approval authority is admin/owner ∪ field owner; the delivery layer already takes an arbitrary user list, so a declared approver is a small change"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: d4dd595f-7813-471b-8289-6923b28b89fa
  modified: 2026-08-17T17:31:00.000Z
---

Traced end to end 2026-08-17.

## Who may DECIDE

`admin/owner role` **∪** `the field's human owner`.

- `approvals.ts:790` `if (isAdminOrOwnerRole(ctx.memberRole)) return;`
- `approvals.ts:721-723` + `:740` — a member may decide a run ONLY when it records
  them as the field owner: `action_input->>'owner_user_id' = ${userId}`
- `owner_user_id` is derived at propose time **from `field_controls`**

## Who is NOTIFIED

- `notifyActionApprovalNeeded` (`notifications/triggers.ts:496`) calls
  **`notifyOrgAdmins`** → `getOrgAdminUserIds` (`role IN ('admin','owner')`)
- `ownerUserId` is a routing tier: *"routes the Slack card to their DM before the
  channel tier"*
- `connectionId`/`channelId`/`teamId` = the policy row's delivery target
- an in-app `approvalUrl` is always minted

## THE GAP

`owner_user_id` is **null for any field no human has ever touched** — which is the
normal case for an agent-written field. So a rule escalating `header_net` routes
to org admins and **only admins can decide it**. A controller or account exec who
is a member but not an admin cannot approve anything. "Over $50k needs controller
approval" actually means "goes to whoever holds org admin".

## Why the fix is SMALL

The delivery layer is already recipient-agnostic:
- `sendNotification(orgId, userIds[], notification)` (`triggers.ts:468`) takes an
  arbitrary array
- the `notify` tool already exposes `recipients: 'admins' | 'all' | string[]`
  and validates them against `member`
- `notifyOrgAdmins` is a SIX-LINE wrapper the approval path happens to call

Three changes: resolve the approver (policy row → field owner → admins), pass the
list instead of the wrapper, add the branch beside the `owner_user_id` predicate.
**Authority is a privilege grant, so it belongs on the POLICY ROW — never as a
parameter on `escalate()`.**

## Two traps

- **Non-member recipients are silently dropped.** `notify` filters ids against
  `member`; zero matches returns `{ notified_count: 0 }` — success with no
  delivery. A declared approver needs an explicit existence check, or an
  escalation to someone who left vanishes. (Precedent for failing closed:
  `resolveAutomationOwner` INNER JOINs `agents`.)
- **There are THREE routing sources**, not two: the policy row's delivery target,
  `ownerUserId`, and `loadConfiguredAutomationDeliveryTarget` (automations carry
  their own channel).

## Delivery target vs decision use DIFFERENT orderings

Decision folds **max-restrictive**; delivery target picks **most-specific**
(`entity_id` 4, `field_path` 2, type 1). Same rows, two sorts. And only a
SINGLE-field escalation can match field-scoped delivery — multi-field falls back
to the type/global row.

Related: [[reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial]]

---
name: reference_entity_write_concurrency_model
description: "Per-row isolate serialization is ALREADY FREE from the lock at :958 — so same-row invariants need zero new machinery; only cross-row aggregates do"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: d4dd595f-7813-471b-8289-6923b28b89fa
  modified: 2026-08-17T17:32:00.000Z
---

## The default path needs NOTHING new

`updateEntity` takes `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` at `entity-management.ts:958`, and the
rule position is `:1101` — *after* the lock, *before* the UPDATE. So a second
writer to the same row **blocks at :958 and its isolate never starts** until the
first commits. **Per-row isolate serialization is already guaranteed by
construction.** No mutex, no advisory lock, no new concept.

That makes every SAME-ROW invariant correct today: freeze, state machines,
cross-field sums, required-when, immutable-once-set, deactivate-blocked-by-count.
Which is the overwhelming majority of real rules.

**Do not present concurrency machinery as part of the design.** It is an opt-in
escape hatch for a narrow minority.

## What per-row serialization does NOT solve

Cross-row aggregates. Two invoices lock two DIFFERENT rows, both read
`customer.open_ar = 6000`, both pass, together they violate. Classic write-skew —
the shared row is the customer and nothing locks it.

It also does **not** bound GLOBAL isolate concurrency: 100 writes to 100 rows =
100 concurrent isolates, and ≥8 zeroes the event loop
([[reference_isolate_per_write_costs_4_5ms]]). Starvation is keyed on the PROCESS,
not the row — two different mechanisms, easy to conflate.

## Four shapes, four answers — two leave the rule system

| shape | example | answer |
|---|---|---|
| uniqueness | PO number per customer | Postgres unique index — not a rule |
| allocation | invoice numbers, no gaps | sequence / counter row — not a rule |
| aggregate threshold | credit limit | materialized total + SSI-retry or declared `locks` |
| advisory / soft | flag trending-over | automation, post-hoc |

## What other systems do (verified from primary docs, 2026-08-17)

- **Convex** — OCC, **no locks**, automatic retry. Works *because* mutations are
  deterministic: *"we can simply re-run the transaction"*. True serializability.
- **Postgres SSI** — detects write-skew; *"predicate locking … these locks do not
  cause any blocking and therefore can not play any part in causing a deadlock"*.
  Docs explicitly say *"Eliminate explicit locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE … where no
  longer needed"* and that Serializable is *"the best performance choice for some
  environments"*. Requires app retry on SQLSTATE `40001`.
- **Odoo** — SERIALIZABLE + auto-retry, and it HURTS: Odoo 14+ locks the last
  journal entry to allocate the invoice number, so concurrent invoice creation
  collides. That is ALLOCATION, not validation — evidence for keeping allocation
  out of the write transaction, not against OCC.
- **Salesforce** — pessimistic `FOR UPDATE`, ~10s wait, then `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW`.

Our rules are pure and deterministic by design, so the Convex retry option is
available to us in a way it is not for general app code. **Caveat:** the whole tx
is not literally replayable — `computeFieldMerge` takes
`nowIso: new Date().toISOString()`.

If declared `locks` is ever built, sort keys by `(type, id)` before acquiring or
two rules touching customers A and B in opposite orders deadlock (ABBA).

Sources: docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/occ ·
postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html · github.com/odoo/odoo/issues/90465

## The default path needs NOTHING new

`updateEntity` takes `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` at `entity-management.ts:958`, and the
rule position is `:1101` — *after* the lock, *before* the UPDATE. So a second
writer to the same row **blocks at :958 and its isolate never starts** until the
first commits. **Per-row isolate serialization is already guaranteed by
construction.** No mutex, no advisory lock, no new concept.

That makes every SAME-ROW invariant correct today: freeze, state machines,
cross-field sums, required-when, immutable-once-set, deactivate-blocked-by-count.
Which is the overwhelming majority of real rules.

**Do not present concurrency machinery as part of the design.** It is an opt-in
escape hatch for a narrow minority.

## What per-row serialization does NOT solve

Cross-row aggregates. Two invoices lock two DIFFERENT rows, both read
`customer.open_ar = 6000`, both pass, together they violate. Classic write-skew —
the shared row is the customer and nothing locks it.

It also does **not** bound GLOBAL isolate concurrency: 100 writes to 100 rows =
100 concurrent isolates, and ≥8 zeroes the event loop
([[reference_isolate_per_write_costs_4_5ms]]). Starvation is keyed on the PROCESS,
not the row — two different mechanisms, easy to conflate.

## Four shapes, four answers — two leave the rule system

| shape | example | answer |
|---|---|---|
| uniqueness | PO number per customer | Postgres unique index — not a rule |
| allocation | invoice numbers, no gaps | sequence / counter row — not a rule |
| aggregate threshold | credit limit | materialized total + SSI-retry or declared `locks` |
| advisory / soft | flag trending-over | automation, post-hoc |

## What other systems do (verified from primary docs, 2026-08-17)

- **Convex** — OCC, **no locks**, automatic retry. Works *because* mutations are
  deterministic: *"we can simply re-run the transaction"*. True serializability.
- **Postgres SSI** — detects write-skew; *"predicate locking … these locks do not
  cause any blocking and therefore can not play any part in causing a deadlock"*.
  Docs explicitly say *"Eliminate explicit locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE … where no
  longer needed"* and that Serializable is *"the best performance choice for some
  environments"*. Requires app retry on SQLSTATE `40001`.
- **Odoo** — SERIALIZABLE + auto-retry, and it HURTS: Odoo 14+ locks the last
  journal entry to allocate the invoice number, so concurrent invoice creation
  collides. That is ALLOCATION, not validation — evidence for keeping allocation
  out of the write transaction, not against OCC.
- **Salesforce** — pessimistic `FOR UPDATE`, ~10s wait, then `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW`.

Our rules are pure and deterministic by design, so the Convex retry option is
available to us in a way it is not for general app code. **Caveat:** the whole tx
is not literally replayable — `computeFieldMerge` takes
`nowIso: new Date().toISOString()`.

If declared `locks` is ever built, sort keys by `(type, id)` before acquiring or
two rules touching customers A and B in opposite orders deadlock (ABBA).

Sources: docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/occ ·
postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html · github.com/odoo/odoo/issues/90465
