| what happened | audited? |
|---|---|
| successful UPDATE | yes — field-level diff, `manage_entity.ts:585` |
| successful CREATE | **no** (`handleCreate` :271 never calls it) |
| delete / merge / link / unlink / update_link | **no** (:1365, :675, :1737) |
| **DENIED write** | **no — structurally** |
| the audit write itself failing | **dropped** |

`recordChangeEvent` (`insert-event.ts:756`) returns `void` — not awaited — and its
`.catch` at `:775` logs
`"change audit event DROPPED after retry — audit trail is missing this row"`.

## Denial invisibility is structural

A deny throws → the transaction rolls back → anything written inside it
disappears. And the audit is POST-COMMIT anyway, so it never runs. Same shape as
the lost approval card in
[[reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial]].

**So you get a diff when nothing went wrong, and nothing when it did.** Adding
write rules makes this materially worse: every `deny` becomes a silent failure,
while case 3 proves a denial can be WRONG and misattributed.

## How to apply

- **Auditing denials is a PREREQUISITE for shipping rules, not a follow-up.**
  Write the audit event after the rollback on a fresh connection — this is the one
  place `getDb()` outside the write tx is correct, because the tx has ended, so
  there is no #2818 risk.
- Record: rule, reason, actor, entity, attempted patch.
- Make the denial audit DURABLE. Fire-and-forget with a DROP log is fine for a
  convenience diff; it is not fine for the record of why a write was refused.
- Auditing creates belongs with whichever phase starts validating creates.

## One thing that already composes

`insertConnectionlessAuditEvent` enforces idempotency via
`metadata._lobu_idempotency_key` + a unique index, handling the unique violation
at `:713-725`. So an SSI **retry** re-running the transaction will not duplicate
audit rows — that integration problem is already solved.

---
name: reference_entity_audit_trail_is_inverted
description: "Audit records successful UPDATES only — creates, deletes, merges and every DENIED write leave no trace, and denial invisibility is structural"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: d4dd595f-7813-471b-8289-6923b28b89fa
  modified: 2026-08-17T18:35:58.989Z
---

Verified 2026-08-17. Supersedes the coverage half of
[[reference_entity_change_history_already_exists]].

| what happened | audited? |
|---|---|
| successful UPDATE | yes — field-level diff, `manage_entity.ts:585` |
| successful CREATE | **no** (`handleCreate` :271 never calls it) |
| delete / merge / link / unlink / update_link | **no** (:1365, :675, :1737) |
| **DENIED write** | **no — structurally** |
| the audit write itself failing | **dropped** |

`recordChangeEvent` (`insert-event.ts:756`) returns `void` — not awaited — and its
`.catch` at `:775` logs
`"change audit event DROPPED after retry — audit trail is missing this row"`.

## Denial invisibility is structural

A deny throws → the transaction rolls back → anything written inside it
disappears. And the audit is POST-COMMIT anyway, so it never runs. Same shape as
the lost approval card in
[[reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial]].

**So you get a diff when nothing went wrong, and nothing when it did.** Adding
write rules makes this materially worse: every `deny` becomes a silent failure,
while case 3 proves a denial can be WRONG and misattributed.

## How to apply

- **Auditing denials is a PREREQUISITE for shipping rules, not a follow-up.**
  Write the audit event after the rollback on a fresh connection — this is the one
  place `getDb()` outside the write tx is correct, because the tx has ended, so
  there is no #2818 risk.
- Record: rule, reason, actor, entity, attempted patch.
- Make the denial audit DURABLE. Fire-and-forget with a DROP log is fine for a
  convenience diff; it is not fine for the record of why a write was refused.
- Auditing creates belongs with whichever phase starts validating creates.

## One thing that already composes

`insertConnectionlessAuditEvent` enforces idempotency via
`metadata._lobu_idempotency_key` + a unique index, handling the unique violation
at `:713-725`. So an SSI **retry** re-running the transaction will not duplicate
audit rows — that integration problem is already solved.

---
name: reference_entity_write_concurrency_model
description: "Per-row isolate serialization is ALREADY FREE from the lock at :958 — so same-row invariants need zero new machinery; only cross-row aggregates do"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: d4dd595f-7813-471b-8289-6923b28b89fa
  modified: 2026-08-17T18:35:47.641Z
---

## The default path needs NOTHING new

`updateEntity` takes `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` at `entity-management.ts:958`, and the
rule position is `:1101` — *after* the lock, *before* the UPDATE. So a second
writer to the same row **blocks at :958 and its isolate never starts** until the
first commits. **Per-row isolate serialization is already guaranteed by
construction.** No mutex, no advisory lock, no new concept.

That makes every SAME-ROW invariant correct today: freeze, state machines,
cross-field sums, required-when, immutable-once-set, deactivate-blocked-by-count.
Which is the overwhelming majority of real rules.

**Do not present concurrency machinery as part of the design.** It is an opt-in
escape hatch for a narrow minority.

## What per-row serialization does NOT solve

Cross-row aggregates. Two invoices lock two DIFFERENT rows, both read
`customer.open_ar = 6000`, both pass, together they violate. Classic write-skew —
the shared row is the customer and nothing locks it.

It also does **not** bound GLOBAL isolate concurrency: 100 writes to 100 rows =
100 concurrent isolates, and ≥8 zeroes the event loop
([[reference_isolate_per_write_costs_4_5ms]]). Starvation is keyed on the PROCESS,
not the row — two different mechanisms, easy to conflate.

## Four shapes, four answers — two leave the rule system

| shape | example | answer |
|---|---|---|
| uniqueness | PO number per customer | Postgres unique index — not a rule |
| allocation | invoice numbers, no gaps | sequence / counter row — not a rule |
| aggregate threshold | credit limit | materialized total + SSI-retry or declared `locks` |
| advisory / soft | flag trending-over | automation, post-hoc |

## What other systems do (verified from primary docs, 2026-08-17)

- **Convex** — OCC, **no locks**, automatic retry. Works *because* mutations are
  deterministic: *"we can simply re-run the transaction"*. True serializability.
- **Postgres SSI** — detects write-skew; *"predicate locking … these locks do not
  cause any blocking and therefore can not play any part in causing a deadlock"*.
  Docs explicitly say *"Eliminate explicit locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE … where no
  longer needed"* and that Serializable is *"the best performance choice for some
  environments"*. Requires app retry on SQLSTATE `40001`.
- **Odoo** — SERIALIZABLE + auto-retry, and it HURTS: Odoo 14+ locks the last
  journal entry to allocate the invoice number, so concurrent invoice creation
  collides. That is ALLOCATION, not validation — evidence for keeping allocation
  out of the write transaction, not against OCC.
- **Salesforce** — pessimistic `FOR UPDATE`, ~10s wait, then `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW`.

Our rules are pure and deterministic by design, so the Convex retry option is
available to us in a way it is not for general app code. **Caveat:** the whole tx
is not literally replayable — `computeFieldMerge` takes
`nowIso: new Date().toISOString()`.

If declared `locks` is ever built, sort keys by `(type, id)` before acquiring or
two rules touching customers A and B in opposite orders deadlock (ABBA).

Sources: docs.convex.dev/database/advanced/occ ·
postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html · github.com/odoo/odoo/issues/90465

---
name: reference_entity_approval_routing_and_authority
description: "TRACED — approval authority is admin/owner ∪ field owner; the delivery layer already takes an arbitrary user list, so a declared approver is a small change"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: d4dd595f-7813-471b-8289-6923b28b89fa
  modified: 2026-08-17T18:35:26.279Z
---

Traced end to end 2026-08-17.

## Who may DECIDE

`admin/owner role` **∪** `the field's human owner`.

- `approvals.ts:790` `if (isAdminOrOwnerRole(ctx.memberRole)) return;`
- `approvals.ts:721-723` + `:740` — a member may decide a run ONLY when it records
  them as the field owner: `action_input->>'owner_user_id' = ${userId}`
- `owner_user_id` is derived at propose time **from `field_controls`**

## Who is NOTIFIED

- `notifyActionApprovalNeeded` (`notifications/triggers.ts:496`) calls
  **`notifyOrgAdmins`** → `getOrgAdminUserIds` (`role IN ('admin','owner')`)
- `ownerUserId` is a routing tier: *"routes the Slack card to their DM before the
  channel tier"*
- `connectionId`/`channelId`/`teamId` = the policy row's delivery target
- an in-app `approvalUrl` is always minted

## THE GAP

`owner_user_id` is **null for any field no human has ever touched** — which is the
normal case for an agent-written field. So a rule escalating `header_net` routes
to org admins and **only admins can decide it**. A controller or account exec who
is a member but not an admin cannot approve anything. "Over $50k needs controller
approval" actually means "goes to whoever holds org admin".

## Why the fix is SMALL

The delivery layer is already recipient-agnostic:
- `sendNotification(orgId, userIds[], notification)` (`triggers.ts:468`) takes an
  arbitrary array
- the `notify` tool already exposes `recipients: 'admins' | 'all' | string[]`
  and validates them against `member`
- `notifyOrgAdmins` is a SIX-LINE wrapper the approval path happens to call

Three changes: resolve the approver (policy row → field owner → admins), pass the
list instead of the wrapper, add the branch beside the `owner_user_id` predicate.
**Authority is a privilege grant, so it belongs on the POLICY ROW — never as a
parameter on `escalate()`.**

## Two traps

- **Non-member recipients are silently dropped.** `notify` filters ids against
  `member`; zero matches returns `{ notified_count: 0 }` — success with no
  delivery. A declared approver needs an explicit existence check, or an
  escalation to someone who left vanishes. (Precedent for failing closed:
  `resolveAutomationOwner` INNER JOINs `agents`.)
- **There are THREE routing sources**, not two: the policy row's delivery target,
  `ownerUserId`, and `loadConfiguredAutomationDeliveryTarget` (automations carry
  their own channel).

## Delivery target vs decision use DIFFERENT orderings

Decision folds **max-restrictive**; delivery target picks **most-specific**
(`entity_id` 4, `field_path` 2, type 1). Same rows, two sorts. And only a
SINGLE-field escalation can match field-scoped delivery — multi-field falls back
to the type/global row.

Related: [[reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial]]

---
name: reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial
description: "REPRODUCED — an approval hold on the state field strips the transition, making a legal write illegal; the write AND the approval card are both lost"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: d4dd595f-7813-471b-8289-6923b28b89fa
  modified: 2026-08-17T18:35:11.740Z
---

Reproduced 2026-08-17 with a passing CONTROL that isolates the cause. Test:
`packages/server/src/__tests__/integration/authz/spike-approval-hold-vs-invariant.test.ts`
(uncommitted, worth promoting to a regression test).

## The sequence

1. invoice in `draft`; spec is `issued: { to:["posted"], frozen:true,
   writableOnExit:{ posted:["einvoice_uuid"] } }`
2. a HUMAN moves `draft → issued` — legal, and claims ownership of `status`
3. an AGENT writes `{ status:"posted", einvoice_uuid:"…" }` — the legal exit plus
   the one field `writableOnExit` permits
4. the gate holds `status` (human-owned), `computeFieldMerge` STRIPS it
5. effective patch = `{ einvoice_uuid }` with NO transition → frozen state,
   non-exempt field → **DENY**

**CONTROL passes:** the identical agent write SUCCEEDS when no human owns
`status`. So the cause is the ownership hold, not the rule.

## Why it is worse than a failed write

- The error says `frozen in state "issued": cannot write einvoice_uuid`. That is
  NOT the real cause (an approval hold on a different field). Misdiagnosed.
- **The approval card is never created.** `entity-management.ts:1134` returns from
  inside the tx; the deferral is built at `:1142`–`:1147` AFTER it. The throw
  skips it. So the agent's work is denied AND dropped with no pending record.

## The general principle

Partial field commits and cross-field invariants are **logically incompatible** —
committing a subset of a consistent set can produce an inconsistent state. Any
system with both must pick. Today Lobu picks silently-lose-the-write.

**Recommended fix:** when a type has a `check`, an approval hold becomes
ALL-OR-NOTHING — defer the whole write rather than partially commit. The
alternative (pass `pending: string[]` into ctx so rules can skip held fields)
pushes platform mechanics into every multi-field rule.

**This is introduced by the validation branch, not pre-existing** — with no rules
there is nothing to deny. So it must be fixed BEFORE rules ship, not after.

Related: [[reference_entity_write_validation_seam_state]],
[[reference_entity_audit_trail_is_inverted]]

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. # Tools

exec – run any PostHog command; its `command` description has the syntax.

Prioritize skills over tools.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_app_state({ include_schema: true, include_canvas_design: true, include_scripts_and_shaders: false }) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. All three flags are required. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

Tools: get_app_state, get_guidelines, execute, get_screenshot, export_nodes, export_html.
Also: browser.

input.content:
Lobu · Technical specification · Final

Write-time entity policy

One place where a write to an entity is judged: a per-type code rule that runs inside the write transaction, after the row lock, before the UPDATE. It can deny, or escalate to a human. It can never grant.

Status spec settled, not built Seam entity-management.ts:1101 Blockers 2, both must land first Dated 2026-08-17

§1 The split, and why it isn't a style choice

Policy in Lobu lives in two tiers, and the boundary between them is forced by where the question gets asked.

TierFormAnswersRuns
Queryable declarative policy rows “may this actor touch this at all?” pre-flight, and on read paths
Enforceable per-type code rule “was this specific attempt legal?” inside the write transaction

Three read paths already gate on action: 'read'. No hook at the write seam can answer a read — there is no write to hook. So the declarative tier stays, and the two tiers are not redundant: they answer different questions at different times. What the code tier removes is the need to express write policy declaratively, which is where the permissions UI was getting expensive.

Load-bearing constraint

The rule is deny-only. Its verbs are deny() and escalate(); there is no allow(). A rule can narrow what the declarative lattice permits, never widen it. That single property is what makes it safe to hand the rule the full actor identity — a rule that cannot grant cannot be tricked into granting.

§2 Surface

One file per entity type, checked into the ontology repo, applied by lobu apply. The access block is data and compiles to policy rows at deploy time. check is a function and compiles to a script that runs at write time. Same file, two compilation targets — the Terraform/CDK shape. 

// ontology/invoice.rules.ts
import { defineEntityRules } from "@lobu/sdk";

export default defineEntityRules({
  type: "invoice",

  // ── data → policy rows at apply time ──────────────────
  access: {
    read:  ["role:member", "agent:billing-clerk", "automation:*"],
    write: ["role:admin", "agent:billing-clerk"],
  },
  approvers: {
    // who may decide an escalation, by field
    header_net: "user:controller@acme.com",
    "*":        "role:admin",
  },

  // ── function → compiled script at the write seam ──────
  async check(ctx) {
    const { committed, next, changed, actor, op } = ctx;

    // state machine
    if (committed.status === "posted" && changed("header_net"))
      ctx.deny("a posted invoice is immutable");

    // legal exits only
    const exits = { draft: ["issued"], issued: ["posted", "void"] };
    if (changed("status") && !exits[committed.status]?.includes(next.status))
      ctx.deny(`cannot go ${committed.status} → ${next.status}`);

    // cross-field invariant
    if (next.status === "posted" && !next.einvoice_uuid)
      ctx.deny("posting requires an e-invoice UUID");

    // threshold → a human decides
    if (changed("header_net") && next.header_net > 50_000)
      ctx.escalate(["header_net"], "over the 50k approval limit");

    // scoped by who is asking — narrowing only
    if (actor.kind === "agent" && changed("customer_id"))
      ctx.deny("reassigning an invoice is a human decision");
  },
});

Everything an ERP needs for one type, in one screen, in the language the team already writes.

The ctx object

FieldTypeMeaning
committedrowthe row as it exists, read under the lock
patchpartial rowthe effective patch, after field-merge
nextrowcommitted merged with patch
changed(f)fn → boolis field f in the effective patch
actor{kind,id,roles}kind ∈ user | agent | automation
openumcreate | update | delete
get(type,id)asynca budgeted read on the write connection — §4
deny(reason)throwsrolls back; the reason reaches the caller
escalate(fields, reason)marksholds those fields, opens an approval — §3

Reserved keys follow the existing validator convention — $name, $slug, $parent_id, $content, $deleted — so the rule sees exactly the shape entity-row-validation.ts already builds.

Deletes

There is no interesting rule about deleting a customer, because in an ERP you don’t. You deactivate — which is a status change on the same row, and is already covered by the state machine above. op: "delete" exists for completeness; it is not the motivating case.

§3 Escalation: who actually gets it

escalate() holds the named fields, commits the rest, and opens a pending approval. The question that matters is who can decide it. Traced end to end, today’s answer is:

admin or owner role  ∪  the field’s human owner, where the owner comes from field_controls at propose time and is written to action_input.owner_user_id.

The gap

owner_user_id is null for any field no human has ever touched — the normal case for a field an agent maintains. So “over 50k needs controller approval” silently means “goes to whoever holds org admin”. A controller or account executive who is a member but not an admin cannot decide anything.

The fix is small because the delivery layer is already recipient-agnostic: sendNotification(orgId, userIds[], …) takes an arbitrary array, and the notify tool already exposes recipients: 'admins' | 'all' | string[]. notifyOrgAdmins is a six-line wrapper that the approval path happens to call. Three changes: resolve an approver (policy row → field owner → admins), pass the list instead of the wrapper, and add the branch beside the owner_user_id predicate that authorizes the decision.

Design call

The approver is declared in approvers — on the policy row, not as an argument to escalate(). Naming an approver is granting a privilege, and the code tier is deny-only. Keeping it in the data tier preserves that invariant and keeps the grant queryable.

Two traps to carry into implementation. Non-member recipients are silently dropped — notify filters ids against member and returns { notified_count: 0 } as a success, so an escalation aimed at someone who left the org evaporates; the declared approver needs an explicit existence check that fails closed. And routing has three sources, not two: the policy row’s delivery target, ownerUserId, and an automation’s own configured channel.

Note also that the decision fold and the delivery target read the same policy rows with different sorts: the decision folds max-restrictive, the delivery target picks most-specific (entity_id 4, field_path 2, type 1). And only a single-field escalation can match a field-scoped delivery row — multi-field falls back to the type-level row.

§4 Reads inside a rule

Banning reads outright would be simpler, and wrong. “Deactivate a customer only if it has no open invoices” is an ordinary ERP rule and it needs one query. Every ontology system that forbids cross-row reads in the cheap tier ships a second tier that allows them.

Reads are allowed, on the write transaction’s own connection, through ctx.get / ctx.query, with a hard budget. The measured cost supports this: a host-function bridge into the isolate costs ~0.079 ms for the first call and ~0.013 ms marginal after — the bridge is not the expense, the query is.

Non-negotiable

The read uses the transaction handle, never getDb(). Calling getDb() inside withEntityWriteTransaction is the exact shape of the #2818 production deadlock: DB_POOL_MAX sessions sitting idle in transaction on the same query. That incident forbids acquiring a second connection, not reading.

§5 Concurrency: the default path needs nothing new

This is the part that looked hard and isn’t. updateEntity takes SELECT … FOR UPDATE at entity-management.ts:958, and the rule position is :1101 — after the lock, before the UPDATE. A second writer to the same row blocks at the lock and its isolate never starts.

Already true

Per-row isolate serialization is guaranteed by construction. Two rules cannot run against one row. No mutex, no advisory lock, no new concept — and therefore every same-row invariant is correct on day one: freeze, state machines, cross-field sums, required-when, immutable-once-set, deactivate-blocked-by-count.

That is the large majority of real rules. What it does not cover is cross-row aggregates: two invoices lock two different rows, each reads customer.open_ar = 6000, each passes, together they violate the credit limit. Classic write-skew — the shared row is the customer, and nothing locked it.

Four shapes, four answers, and two of them leave the rule system entirely:

ShapeExampleAnswer
uniquenessPO number per customernot a rule Postgres unique index
allocationgapless invoice numbersnot a rule sequence, outside the write tx
aggregate thresholdcredit limitopt-in materialized total + SSI retry, or declared locks
advisoryflag “trending over”not a rule automation, post-hoc

So the concurrency machinery is an escape hatch on one row of that table, not a pillar of the design. It ships when a customer needs it.

What the field does

  • Convex — OCC, no locks, automatic retry. It works precisely because mutations are deterministic: “we can simply re-run the transaction.”
  • Postgres SSI — detects write-skew via predicate locks that “do not cause any blocking and therefore can not play any part in causing a deadlock.” The docs recommend eliminating explicit SELECT FOR UPDATE where it is no longer needed, and call Serializable the best performance choice in some environments. Lobu · technical specification · final

Write-time entity policy

One place where a write to an entity is judged: a per-type code rule that runs inside the write transaction, after the row lock and before the UPDATE. It can deny, or escalate to a human. It can never grant.

Status settled, not built Seam entity-management.ts:1101 Blockers 2 — both land first Dated 2026-08-17

§1 The split, and why it isn’t a style choice

Policy lives in two tiers, and the boundary is forced by where the question gets asked.

TierFormAnswersRuns
Queryable declarative policy rows “may this actor touch this at all?” pre-flight, and on read paths
Enforceable per-type code rule “was this attempt legal?” inside the write transaction

Three read paths already gate on action: 'read'. No hook at the write seam can answer a read — there is no write to hook. So the declarative tier stays, and the two are not redundant: different questions, different times. What the code tier removes is the need to express write policy declaratively, which is exactly where the permissions UI was getting expensive.

The load-bearing constraint

The rule is deny-only. Its verbs are deny() and escalate(); there is no allow(). A rule can narrow what the declarative lattice permits, never widen it. That single property is what makes it safe to hand the rule full actor identity — a rule that cannot grant cannot be tricked into granting.

§2 Surface

One file per entity type, checked into the ontology repo, applied by lobu apply. access is data and compiles to policy rows at deploy time; check is a function and compiles to a script that runs at write time. Same file, two compilation targets — the Terraform/CDK shape. 

// ontology/invoice.rules.ts
import { defineEntityRules } from "@lobu/sdk";

export default defineEntityRules({
  type: "invoice",

  // ── data → policy rows, at apply time ────────────────────
  access: {
    read:  ["role:member", "agent:billing-clerk", "automation:*"],
    write: ["role:admin", "agent:billing-clerk"],
  },
  approvers: {
    header_net: "user:controller@acme.com",   // see §3
    "*":        "role:admin",
  },

  // ── function → compiled script, at the write seam ────────
  async check(ctx) {
    const { committed, next, changed, actor } = ctx;

    // immutability
    if (committed.status === "posted" && changed("header_net"))
      ctx.deny("a posted invoice is immutable");

    // legal exits only
    const exits = { draft: ["issued"], issued: ["posted", "void"] };
    if (changed("status") && !exits[committed.status]?.includes(next.status))
      ctx.deny(`cannot go ${committed.status} → ${next.status}`);

    // cross-field invariant
    if (next.status === "posted" && !next.einvoice_uuid)
      ctx.deny("posting requires an e-invoice UUID");

    // threshold → a human decides
    if (changed("header_net") && next.header_net > 50_000)
      ctx.escalate(["header_net"], "over the 50k limit");

    // scoped by who is asking — narrowing only
    if (actor.kind === "agent" && changed("customer_id"))
      ctx.deny("reassigning an invoice is a human decision");
  },
});

Everything an ERP needs for one type, on one screen, in the language the team already writes.

The ctx object

FieldTypeMeaning
committedrowthe row as it exists, read under the lock
patchpartialthe effective patch, after field-merge
nextrowcommitted merged with patch
changed(f)→ boolis f in the effective patch
actorobject{ kind, id, roles }; kind ∈ user | agent | automation
openumcreate | update | delete
get(type, id)asyncbudgeted read on the write connection — §4
deny(reason)throwsrolls back; the reason reaches the caller
escalate(fields, why)marksholds those fields, opens an approval — §3

Reserved keys follow the existing validator convention — $name, $slug, $parent_id, $content, $deleted — so a rule sees exactly the shape entity-row-validation.ts already builds.

There is no interesting rule about deleting a customer, because in an ERP you don’t delete one — you deactivate, which is a status change on the same row and is already covered by the state machine above. op: "delete" exists for completeness; it is not the motivating case.

§3 Escalation: who actually gets it

escalate() holds the named fields, commits the rest, and opens a pending approval. The question that matters is who can decide it. Traced end to end, today’s answer is:

admin or owner role  ∪  the field’s human owner — where the owner is resolved from field_controls at propose time and written to action_input.owner_user_id.

The gap

owner_user_id is null for any field no human has ever touched, which is the normal case for a field an agent maintains. So “over 50k needs controller approval” silently means “goes to whoever holds org admin.” A controller or account executive who is a member but not an admin cannot decide anything.

The fix is small, because the delivery layer is already recipient-agnostic: sendNotification(orgId, userIds[], …) takes an arbitrary array, and the notify tool already exposes recipients: 'admins' | 'all' | string[]. notifyOrgAdmins is a six-line wrapper the approval path happens to call. Two traps for implementation. Non-member recipients are silently dropped — notify filters ids against member and returns { notified_count: 0 } as a success, so an escalation aimed at someone who has left the org simply evaporates; a declared approver needs an explicit existence check that fails closed. And routing has three sources, not two: the policy row’s delivery target, ownerUserId, and an automation’s own configured channel.

Note also that decision and delivery read the same policy rows with different sorts: the decision folds max-restrictive, the delivery target picks most-specific (entity_id 4, field_path 2, type 1). Banning reads outright would be simpler, and wrong. “Deactivate a customer only if it has no open invoices” is an ordinary ERP rule and it needs one query. Every ontology system that forbids cross-row reads in its cheap tier ships a second tier that allows them.

So reads are allowed, on the write transaction’s own connection, through ctx.get / ctx.query, under a hard budget. The measured cost supports it: a host-function bridge into the isolate costs ~0.079 ms for the first call and ~0.013 ms marginal after. The bridge is not the expense — the query is.

The read uses the transaction handle, never getDb(). ShapeExampleAnswer

There is no interesting rule about deleting a customer, because in an ERP you don’t delete one — you deactivate, which is a status change on the same row and is already covered by the state machine above. op: "delete" exists for completeness; it is not the motivating case.

§3 Escalation: who actually gets it

escalate() holds the named fields, commits the rest, and opens a pending approval. The question that matters is who can decide it. Traced end to end, today’s answer is:

admin or owner role  ∪  the field’s human owner — where the owner is resolved from field_controls at propose time and written to action_input.owner_user_id.

The gap

owner_user_id is null for any field no human has ever touched, which is the normal case for a field an agent maintains. So “over 50k needs controller approval” silently means “goes to whoever holds org admin.” A controller or account executive who is a member but not an admin cannot decide anything.

The fix is small, because the delivery layer is already recipient-agnostic: sendNotification(orgId, userIds[], …) takes an arbitrary array, and the notify tool already exposes recipients: 'admins' | 'all' | string[]. notifyOrgAdmins is a six-line wrapper the approval path happens to call. Three changes: resolve an approver (policy row → field owner → admins), pass the list instead of the wrapper, and add a branch beside the owner_user_id predicate that authorizes the decision.

Design call

The approver is declared in approvers — on the policy row, not as an argument to escalate(). Naming an approver is granting a privilege, and the code tier is deny-only. Keeping it in the data tier preserves that invariant and keeps the grant queryable.

Two traps for implementation. Non-member recipients are silently dropped — notify filters ids against member and returns { notified_count: 0 } as a success, so an escalation aimed at someone who has left the org simply evaporates; a declared approver needs an explicit existence check that fails closed. And routing has three sources, not two: the policy row’s delivery target, ownerUserId, and an automation’s own configured channel.

Note also that decision and delivery read the same policy rows with different sorts: the decision folds max-restrictive, the delivery target picks most-specific (entity_id 4, field_path 2, type 1). And only a single-field escalation can match a field-scoped delivery row — multi-field falls back to the type-level one.

§4 Reads inside a rule

Banning reads outright would be simpler, and wrong. “Deactivate a customer only if it has no open invoices” is an ordinary ERP rule and it needs one query. Every ontology system that forbids cross-row reads in its cheap tier ships a second tier that allows them.

So reads are allowed, on the write transaction’s own connection, through ctx.get / ctx.query, under a hard budget. The measured cost supports it: a host-function bridge into the isolate costs ~0.079 ms for the first call and ~0.013 ms marginal after. The bridge is not the expense — the query is.

Non-negotiable

The read uses the transaction handle, never getDb(). Calling getDb() inside withEntityWriteTransaction is the exact shape of the #2818 production deadlock — DB_POOL_MAX sessions sitting idle in transaction on the same query. That incident forbids acquiring a second connection; it does not forbid reading.

§5 Concurrency: the default path needs nothing new

This is the part that looked hard and isn’t. updateEntity takes SELECT … FOR UPDATE at entity-management.ts:958, and the rule position is :1101 — after the lock, before the UPDATE. A second writer to the same row blocks at the lock, and its isolate never starts.

Already true today

Per-row isolate serialization is guaranteed by construction. Two rules cannot run against one row. No mutex, no advisory lock, no new concept — and therefore every same-row invariant is correct on day one: freeze, state machines, cross-field sums, required-when, immutable-once-set, deactivate-blocked-by-count.

That is the large majority of real rules. What it does not cover is cross-row aggregates: two invoices lock two different rows, each reads customer.open_ar = 6000, each passes, together they breach the credit limit. Classic write-skew — the shared row is the customer, and nothing locked it.

Four shapes, four answers, and two of them leave the rule system entirely:

ShapeExampleAnswer
uniquenessPO number per customernot a rule Postgres unique index
allocationgapless invoice numbersnot a rule sequence, outside the write tx
aggregate thresholdcredit limitopt-in materialized total + SSI retry, or declared locks
advisoryflag “trending over”not a rule automation, post-hoc

So the concurrency machinery is an escape hatch on one row of that table, not a pillar of the design. It ships when a customer needs it, and not before.

What the field does

  • Convex — OCC, no locks, automatic retry. It works precisely because mutations are deterministic: “we can simply re-run the transaction.”
  • Postgres SSI — detects write-skew via predicate locks that “do not cause any blocking and therefore can not play any part in causing a deadlock.” The docs recommend eliminating explicit SELECT FOR UPDATE where it is no longer needed, and call Serializable the best performance choice in some environments. Requires app retry on 40001.
  • Odoo — serializable with auto-retry, and it hurts: the pain traces to locking the last journal entry to allocate an invoice number. That is allocation, not validation — evidence for keeping allocation out of the write transaction, not evidence against OCC.
  • Salesforce — pessimistic FOR UPDATE, ~10 s wait, then UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW.

Our rules are pure and deterministic by design, so Convex-style retry is available to us in a way it is not for general application code. One honest caveat: the transaction is not literally replayable — computeFieldMerge takes a fresh nowIso. And if declared locks ever ships, keys must be sorted by (type, id) before acquisition, or two rules touching customers A and B in opposite orders deadlock.

The risk that is actually real

Not row contention — event-loop starvation, which is keyed on the process, not the row. A hundred writes to a hundred different rows means a hundred concurrent isolates. Measured on node 22, the production runtime:

Two conclusions. Throughput plateaus at ~2,250/s from four workers and does not scale with cores — isolated-vm is not buying parallelism here. And the event loop dies between 4 and 8 concurrent isolates. So the mitigation is a global concurrency cap of 4 on rule execution, which costs nothing at the plateau, plus the existing timeout. That is the one operational control this design needs.

Per-write cost is 0.63 ms for a bare isolate and 4.5 ms through the full SDK harness (jail, four bridges, manifest, timeout wrapper). The gap is harness, not V8 — and compilation is per module, which is why the unit is one rule script per entity type rather than one per rule.

§6 Audit: the trail is currently inverted

Before rules can ship, the record has to work in the direction that matters. Today it works in exactly the wrong one.

What happenedRecorded?Where
successful updateyesfield-level diff, manage_entity.ts:585
successful createnohandleCreate never calls it
delete / merge / link / unlinkno—
denied writeno — structurallyrollback + post-commit placement
the audit write itself failingdroppedfire-and-forget; logs and moves on

A denial throws, the transaction rolls back, and anything written inside it disappears — and the audit hook is post-commit anyway, so it never runs. You get a detailed diff when nothing went wrong, and nothing at all when it did. Adding write rules makes that materially worse, because every deny becomes a silent failure — and §7 proves a denial can be both wrong and misattributed.

Fix: write the denial audit after the rollback, on a fresh connection. This is the one place getDb() outside the write transaction is correct — the transaction has ended, so there is no #2818 exposure. Record rule, reason, actor, entity, and attempted patch, and make it durable: fire-and-forget with a drop-log is acceptable for a convenience diff, not for the record of why a write was refused.

Already composes

Audit inserts enforce idempotency through metadata._lobu_idempotency_key plus a unique index, handling the violation inline. An SSI retry that re-runs the transaction therefore will not duplicate audit rows — that integration problem is already solved.

§7 Blocker: an approval hold turns a legal write into a denial

Reproduced, with a passing control that isolates the cause — __tests__/integration/authz/spike-approval-hold-vs-invariant.test.ts.

  1. Invoice in draft. Spec: issued exits to posted, frozen, with einvoice_uuid writable on exit.
  2. A human moves draft → issued. Legal — and this claims human ownership of status.
  3. An agent writes { status: "posted", einvoice_uuid: "…" } — the legal exit plus the one field the spec permits.
  4. The gate holds status because a human owns it. The field merge strips it.
  5. Effective patch is { einvoice_uuid } with no transition → frozen state, non-exempt field → DENY.

The control — the identical agent write with no human owner on status — succeeds. So the cause is the ownership hold, not the rule.

Why this is worse than a failed write

The error reads frozen in state "issued": cannot write einvoice_uuid, which is not the cause — the cause is an approval hold on a different field. And the approval card is never created: the write path returns from inside the transaction, and the deferral is constructed after that point, so the throw skips it. The agent’s work is denied, misattributed, and dropped with no pending record anyone can act on.

The general principle: partial field commits and cross-field invariants are logically incompatible. Committing a consistent subset can produce an inconsistent whole. Any system with both must pick one — today Lobu silently picks lose-the-write.

Recommended fix: when a type has a check, an approval hold becomes all-or-nothing — defer the entire write rather than partially commit it. The alternative, passing pending: string[] into ctx so each rule can skip held fields, pushes platform mechanics into every multi-field rule an ontology author writes.

This is introduced by the validation branch, not pre-existing — with no rules there is nothing to deny. So it must be fixed before rules ship, not after.

§8 Phasing

PhaseContentsGate to the next
0 · prerequisites All-or-nothing approval hold (§7). Durable denial audit plus create and delete coverage (§6). Global isolate cap of 4 (§5). Both blockers closed; cap verified under load.
1 · rules, inert defineEntityRules, compiled at apply, run at :1101, log-only. No denial reaches a caller. A week of production shadow output with no surprise denials.
2 · enforcing Arm deny. Delete entity-transition-rules.ts outright — the DSL is strictly less expressive than the function replacing it, so it goes entirely: no alias, no deprecation. Escalation routing ready.
3 · escalation escalate(), declared approvers, and the authority branch beside owner_user_id (§3). —
4 · opt-in Cross-row aggregates: materialized totals, SSI plus retry, or declared locks. Built on demand, not speculatively. —

The inert-then-arm shape across phases 1 → 2 is the same one the ACL trigger needed: classification, not the mechanism, is what breaks a rolling deploy, so the two must land in separate deploys.

§9 Decisions still yours

  • Case-3 fix shape — all-or-nothing hold (recommended) vs pending exposed in ctx.
  • Clock in ctx — exposing now makes rules non-replayable and forecloses OCC retry. Recommend withholding it and passing effective dates as fields.
  • Read budget — the numeric cap on ctx.get calls per write.
  • Deny-message disclosure — a reason string can leak the existence of rows the caller cannot read.
  • Transforms — whether a rule may normalize a value or only judge it. Judge-only is the safer start.
  • Permission UI — hide the write half, or delete it, once §3 lands.
  • Merge semantics — whether a rule runs on entity merge, where two committed rows each claim to be valid.

content.text:
Spec is finalized and republished to the same URL: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9af4a098-8d23-4646-92fd-09f4b0d5cc99

Two things changed structurally from the working draft:

**Concurrency is no longer a pillar.** It now opens with the fact that the lock at `:958` precedes the rule position at `:1101`, so per-row isolate serialization is already free — every same-row invariant works on day one with no new machinery. Cross-row aggregates are one row in a four-row table, and the SSI/locks work is Phase 4, built on demand. The risk that *is* real got promoted in its place: event-loop starvation is per-process, not per-row, and the measurements say the mitigation is a global cap of 4.

**Denial auditing became a Phase 0 prerequisite,** alongside the case-3 fix. Both are now gates, not follow-ups — the argument being that arming `deny` on a system where denials are structurally invisible turns every rejected write into a silent, misattributed failure.

Memory before compaction — four files written, all cross-linked:

| file | what it preserves |
|---|---|
| `reference_entity_write_concurrency_model` | the lock/rule ordering, the four shapes, Convex/SSI/Odoo/Salesforce primary-source quotes |
| `reference_entity_audit_trail_is_inverted` | the coverage table, why denials can't be audited in-transaction, the idempotency-key composition |
| `reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial` | the reproduced sequence, the lost approval card, the all-or-nothing recommendation |
| `reference_entity_approval_routing_and_authority` | authority = admin ∪ field owner, the null-`owner_user_id` gap, the silent-drop trap |

`MEMORY.md` got a new write-policy line at the top of Open work, and I compacted it from 20KB to ~17KB (the hook was warning it was near the read limit) by folding shipped ACL/release detail into their topic files and dropping a handful of low-value index entries — those stay recallable by `description:` grep.

**Confidence**

- Measurements (isolate throughput, heartbeat, bridge cost): **high** — ran on node 22 from inside the repo tree, idle baseline included.
- Case-3 bug: **high** — reproduced with a passing control that isolates the ownership hold as the cause.
- Audit coverage table: **high** — read every call site.
- Approval authority/routing: **medium-high** — traced the code paths, but not exercised against a live escalation with a non-admin approver.
- The proposed API surface: **low-medium** — it's a design, nothing is built. `defineEntityRules` doesn't exist.

**Next actions to pick from**

1. Promote `spike-approval-hold-vs-invariant.test.ts` out of scratch into a real regression test and commit it — right now it's uncommitted in the worktree and it's the only proof of the blocker.
2. Fix the all-or-nothing hold (§7) as its own PR, before any rule work starts.
3. Land durable denial auditing + create/delete coverage (§6) as a second PR.
4. Answer the §9 decisions — the clock-in-ctx one is the only one that constrains the API shape, so it's worth settling before Phase 1.

content.text:
Dug into it. It's smaller than the spec implies, because you've already built this pipeline once — for automation reactions.

## The pipeline exists end to end

`reaction_script` is TS source authored in the ontology repo, compiled at apply, stored on the owning row, and run in an isolate when it fires. That is exactly the shape rules need. Every stage has a working implementation to copy:

| Stage | Exists as | Reuse |
|---|---|---|
| Author a sibling `.ts`, brand the path | `reactionFromFile` → `{kind, path}` (`cli/src/config/define.ts:526`) | verbatim, ~5 lines for a `rulesFromFile` twin |
| Resolve + read the file at apply | `desired-state.ts:948` | copy-adapt |
| TS → JS + content hash | `compileSource`, `computeCodeHash` (`compiler-core.ts`) | verbatim |
| Store source + compiled | `watchers.reaction_script` / `_compiled` | mirror the two columns on `entity_types` |
| Run in an isolate | `runScript` | verbatim |
| Executor wrapper | `reaction-executor.ts`, 200 lines | ~150-line analogue |
| Deny → throw → rollback | `EntityRowValidationError` | verbatim |
| Escalate | `deferEntityFieldChange` + mutation gate | verbatim |
| Notify | `sendNotification(orgId, userIds[])` | verbatim |

## The seam is a one-line swap

This is the part I under-sold in the spec. `validateEntityRowPatch` is **already async**, already does the `SELECT` of the committed rows inside the locked transaction, and already builds `committedState(row)` and `flatten(patch, patch.metadata)`. The rule call replaces exactly this:

```ts
const reason = evaluateTransition({ spec, committed, patch });
if (reason !== null) throw new EntityRowValidationError(`entity ${row.id}: ${reason}`);
```

Same inputs, same `string | null` contract, same throw. Nothing upstream moves.

## Net new code is close to zero

`entity-transition-rules.ts` is 206 lines with **two** importers, one of which is its own test. It all goes — parser, validator, evaluator, and the whole `x-transitions.states.foo.writableOnExit` error vocabulary, which TypeScript replaces at authoring time in the developer's IDE. Rough shape of the trade:

```
-206  entity-transition-rules.ts (deleted)
+150  entity-rule-executor.ts        (adapted from reaction-executor)
 +80  apply: read/compile/send       (adapted from reaction handling)
 +60  defineEntityRules + rulesFromFile
 +30  seam swap in entity-row-validation.ts
 +30  concurrency semaphore
 +20  migration (2 columns)
```

Phase 1 lands at roughly **+170 net**, and most of the additions are copy-adapted from a file that has been running in production.

## Three simplifications worth taking

**No new table.** Two columns on `entity_types`, exactly mirroring `watchers`. Still needs your sign-off as a DB change, but it's the smallest possible one.

**Add `SDKMode: "none"`.** Today it's `"read" | "full"`, and the reaction path always builds a full ClientSDK — jail, four bridges, manifest. That's the entire gap between the 0.63 ms bare isolate and the 4.5 ms harness I measured. A rule with no `ctx.get` needs none of it, and a third mode makes the §4 read-budget decision enforceable by construction rather than by convention: rules that don't declare reads literally cannot make one.

**One seam, not two.** Transition validation lives in `entity-row-validation.ts`; approval and escalation live in the mutation gate. Two mechanisms answering "may this write proceed." Folding the write half of the gate into the rule is the consolidation you've been pushing for — but it's only available *after* escalation is expressible from a rule, which is why §3 gates it.

## Where it is genuinely not small

The Phase 0 blockers, and they're the reverse of the feature work — small in lines, high in risk, because they change behavior that already ships.

The all-or-nothing hold is the hard one. `entity-management.ts` returns from inside the transaction at `:1134` and builds the deferral at `:1142`, so fixing it means restructuring the commit boundary of a path that currently works. Call it 60–100 lines and the majority of the total risk in this project.

Denial auditing is mechanically easy (~80 lines) but touches the audit contract, and the create/delete coverage gap rides along with it.

One thing to flag: `validateEntityRowPatch` takes `ids: number[]` — it's a batch function. A batch write of 20 rows spawns 20 isolates, which is well past where the event loop dies. The semaphore is not optional, and it has to sit inside the batch loop, not around it.

---

**Confidence: high (85)** on the reuse map and the seam being a one-line swap — I read `reactionFromFile`, `reaction-executor.ts`, `compileSource`, `validateEntityRowPatch`, the `watchers` columns, and confirmed `SDKMode` has only two members. **Medium (55)** on the line estimates; they're informed by reading the analogue files, not by writing the code. **Low** on the all-or-nothing fix being 60–100 lines — I've read the shape of the problem but not attempted it.

**Next actions**

1. Spike just the seam swap: a hardcoded compiled rule string run at `validateEntityRowPatch`, log-only, no CLI or storage. Half a day, and it validates the whole reuse thesis or kills it.
2. Decide the `entity_types` column addition — it's the one thing here that needs your sign-off before any code.
3. Take a real run at the all-or-nothing hold, since it's the only genuinely uncertain estimate and it gates everything else.
4. Add `SDKMode: "none"` as a standalone PR — it's independently useful and it's how §4's read budget gets teeth.

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- `core` types/utils · `plugin-api` plugin contracts · `plugin-host` plugin composition · `server` gateway + embedded runtime · `agent-worker` agent execution · `connectors` built-in connectors · `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Read the nearest package `AGENTS.md` before editing that package; grep `docs/GOTCHAS.md` when something looks inexplicable.

## Unrecoverable — never do these
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout — other sessions share it. For a pure submodule-pointer bump, `make bump SUBMODULE=packages/owletto` is the lightweight isolated-worktree exception; it also posts the required statuses.
- **Stage by explicit path** (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`). A commit is a snapshot, so a stale file copy left by earlier work in the same worktree silently reverts merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal your intended file list; extras = stop.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone or supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are usually real signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI** — it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work. Rebase locally against `origin/main`; submodule-pointer branches `git merge` instead (`docs/GOTCHAS.md`).
- **Two writing agents must never share a worktree** — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work. Every subagent with Edit/Write/Bash gets its own through `make task-setup` (only task-setup does submodule pinning, `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation); only read-only agents share the parent.
- **Never add a table or change DB design, API surface, or SDK surface** without surfacing the proposal and receiving confirmation first.
- **Never auto-submit an interactive browser draft, in any package.** Drafts are page-activated: persist the operation, notify normally, and let the extension activate the run only when the user visits a pending URL in a user-owned tab. Only scrape-owned scratch tabs may be opened and closed automatically. Server, connector, and Owletto code all obey this (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`).

## Facts you cannot derive
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** A resync supersedes the row and mints a new id for the same source item, so cross-sync identity and dedupe must key on the connector's `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over `events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, … on a user-facing read path: history grows, the answer doesn't. Materialize at write time, read back by index, backfill in a migration. Bounded config tables (`connections`, `automations`, `agent_users`) are fine.
- **Shared state must be Postgres-mediated.** An in-memory Map or singleton is invisible to other replicas — correct in dev, broken in prod.
- **Workers never receive real credentials** — placeholders or proxied access only. The exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived leases (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one.
- **Automation is the product, API, and storage vocabulary.** Use it consistently in public contracts and internal identifiers; `make pre-pr-remote` rejects retired product and engine terminology.
- **`make review` is the semantic review gate, not CI.** It runs no typecheck, knip, or tests; a verdict or safe-class skip is not evidence CI will pass.
- **Depot serializes org-wide.** A newer dispatch silently cancels a peer session's running gate, and `gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch. Check `pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"` before dispatching.
- Default to static `import`; a new production dynamic import needs measured justification plus a call-site rationale comment. Tests may import dynamically after mocks; two Node-version gates are grandfathered (playbook).

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce red → fix → prove green, and paste both outputs in the PR. Cannot reproduce = report the dead end; never ship a speculative fix.
3. Iterate on focused tests: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. `make pre-pr-remote-fast` gives interim breadth and never substitutes for the final gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff, then re-read what it touched. Safe-class changes self-skip before selecting an LLM. Otherwise it runs BEFORE the first `make review` — never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop, since each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
5. Stage by explicit path, then `make pre-pr-remote`; it fails closed on unstaged or untracked changes. Reviewed workflow/action changes need `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1`.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD; it posts the required `pi-review` status. Narrow path/content-gated safe classes skip the cross-harness review; this includes pure `packages/owletto` pointer bumps and exact `model:` literal swaps, but not mixed runtime and source changes. The submodule's own repo owns its content review.
9. `make ui-review`. Non-Owletto changes and complete, forward-only Owletto pointer diffs confined to `deploy/` pass as not applicable; other pointer changes need exact hosted proof (`ARTIFACT=<url>`; see the playbook).
10. `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin` once green — never `--admin` past a check that has not reported. Lobu's required `integration` fan-in is absent from `gh pr checks` until it starts, not pending, so diff against the branch-protection list (playbook).
11. Prod-visible surface? Verify live after rollout: gate on the **squash commit**, not your branch head, keeping the argument order `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"`. Record the result.

## How to work
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create; no new `*.md` unless asked.
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- **Evidence, not assertion.** Never report done off a green typecheck — boot it, exercise every branch you touched, and clean up test data; if "compiles" is all you ran, say so. Show `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`, including for a dispatched agent's work.
- **Absence needs `origin/main`:** `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main`. A working-tree grep proves nothing, and the fetch is load-bearing.
- Deleting code needs structural evidence — a dangling import, a completed migration, a superseded implementation. Low prod usage is not evidence, and docs and help text are load-bearing.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other occurrence and fix in one pass. A diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one.
- One branch = one concern. Never `git stash`; use WIP commits.
- Prefer `bun`, never npm/yarn/pnpm. Before adding an env var, grep for the one already read, and do not rename existing vars unasked.
- Block only on irreversible or destructive actions and decisions genuinely the user's; otherwise take the recommended option and flag it in your summary.
- Never poll in the foreground — run long waits in the background and act on the notification. Poll delegated CLIs at most once every 4.5 minutes unless they finish or request input.
- Prefer DOM reads over screenshots, the top context-bloat source. The paired Owletto extension drives the user's real logged-in browser; CDP is not required (`docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`).
- Slack link pasted → run `scripts/slack-thread-viewer.js "<link>"` first.
- `make dev-remote` runs the live app on remote compute (commit first; `make dev-remote-pause` when finished).
