git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(server): per-type entity write rules, enforced at the write seam

Replaces the `x-transitions` JSON DSL with per-type TypeScript compiled at
apply time and executed at the entity row-write seam. The DSL was never
authorable through the CLI (raw SQL only) and could only express transitions;
a rule is code, so it can express any invariant its author can write.

Storage mirrors `automations.reaction_script`: `entity_types.rules_source`
holds the authored text, `rules_compiled` the build output, so the write path
never invokes esbuild. Both columns default to NULL, which every existing type
already reads as "no rule".

Batch-shaped by construction — one isolate per (type, batch), not per row.
Measured on node 22: per-row tops out near 300 evals/sec and takes ~21s for
5,000 rows; the same rows share one isolate in ~13.5ms.

Creates no longer bypass validation. `insertEntityRow`/`tryInsertEntityRow`
now take the same brand `patchEntityRows` already required, so skipping the
check is a compile error. That found FIVE create sites, not the two a grep
predicted: createEntity, automation-output promotion and connector link
auto-create now validate; eval scaffolding and the platform canvas container
take an explicit `unvalidatedEntityRowInsert({ reason })`.

Fixes an approval-hold bug that predates rules but only became visible with
them. An agent proposing a legal `issued -> posted` plus the field that move
unlocks had `status` stripped by an ownership hold, leaving a naked field edit
on a frozen row — rejected under a reason describing neither what was proposed
nor why it failed, and because the deferral is built after the transaction
returns, the throw dropped the approval card too. An approval hold may not
manufacture an illegal state: when the residual fails and fields were held,
nothing commits and the entire proposal defers as one approval unit. A rule
that rejects a write the caller actually proposed, with nothing held, still
throws.

`escalate(fields, reason)` is wired to that same path, holding the whole write
rather than applying part of it. `deny` beats `escalate`: approval cannot make
an illegal state legal.

Authored via `rulesFromFile("./rules/invoice.ts")`. The CLI ships raw source
and diffs source, never the compiled artifact, so a compiler change does not
read as a rule change; the server compiles on save and rejects a rule that
does not compile at apply time, while the author is still there.

Known gaps, documented in place: soft-delete, merge and unmerge still bypass
the seam, and a create cannot escalate (there is no row to hold fields against).
EOF

## Summary
- Replaces the `x-transitions` JSON DSL with per-type TypeScript compiled at apply time and run at the entity row-write seam. The DSL was never authorable through the CLI (raw SQL only) and could only express transitions.
- Closes the create bypass: `insertEntityRow`/`tryInsertEntityRow` now take the same brand `patchEntityRows` already required, so skipping validation is a compile error. The compiler found **five** create sites, not the two a grep predicted.
- Fixes an approval-hold bug that predates rules: an ownership hold could split a write, leave an illegal residual, reject it under a misattributed reason, and drop the approval card with it.

## Test plan
- [x] Intended files staged explicitly, then `make pre-pr-remote` clean — Depot run `djp21wcx0k`, 19/19 jobs passed
- [x] Tests run: 293 server tests / 37 files (`src/__tests__/integration/authz`, `integration/entity-schema`, `src/authz/__tests__`, entity-adjacent unit suites) · 341 CLI apply tests · `tsc --noEmit` clean in core/cli/server
- [x] Bug fix: red→fix→green below
- [ ] Bot runtime unchanged

### red → green

The approval-hold bug, reproduced before the fix (`entity-approval-hold-vs-rule.test.ts`):

```
× BUG: the identical write is denied once a human owns `status`
  EntityRowValidationError: entity 3: issued is frozen: einvoice_uuid is not writable
```

An agent proposed the legal exit `issued -> posted` plus `einvoice_uuid`, the one field that move unlocks. The permission gate held `status` (human-owned) and stripped it, so what reached the rule was a naked field edit on a frozen row. The rule rejected a write the agent never proposed — and because the deferral is built *after* the transaction returns, the throw skipped it, so no approval card was queued either. The work was denied, misattributed, and dropped.

After — the same four cases, green:

```
✓ CONTROL: the agent's legal exit succeeds when no human owns `status`
✓ defers the WHOLE write once a human owns `status`, instead of denying it
✓ defers the whole write when a RULE escalates, carrying the rule's own reason
✓ still DENIES outright when nothing was held and the caller's own proposal is illegal
```

The create bypass, proven then closed (`entity-create-validation.test.ts`) — this file began as a spike asserting the bypass existed:

```
✓ denies an invoice born DIRECTLY in the terminal frozen state
✓ permits the legal create and still denies the same end state by update
```

## Notes

**The fix.** The root cause was not validation being too strict — it was that an approval hold splits a write and commits half of it, which was already wrong before rules existed. New invariant: *an approval hold may not manufacture an illegal state.* When the residual fails validation and fields were held, nothing commits and the entire proposal defers as one approval unit. `escalate` routes the same way, holding the whole write rather than applying part of it. A rule rejecting a write the caller actually proposed, with nothing held, still throws — there is a dedicated case for that so the fix cannot quietly swallow real denials.

**Performance.** Batch-shaped by construction: one isolate per (type, batch), not per row. Measured on node 22 — per-row tops out near 300 evals/sec and takes ~21s for a 5,000-row sync; the same rows share one isolate in ~13.5ms. Types with no rule never reach an isolate at all, so an unruled org's writes cost exactly what they do today.

**Two subtleties for rule authors**, both because `patch` is the fully merged value set rather than a delta: a transition check must compare `from !== to` or a rename reads as an illegal self-transition, and a frozen-field check must skip values equal to `committed` or every unrelated write is denied. Documented on `EntityWriteRow` and exercised in the tests.

**Rollout.** Both columns default to NULL, which every existing type already reads as "no rule" — nothing changes for anyone until an author declares one. Schema ships ahead of code so a rolling deploy never runs new code against an old table.

**Publish ordering.** The server change is additive, so an older `@lobu/cli` is unaffected. `rulesFromFile` needs an `@lobu/cli` publish before anyone can author a rule.

**Known gaps, documented in place:** soft-delete, merge and unmerge still bypass the seam; a create cannot escalate (no row to hold fields against); `ctx.actor` is deliberately absent, since this seam answers "is the resulting state legal", which has no principal in it.
EOF

content.text:
You're right, and it's a real defect, not a style disagreement. I proved it:

A rule that says "deny if `changed("status")`" **denies an update that only touches `amount`.**

`changed()` is `hasOwnProperty(patch, f)`, and at the seam `flatten()` spreads the *fully merged* metadata into `patch`. So every metadata key is present on every metadata write. `row.changed("status")` is true whenever the writer touched any metadata at all. I named it `changed`, then wrote a doc comment admitting it doesn't mean changed — and shipped that as the primitive every rule is built on.

Three things follow, and they're all mine:

**My unit test passed because its fixtures are shapes production never produces.** Line 55 passes `patch: { $name: "renamed" }` with no `status`. The real seam sends `{ status: "draft", $name: "renamed" }`. I tested a delta; the seam only ever sends a merge. That's the same false-green class I flagged earlier this session on the wrong-signature spike — and I walked straight into it.

**The two "subtleties for rule authors" I documented are not subtleties.** `from !== to` and the `same(committed, patch)` deep-compare exist *only* to work around the broken primitive. I wrote them down instead of fixing the cause. Documenting a footgun is not the same as not having one.

**That's why all three of my test files re-implement the identical transition table.** I deleted a declarative transitions DSL and replaced it with a blank sheet whose one helper lies. The DSL at least encoded `from → to` correctly. Every author now rebuilds a state machine by hand on top of a primitive that mis-fires.

The fix for `changed()` is unambiguous and I'll do it regardless: compare values — `!deepEqual(committed[f], next[f])`. That makes both workarounds disappear, since `changed("status")` *becomes* the `from !== to` check and the frozen-field loop just asks `changed(f)`.

What I want your call on is the layer above it, because that's the part I removed without a replacement:

content.text:
Yes — exactly right, and that distinction is the whole point.

**Options 2 and 3: the app is blind.** The transition table is a `const ALLOWED = {...}` inside a compiled JS bundle. Only the isolate ever sees it. The server can't read it, Owletto can't read it, the agent prompt can't read it. The single way to discover whether `draft → posted` is legal is to attempt the write and get denied. Option 3's SDK helper only moves the boilerplate into one tested place — the data is still trapped in the bundle.

**Option 1: the server knows it as data.** `transitions` is stored structured, so anything can read it:

- Owletto can render only the buttons that lead somewhere legal, instead of showing all of them and letting the write fail
- the agent's prompt can say "this invoice is `issued`; the only legal move is `posted`, which needs `einvoice_uuid`" — so it proposes something legal the first time instead of burning a turn on a denial
- you can query "which invoices are stuck in `issued`" without executing anything

You already have this exact failure mode twice in this codebase: Owletto shows **dead 403 buttons** on `member_of`, and the authorization-purpose work left the **agent prompt blind** to the same policy the server enforces. Both are enforcement the UI and the agent can't see. Code-only rules would be a third instance, and a worse one, because a state machine is precisely the thing a UI wants to render.

The catch is that declarative can't express everything — "posting requires an e-invoice UUID", cross-field arithmetic, thresholds. So it isn't either/or: transitions declarative because the app needs to read them, code rules for the rest. That's the queryable/enforceable split, and I collapsed it into code-only when I deleted the DSL.

**Note that option 1 means a new stored column and a new public config surface**, which is why I asked rather than just building it.

---

Now the part I owe you: **the review found a blocker that proves your pushback right.**

`escalate` creates an approval card **that can never be applied.** Approving it re-runs the same rule against the same committed state, which escalates again and throws out of `applyEntityFieldChangeProposal`. Nothing commits, ever. My test called `queue()` and stopped there; the reviewer went one step further and called the apply path. I built a review mechanism and never tested approving anything.

Second real finding: my module and migration comments claim "the write path never invokes esbuild." **On this branch that's false** — ~9-10ms of esbuild per batch, inside the row-locked transaction. The compile memo from #2838 is on `origin/main`; this branch was cut before it and never rebased. So my measured 13.5ms/5000-rows figure doesn't hold as shipped. A rebase fixes it, but I stated it as fact without checking the branch actually had the memo.

Verdict was `bug_free 55, simplicity 64, 1 blocker, risk high, tests_adequate: false`. That's a fair read.

So: three defects, all of the same kind — I asserted behavior I hadn't exercised end to end. `changed()`, escalate-then-approve, and the esbuild claim.

I'd like your call on the transitions question before I rewrite, since it changes what `changed()` and the rule surface even need to do. My recommendation is **option 1** — declarative transitions the app can read, plus code rules — specifically because of the dead-403-button precedent. But it's a new column and public surface, so it's yours to sign off.

content.text:
You're right, and I talked myself into a bad idea. Rules cover transitions completely — a code rule can enforce any transition table, so a declarative `transitions` block would be a **second mechanism doing the same enforcement job**. That's exactly the duplication you don't want, and it'd cost a new column and a new public config surface to boot. Dropping it.

Worse: my main argument for it was that "every author rebuilds the same state machine boilerplate." That boilerplate is an artifact of *my own bug*. The `from !== to` dance and the `same(committed, patch)` helper exist only because `changed()` is broken. Once `changed()` actually means changed, a transition rule is three lines:

```js
if (!row.changed('status')) return
if (!(ALLOWED[row.committed.status] ?? []).includes(row.next.status))
  row.deny(`cannot move ${row.committed.status} -> ${row.next.status}`)
```

Nothing there justifies inventing a subsystem. I was proposing to build one to work around a bug I introduced.

The one thing genuinely lost is that the app can't *read* the state machine — but that's a separate concern about UI and agent prompts, not an enforcement gap, and it doesn't belong in this PR.

So the work is the three real defects, nothing more:

1. **`changed()` must compare values**, not key presence — proven broken
2. **escalate → approve is a dead end** — the reviewer's blocker; approving re-runs the rule, re-escalates, throws forever
3. **the "never invokes esbuild" claim is false on this branch** — the #2838 memo is on `origin/main`, this branch predates it

content.text:
You were right, and dropping the transitions idea was the right call — it would have been a second mechanism for enforcement rules already do, plus a column and a public surface, to work around a bug I'd introduced. Here's what the three real defects turned out to be.

**`changed()` didn't mean changed.** Proven end to end: a rule guarding only `status` denied an update that touched only `amount`. It was `hasOwnProperty(patch, f)`, and the seam hands over the *merged* value set, so every metadata key is present on every metadata write. Now it compares values structurally. The payoff is that your point lands directly — the transition rule got *shorter*:

```js
if (row.changed('status') && !(ALLOWED[from] || []).includes(to))
  row.deny(...)
```

The `same()` deep-compare helper and the `from !== to` dance are deleted from all three rules. That boilerplate was never inherent to code rules; it was my bug leaking into every author's file.

**Escalate created a card that could never be applied.** The reviewer reproduced it: approving re-ran the rule against the same committed state, re-escalated, and threw. I'd built a review mechanism and never tested approving anything. Fixed by threading `onEscalate: "approved"` through the one path applying a human-approved proposal — `deny` still throws in both modes, since approval can't make an illegal state legal. I mutation-tested it: flipping the flag back makes the new assertion fail.

**The "never invokes esbuild" claim was false.** The #2838 memo was on `origin/main`; this branch predated it and I never rebased. Rebased, then *measured* instead of asserting — and found my documented numbers were wrong by 3x. Real figures: ~1.6ms fixed per batch, ~0.002ms/row, 1000 rows ~3.2ms, 5000 rows ~29.7ms.

That measurement also changed a decision: I'd set `MAX_RULE_BATCH = 2000` from the bad numbers. Cost grows faster than linearly, so at 1000 the same 5000 rows take **29.7ms instead of 42.5ms**, with each event-loop block ~3.2ms instead of ~14–19ms. Better on both axes, so it's 1000 now — and the comment says why, with the numbers.

The common thread in all three: I asserted behavior I hadn't exercised end to end, and my unit test fixtures used a delta shape the seam never produces, so it passed while the API misfired in production.

299 tests / 37 files green, tsc clean in all three packages, gate running now.

**Confidence**
- `changed()` fix — **90**. Proven broken at the seam first, then fixed, with regressions at both unit and integration level and merged-shaped fixtures.
- Escalate round trip — **85**. Mutation-tested; the assertion fails without the fix.
- Perf numbers — **85**. Measured in-process just now, not quoted from a spike. Not measured under concurrent load.

**Next**
1. Read the gate, then `make review` again — the previous verdict is stale and its blocker is fixed.
2. The old PR body still quotes 13.5ms and the pre-rebase claims; needs updating before merge.
3. Still open from the review: `tests_adequate: false`, and merge/unmerge/soft-delete still bypass the seam.
4. The thing genuinely lost with transitions-as-data — UI and agent can't read the state machine — is worth its own issue if the dead-403-button problem bothers you, but it's not enforcement and not this PR.

git commit -q --amend -F - <<'EOF'
feat(server): per-type entity write rules, enforced at the write seam

Replaces the `x-transitions` JSON DSL with per-type TypeScript compiled at
apply time and executed at the entity row-write seam. The DSL was never
authorable through the CLI (raw SQL only) and could only express transitions;
a rule is code, so it can express any invariant its author can write.

Storage mirrors `automations.reaction_script`: `entity_types.rules_source`
holds the authored text, `rules_compiled` the build output, so the write path
never bundles the author's TypeScript. Both columns default to NULL, which
every existing type already reads as "no rule".

`row.changed(field)` compares VALUES between `committed` and `next`. It cannot
be key presence: the seam hands a rule the fully MERGED value set, not a delta,
so `hasOwnProperty` is true for every metadata key on every metadata write.
An earlier cut had exactly that bug — a rule guarding only `status` denied an
update touching only `amount` — which then forced every rule to hand-roll
`from !== to` and a deep-compare helper. With the comparison fixed, a
transition rule is three lines and those workarounds are gone.

Batch-shaped by construction: one isolate per (type, batch), not per row. A
per-row design was built and measured first at ~300 evals/sec. Measured warm on
node 22: ~1.6ms fixed per batch, ~0.002ms marginal per row, 1,000 rows ~3.2ms,
5,000 rows ~29.7ms. MAX_RULE_BATCH is 1,000 rather than larger because cost
grows faster than linearly — over the same 5,000 rows, 2,000/batch took 42.5ms
with ~14-19ms event-loop blocks against 29.7ms with ~3.2ms blocks.

Creates no longer bypass validation. `insertEntityRow`/`tryInsertEntityRow`
now take the same brand `patchEntityRows` already required, so skipping the
check is a compile error. That found FIVE create sites, not the two a grep
predicted: createEntity, automation-output promotion and connector link
auto-create now validate; eval scaffolding and the platform canvas container
take an explicit `unvalidatedEntityRowInsert({ reason })`.

Fixes an approval-hold bug that predates rules but only became visible with
them. An agent proposing a legal `issued -> posted` plus the field that move
unlocks had `status` stripped by an ownership hold, leaving a naked field edit
on a frozen row — rejected under a reason describing neither what was proposed
nor why it failed, and because the deferral is built after the transaction
returns, the throw dropped the approval card too. An approval hold may not
manufacture an illegal state: when the residual fails and fields were held,
nothing commits and the entire proposal defers as one approval unit. A rule
that rejects a write the caller actually proposed, with nothing held, still
throws.

`escalate(fields, reason)` routes to that same path, holding the whole write
rather than applying part of it. Applying an approved proposal passes
`onEscalate: "approved"` so the rule that escalated does not escalate the very
write its escalation asked for — without it the card could never be cleared.
`deny` still throws in both modes: approval cannot make an illegal state legal.

Authored via `rulesFromFile("./rules/invoice.ts")`. The CLI ships raw source
and diffs source, never the compiled artifact, so a compiler change does not
read as a rule change; the server compiles on save and rejects a rule that
does not compile at apply time, while the author is still there.

Known gaps, documented in place: soft-delete, merge and unmerge still bypass
the seam, and a create cannot escalate (there is no row to hold fields against).
EOF

  row.deny(`cannot move ${from} -> ${to}`)
```

```

After — all four cases green, and the escalate case now runs past `queue()` into `applyEntityFieldChangeProposal` and asserts the metadata commits:

```

✓ defers the WHOLE write once a human owns `status`, instead of denying it
✓ defers the whole write when a RULE escalates, carrying the rule's own reason
✓ still DENIES outright when nothing was held and the caller's own proposal is illegal
```

**The approval-hold fix.** The root cause was not validation being too strict — it was that an approval hold splits a write and commits half of it, which was already wrong before rules existed. New invariant: *an approval hold may not manufacture an illegal state.* When the residual fails validation and fields were held, nothing commits and the entire proposal defers as one approval unit. `escalate` routes the same way. content.text:
Confirmed — the only hits are unrelated prose in other subsystems. There is **no transitions concept in the product**. The schema gained exactly two text columns.

## What Lobu ships

Four things, none of which know what a state machine is:

1. **Two columns** — `entity_types.rules_source` (what you wrote) and `rules_compiled` (the build output)
2. **A way to point at a file** — `rulesFromFile('./rules/invoice.ts')` in your config
3. **Compile on save** — `lobu apply` sends raw source, the server compiles it and rejects it if it doesn't build
4. **Execution at the write seam** — every entity write runs it, with six primitives: `committed`, `patch`, `next`, `op`, `changed()`, `deny()` / `escalate()`

That's the whole first-party surface. Lobu sees a function that either says nothing, calls `deny`, or calls `escalate`.

## What lives in your project

Everything about *invoices*. In your repo, your git, your PR review:

```js
// rules/invoice.ts — yours, not ours
const ALLOWED = { draft: ['issued'], issued: ['posted'], posted: [] }

export default (row) => {
  if (row.op === 'create' && row.next.status !== 'draft')
    row.deny('an invoice is created in draft')

  if (row.changed('status') && !(ALLOWED[row.committed.status] ?? []).includes(row.next.status))
    row.deny(`cannot move ${row.committed.status} -> ${row.next.status}`)

  if (row.next.status === 'posted' && !row.next.einvoice_uuid)
    row.deny('posting requires an e-invoice UUID')

  if (row.next.amount > 50000)
    row.escalate(['amount'], 'over the 50k limit')
}
```

The state names, the transition table, the frozen states, the threshold — none of that is a Lobu concept. `ALLOWED` is just a JS object in your file. If you'd rather express the lifecycle as nested ifs, or a lookup keyed on two fields, or something that isn't a state machine at all, nothing stops you.

Note the last two lines: "posting requires a UUID" and a 50k threshold aren't transitions at all. A DSL couldn't have expressed them. That's the argument for your call — one mechanism covers both, where first-party transitions would have covered a subset and still needed rules alongside.

## What you get from the platform side

Not nothing, and it's the part worth paying for:

- **It binds every writer.** Agent, API, connector sync, a human in the UI — all converge on the same physical writer, so the rule can't be routed around. Creates included, which is what the branded-type work closed.
- **It runs inside the write transaction**, under the row lock, so there's no window where an illegal state exists.
- **Fail-closed by default.** Crash, timeout, or a module that doesn't export a function all deny.
- **Isolated and bounded** — separate V8 isolate, 2s per batch, no SDK, no network, no DB.
- **`escalate` reaches your existing approval flow**, so a rule can send something to a human rather than only rejecting it.

## The one thing it costs

Because your state machine is code, Lobu can't *read* it. Owletto can't render "what can this invoice do next", and the agent's prompt can't be told the legal moves in advance — it finds out by being denied. That's the tradeoff you took, and I think correctly: it's a UI/prompt problem, not an enforcement gap, and it doesn't justify a second enforcement mechanism to solve.

Worth an issue on its own if the dead-button behavior bothers you later.

---

Review is still running on the fixed SHA; I'll report the verdict when it lands rather than guess at it.

content.text:
Two things confirmed: a rule gets **no SDK at all** (no DB, no network, no side effects), and the evaluator already takes **N independent `(committed, patch)` pairs and returns N verdicts**. That changes the answer.

I conflated three different things. Separating them:

**1. Reading the source — already possible.** `rules_source` is a plain text column holding exactly what the author wrote. You can render it on the entity-type page today. Nothing is hidden.

**2. Statically deriving structure — genuinely not possible.** You can't parse arbitrary JS and extract "the states are draft/issued/posted and `issued` leads to `posted`." `ALLOWED` could be built from a loop, a lookup, an import. That's the real limitation, and it's inherent to code-over-DSL.

**3. Answering "what can this row do next" — possible, and I was wrong to say otherwise.**

You don't need to *understand* the rule to answer that. You can **ask it**. The evaluator takes candidate `(committed, patch)` pairs and returns a verdict for each, and a rule is pure — no SDK, no DB, no network, nothing to roll back. So you can run it speculatively against a row that isn't being written:

```
committed = the invoice as it stands
candidates = [{status:'draft'}, {status:'issued'}, {status:'posted'}]
→ one isolate call → [deny, deny, allow]
```

That's the legal-moves list. One batch, ~2ms, all candidates in a single isolate — the batch shape that exists for syncs happens to be exactly the shape a preview needs.

And you already have the candidate set: `metadata_schema.properties.status.enum` is declared on the entity type. Enum values × dry-run = the buttons to enable. Same trick gives the agent prompt "legal moves from here" instead of letting it guess and get denied.

So the honest cost is narrower than I said: **you lose static introspection, not the ability to answer the question.** The UI can't draw a state-machine diagram without executing anything, but it can absolutely gray out the illegal buttons — which is the dead-403-button problem, and it's solvable.

To be clear about what's actually true right now: none of that preview path is built. There's no endpoint, and `runEntityRules` is only called from the write seam. But it's a read-only caller over an existing pure, batch-shaped evaluator — a genuinely small addition, not a redesign.

Worth its own issue after this merges. It'd be the piece that makes rules visible to the UI without giving up the single enforcement mechanism you chose.

This session continued a long design/implementation conversation about write-time entity policy in Lobu, on worktree `/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/.claude/worktrees/entity-transitions` (branch `feat/entity-transitions`).

User requests chronologically:

1. **(carried over) "yes do those as well"** — approve all three: `entity_types` rules columns, deleting the `x-transitions` DSL, and branding `EntityRowInsert`.
2. **"fix the issue properly go do next steps in the same PR"** — fix the approval-hold bug properly (not a workaround), and do the next steps I had listed (escalate wiring, apply path) in the same PR rather than splitting.
3. **"explain approval or escalate what's the difference"** — conceptual explanation request.
4. **"not doing the entity transition stuff right"** — pushback on the approach.
5. **"can you explain? this transitions our app doesn't know i gues right, the rules read it?"** — clarifying question in response to my AskUserQuestion about declarative transitions (no option selected).
6. **"i don't understand, doesnt rules cover the transcitions stuff already"** — challenge to my proposal to add a declarative transitions layer.

8. **"what do you mean lobu can't read it? you mean we can't render in the ui?"** — asking me to clarify an overstated limitation (CURRENT, unanswered).

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

- **Branded types as structural enforcement**: `declare const validatedBrand: unique symbol`; no public constructor, so bypass is a compile error. Shared by `ValidatedEntityRowPatch` and `ValidatedEntityRowInsert`.
- **Deny-only verbs**: `deny(reason)`, `escalate(fields, reason)`. No `allow` — a rule can only NARROW the lattice.
- **Two-tier split**: `runMutationGate` = PERMISSION ("may this principal write this field", keyed on principalKind/ownership); `validateEntityRowPatch` = VALIDATION ("is the resulting state legal", no principal).
- **Batch-shaped isolate execution**: one isolate per (type, batch), not per row.
- **Two-pass compile**: `runScript` re-esbuilds its `source`, so stored artifacts must be IIFE + one ESM runner.
- **Guest-side control flow**: `deny`/`escalate` need zero `ivm.Reference` bridges.
- **"An approval hold may not manufacture an illegal state"** — the core invariant of the fix.
- **`changed()` must compare VALUES, not key presence** — because the seam passes the fully MERGED value set.
- **Rules are pure** — `noSdk` stub, no network/DB/fs, in an isolated-vm isolate. This makes speculative dry-run execution safe.
- `REVIEWER_CLI` has only TWO quota pools (pi is codex-backed); model via `CLAUDE_REVIEW_MODEL`.

### `db/migrations/20260817210000_entity_type_write_rules.sql` (NEW)

### `packages/server/src/authz/entity-rule-executor.ts` (heavily rewritten)

```ts
const RULE_BATCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_000;
export const MAX_RULE_BATCH = 1_000;   // was 2_000; changed by measurement

const RULE_RUNNER = `
const __lobuRule = __lobuRuleModule.default;
const __lobuNorm = (v) => (v === undefined ? null : v);
const __lobuDiffers = (a, b) =>
  JSON.stringify(__lobuNorm(a)) !== JSON.stringify(__lobuNorm(b));
export default async (ctx) => {
  if (typeof __lobuRule !== "function") {
    throw new Error("entity rule must export default a function");
  }
  const verdicts = [];
  for (const row of ctx.rows) {
    let verdict = { outcome: "allow" };
    const next = { ...row.committed, ...row.patch };
    const api = {
      committed: row.committed,
      patch: row.patch,
      next,
      op: ctx.op,
      changed: (f) => __lobuDiffers(row.committed[f], next[f]),
      deny: (reason) => { const err = new Error(String(reason)); err.__lobuDeny = true; throw err; },
      escalate: (fields, reason) => { verdict = { outcome: "escalate", fields: Array.isArray(fields) ? fields : [fields], reason: String(reason) }; },
    };
    try { await __lobuRule(api); }
    catch (err) { if (err && err.__lobuDeny) verdict = { outcome: "deny", reason: err.message }; else throw err; }
    verdicts.push(verdict);
  }
  return verdicts;
};`;

export async function compileEntityRule(source: string): Promise<string> {
  const { compiledCode } = await compileSource(source, {
    tmpPrefix: ".entity-rule-compile-",
    label: "EntityRuleCompiler",
    buildOptions: { format: "iife", globalName: "__lobuRuleModule", target: "esnext", platform: "node", external: [] },
  });
  return `${compiledCode}\n${RULE_RUNNER}`;
}

export async function runEntityRules(batch: EntityRuleBatch): Promise<EntityRuleVerdict[]>
```

- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout.
- **Stage by explicit path** (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`).

- Do NOT add backwards-compatibility shims, deprecated annotations, or fallback aliases; no `@deprecated` tags — just delete the old thing.

The user asked, immediately before the summary request: **"what do you mean lobu can't read it? you mean we can't render in the ui?"**

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- frontend-typescript-tailwind: Use this agent when you need to develop frontend applications or components using TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui. This includes creating React components, implementing UI designs, setting up frontend projects, refactoring existing frontend code to follow best practices, or solving frontend-specific issues. The agent specializes in modern frontend development patterns and component-based architecture.

Examples:
- <example>
  Context: The user needs to create a new React component with TypeScript and Tailwind.
  user: "Create a card component that displays user information"
  assistant: "I'll use the frontend-typescript-tailwind agent to create a properly typed React component with Tailwind styling following best practices."
  <commentary>
  Since the user is asking for frontend component creation, use the frontend-typescript-tailwind agent to ensure TypeScript types, Tailwind classes, and shadcn/ui patterns are properly implemented.
  </commentary>
</example>
- <example>
  Context: The user wants to refactor existing frontend code.
  user: "Can you review and improve this dashboard component to use better TypeScript types and Tailwind conventions?"
  assistant: "I'll use the frontend-typescript-tailwind agent to analyze and refactor your dashboard component following TypeScript and Tailwind best practices."
  <commentary>
  The user is asking for frontend code improvement, so the frontend-typescript-tailwind agent should be used to ensure proper typing and styling conventions.
  </commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

## claude.ai PostHog
# PostHog `exec` covers

action|agent-feedback|alert|annotation|apm|approval|batch-export|cdp-function|channel|cohorts|comment|conversations|dashboard|data-warehouse|docs-search|early-access-feature|endpoint|error-tracking|event-definition|execute-sql|experiment|experiment-activity|experiment-archive|experiment-calculate|experiment-copy|experiment-duplicate|experiment-end|experiment-freeze|experiment-launch|experiment-metrics|experiment-pause|experiment-prompt|experiment-reset|experiment-results|experiment-resume|experiment-saved|experiment-ship|experiment-stats|experiment-timeseries|experiment-unarchive|experiment-unfreeze|external-data-schemas|external-data-sources|external-data-sync|feature-flag|file-download-batch|generate-app-url|health-issues|heatmaps|inbox|insight|integration|llm-total-costs|llma-clustering|llma-evaluation|llma-parser|llma-personal|llma-prompt|llma-review|llma-score|llma-skill|llma-summarization|llma-tagger|llma-trace|logs|marketing-analytics|mcp|notebooks|opt-outs|org-member|organization|path-cleaning-rules|persons|project|proxy|query|read-data-schema|reminder|role|saved-query-column|scheduled-changes|scout|session-recording|signals-scout|skill|sql-variables|subscriptions|survey|switch|usage-metrics|user|view|vision|warehouse|web-analytics-weekly|workflows|workflows-archive|workflows-blast|workflows-discard|workflows-enable|workflows-global|workflows-logs|workflows-patch|workflows-publish|workflows-restore|workflows-schedule|workflows-show|workflows-stats|workflows-test

# Tools

exec – run any PostHog command; its `command` description has the syntax.

Prioritize skills over tools.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_app_state({ include_schema: true, include_canvas_design: true, include_scripts_and_shaders: false }) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. All three flags are required. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

Tools: get_app_state, get_guidelines, execute, get_screenshot, export_nodes, export_html.
Also: browser.

<!-- Per-repo agent rules loaded into every Claude Code session in this repo. Inlines AGENTS.md (shared project rules) first, then layers local-only notes below. User memory entries live under ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/. Don't add anything here unless it's only relevant to Claude agent specific. If other harnesses like pi or codex need it, modify AGENTS.md -->

@AGENTS.md

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- `core` types/utils · `plugin-api` plugin contracts · `plugin-host` plugin composition · `server` gateway + embedded runtime · `agent-worker` agent execution · `connectors` built-in connectors · `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Read the nearest package `AGENTS.md` before editing that package; grep `docs/GOTCHAS.md` when something looks inexplicable.

## Unrecoverable — never do these
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout — other sessions share it. For a pure submodule-pointer bump, `make bump SUBMODULE=packages/owletto` is the lightweight isolated-worktree exception; it also posts the required statuses.
- **Stage by explicit path** (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`). A commit is a snapshot, so a stale file copy left by earlier work in the same worktree silently reverts merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal your intended file list; extras = stop.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone or supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are usually real signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI** — it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work. Rebase locally against `origin/main`; submodule-pointer branches `git merge` instead (`docs/GOTCHAS.md`).
- **Two writing agents must never share a worktree** — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work. Every subagent with Edit/Write/Bash gets its own through `make task-setup` (only task-setup does submodule pinning, `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation); only read-only agents share the parent.
- **Never add a table or change DB design, API surface, or SDK surface** without surfacing the proposal and receiving confirmation first.
- **Never auto-submit an interactive browser draft, in any package.** Drafts are page-activated: persist the operation, notify normally, and let the extension activate the run only when the user visits a pending URL in a user-owned tab. Only scrape-owned scratch tabs may be opened and closed automatically. Server, connector, and Owletto code all obey this (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`).

## Facts you cannot derive
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** A resync supersedes the row and mints a new id for the same source item, so cross-sync identity and dedupe must key on the connector's `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over `events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, … on a user-facing read path: history grows, the answer doesn't. Materialize at write time, read back by index, backfill in a migration. Bounded config tables (`connections`, `automations`, `agent_users`) are fine.
- **Shared state must be Postgres-mediated.** An in-memory Map or singleton is invisible to other replicas — correct in dev, broken in prod.
- **Workers never receive real credentials** — placeholders or proxied access only. The exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived leases (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one.
- **Automation is the product, API, and storage vocabulary.** Use it consistently in public contracts and internal identifiers; `make pre-pr-remote` rejects retired product and engine terminology.
- **`make review` is the semantic review gate, not CI.** It runs no typecheck, knip, or tests; a verdict or safe-class skip is not evidence CI will pass.
- **Depot serializes org-wide.** A newer dispatch silently cancels a peer session's running gate, and `gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch. Check `pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"` before dispatching.
- Default to static `import`; a new production dynamic import needs measured justification plus a call-site rationale comment. Tests may import dynamically after mocks; two Node-version gates are grandfathered (playbook).

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce red → fix → prove green, and paste both outputs in the PR. Cannot reproduce = report the dead end; never ship a speculative fix.
3. Iterate on focused tests: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. `make pre-pr-remote-fast` gives interim breadth and never substitutes for the final gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff, then re-read what it touched. Safe-class changes self-skip before selecting an LLM. Otherwise it runs BEFORE the first `make review` — never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop, since each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
5. Stage by explicit path, then `make pre-pr-remote`; it fails closed on unstaged or untracked changes. Reviewed workflow/action changes need `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1`.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD; it posts the required `pi-review` status. Narrow path/content-gated safe classes skip the cross-harness review; this includes pure `packages/owletto` pointer bumps and exact `model:` literal swaps, but not mixed runtime and source changes. The submodule's own repo owns its content review.
9. `make ui-review`. Non-Owletto changes and complete, forward-only Owletto pointer diffs confined to `deploy/` pass as not applicable; other pointer changes need exact hosted proof (`ARTIFACT=<url>`; see the playbook).
10. `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin` once green — never `--admin` past a check that has not reported. Lobu's required `integration` fan-in is absent from `gh pr checks` until it starts, not pending, so diff against the branch-protection list (playbook).
11. Prod-visible surface? Verify live after rollout: gate on the **squash commit**, not your branch head, keeping the argument order `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"`. Record the result.

## How to work
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create; no new `*.md` unless asked.
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- **Evidence, not assertion.** Never report done off a green typecheck — boot it, exercise every branch you touched, and clean up test data; if "compiles" is all you ran, say so. Show `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`, including for a dispatched agent's work.
- **Absence needs `origin/main`:** `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main`. A working-tree grep proves nothing, and the fetch is load-bearing.
- Deleting code needs structural evidence — a dangling import, a completed migration, a superseded implementation. Low prod usage is not evidence, and docs and help text are load-bearing.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other occurrence and fix in one pass. A diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one.
- One branch = one concern. Never `git stash`; use WIP commits.
- Prefer `bun`, never npm/yarn/pnpm. Before adding an env var, grep for the one already read, and do not rename existing vars unasked.
- Block only on irreversible or destructive actions and decisions genuinely the user's; otherwise take the recommended option and flag it in your summary.
- Never poll in the foreground — run long waits in the background and act on the notification. Poll delegated CLIs at most once every 4.5 minutes unless they finish or request input.

<!-- Rules for agents (Claude, pi, codex); CLAUDE.md inlines this into every session. Keep it to facts an agent cannot derive and boundaries it must not cross. Reasoning and recipes go in docs/AGENT_PLAYBOOK.md, package specifics in the nearest package AGENTS.md. -->

## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- `core` types/utils · `plugin-api` plugin contracts · `plugin-host` plugin composition · `server` gateway + embedded runtime · `agent-worker` agent execution · `connectors` built-in connectors · `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Read the nearest package `AGENTS.md` before editing that package; grep `docs/GOTCHAS.md` when something looks inexplicable.

## Unrecoverable — never do these
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout — other sessions share it. For a pure submodule-pointer bump, `make bump SUBMODULE=packages/owletto` is the lightweight isolated-worktree exception; it also posts the required statuses.
- **Stage by explicit path** (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`). A commit is a snapshot, so a stale file copy left by earlier work in the same worktree silently reverts merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal your intended file list; extras = stop.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone or supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are usually real signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI** — it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work. Rebase locally against `origin/main`; submodule-pointer branches `git merge` instead (`docs/GOTCHAS.md`).
- **Two writing agents must never share a worktree** — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work. Every subagent with Edit/Write/Bash gets its own through `make task-setup` (only task-setup does submodule pinning, `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation); only read-only agents share the parent.
- **Never add a table or change DB design, API surface, or SDK surface** without surfacing the proposal and receiving confirmation first.
- **Never auto-submit an interactive browser draft, in any package.** Drafts are page-activated: persist the operation, notify normally, and let the extension activate the run only when the user visits a pending URL in a user-owned tab. Only scrape-owned scratch tabs may be opened and closed automatically. Server, connector, and Owletto code all obey this (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`).

## Facts you cannot derive
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** A resync supersedes the row and mints a new id for the same source item, so cross-sync identity and dedupe must key on the connector's `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over `events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, … on a user-facing read path: history grows, the answer doesn't. Materialize at write time, read back by index, backfill in a migration. Bounded config tables (`connections`, `automations`, `agent_users`) are fine.
- **Shared state must be Postgres-mediated.** An in-memory Map or singleton is invisible to other replicas — correct in dev, broken in prod.
- **Workers never receive real credentials** — placeholders or proxied access only. The exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived leases (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one.
- **Automation is the product, API, and storage vocabulary.** Use it consistently in public contracts and internal identifiers; `make pre-pr-remote` rejects retired product and engine terminology.
- **`make review` is the semantic review gate, not CI.** It runs no typecheck, knip, or tests; a verdict or safe-class skip is not evidence CI will pass.
- **Depot serializes org-wide.** A newer dispatch silently cancels a peer session's running gate, and `gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch. Check `pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"` before dispatching.
- Default to static `import`; a new production dynamic import needs measured justification plus a call-site rationale comment. Tests may import dynamically after mocks; two Node-version gates are grandfathered (playbook).

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce red → fix → prove green, and paste both outputs in the PR. Cannot reproduce = report the dead end; never ship a speculative fix.
3. Iterate on focused tests: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. `make pre-pr-remote-fast` gives interim breadth and never substitutes for the final gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff, then re-read what it touched. Safe-class changes self-skip before selecting an LLM. Otherwise it runs BEFORE the first `make review` — never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop, since each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
5. Stage by explicit path, then `make pre-pr-remote`; it fails closed on unstaged or untracked changes. Reviewed workflow/action changes need `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1`.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD; it posts the required `pi-review` status. Narrow path/content-gated safe classes skip the cross-harness review; this includes pure `packages/owletto` pointer bumps and exact `model:` literal swaps, but not mixed runtime and source changes. The submodule's own repo owns its content review.
9. `make ui-review`. Non-Owletto changes and complete, forward-only Owletto pointer diffs confined to `deploy/` pass as not applicable; other pointer changes need exact hosted proof (`ARTIFACT=<url>`; see the playbook).
10. `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin` once green — never `--admin` past a check that has not reported. Lobu's required `integration` fan-in is absent from `gh pr checks` until it starts, not pending, so diff against the branch-protection list (playbook).
11. Prod-visible surface? Verify live after rollout: gate on the **squash commit**, not your branch head, keeping the argument order `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"`. Record the result.

- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create; no new `*.md` unless asked.
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.

- One branch = one concern. Never `git stash`; use WIP commits.
- Prefer `bun`, never npm/yarn/pnpm. Before adding an env var, grep for the one already read, and do not rename existing vars unasked.

content.text:
Here's the whole thing end to end, then the gaps — including one I think is still live.

## How a rule gets there

You write a plain TS file in your own project and point at it from your config:

```ts
entities: [{ slug: "invoice", rules: rulesFromFile("./rules/invoice.ts") }]
```

`lobu apply` reads that file (`desired-state.ts`, capped at 32KB), sends the **source** to the server, and the server compiles it once (`manage_entity_schema.ts` → `compileEntityRule`) and stores both halves on the entity type: `rules_source` (what you wrote, for diffing and display) and `rules_compiled` (the artifact the write path runs). Apply diffs on source only, so a recompile alone never shows as drift.

The compile is a two-step wrap that matters more than it looks: your module is built as an **IIFE** bound to a global, and a small ESM runner is appended. That's because `runScript` re-esbuilds whatever it's handed — concatenating a CJS module with the runner would put two module formats in one file, your `export default` would resolve against the wrapper, and every write would fail closed while looking like working enforcement.

## What happens on a write

Inside `updateEntity`, one transaction, in this order:

```
sql.begin                              :979
  SELECT … FOR UPDATE   ← row lock     :986
  runMutationGate       ← PERMISSION   :1062
  computeFieldMerge     ← strips held  :1098
  validateEntityRowPatch← YOUR RULE    :1166
  patchEntityRows       ← commit
```

Two things fall out of that ordering. The lock is taken *before* the rule runs, so same-row invariants are already serialized — you get that for free, no new machinery. And the rule sees the **effective** patch, not what the caller asked for: the permission gate has already stripped fields the caller may not write.

The split between those two stages is the design's spine. `runMutationGate` answers *"may this principal write this field"* — it knows about agents vs humans and field ownership. Your rule answers *"is the resulting state legal"* — it has no principal in it at all. That's why the test at `entity-row-validation.test.ts:198` asserts an **owner** is denied editing a frozen invoice. Being an admin doesn't make a posted invoice mutable.

Your rule gets `committed`, `patch`, `next`, `op`, and `changed(field)`, and can call `deny(reason)` or `escalate(fields, reason)`. There's no `allow` — a rule can only narrow. `changed()` compares **values**, not key presence, which was a real bug I shipped and had to fix: the seam hands you the fully merged metadata, so `hasOwnProperty` is true for every key on every write, and a rule guarding `status` was denying edits to `amount`.

Execution is one isolate per (type, batch), not per row — per-row tops out around 300/sec, or ~21s for a 5,000-row sync. Batched, 5,000 rows is ~29.7ms. Batches cap at 1,000 because cost grows faster than linearly. The rule gets **no SDK** — no DB, no network, no filesystem. Pure function.

## The three outcomes

**deny** → the write throws, nothing commits.

**escalate** → the write becomes an approval card carrying the *whole* proposal, not the fragment. When a human approves it, the apply path re-runs the rule with `onEscalate: "approved"`, which treats escalate as allow. That flag is the entire reason approval works — without it, approving re-runs the rule, it escalates again, and the card can never be cleared. A `deny` still throws in approved mode: a human can't bless an illegal state.

**allow** → commits.

The subtle case the branch exists to fix: an agent proposes a legal `issued → posted` plus the field that move unlocks, the gate strips `status` because a human owns it, and what's left is a naked field edit in a frozen state — illegal. The agent proposed something legal; the *split* made it illegal. So when validation fails and fields were held, nothing commits and the entire proposal defers as one unit.

---

## Gaps

**Merge and unmerge bypass completely.** `entity-merge.ts:345` and `:360` write `UPDATE entities SET deleted_at = …` as raw SQL, never through `patchEntityRows`. Worse than the other gaps: it carries no `unvalidated*` marker, so it doesn't show up when you grep for exemptions. A rule that freezes a posted invoice does not stop that invoice being merged away.

**Soft-delete is exempt, honestly.** `entity-management.ts:1678` documents why — that path is a single pool-level statement, not a transaction, so a check there could be overtaken between read and write. A racy check that looks like enforcement is worse than an admitted hole. Closing it needs a transaction boundary.

**Three deliberate platform exemptions**, all marked: membership deprovisioning (`member-entity.ts:267` — removing a user must never be blockable by a tenant rule), automation canvases, eval cases. Those read as correct.

**Creates can't escalate.** `validateEntityRowInsert` throws an explicit error on escalate, because there's no row to hold fields against and no create-approval surface. Deny works on creates; escalate doesn't.

**A crashed rule may produce an unclearable card — I have not verified this.** Reading `entity-management.ts:1174`, the `else if (heldFields.length > 0)` branch catches *any* validation error when a field was held, and a rule that crashes or times out fails closed as a `deny`. So a buggy rule plus any held field looks like it becomes an approval card — and at apply time a deny still throws, so that card would never clear. Same shape as the blocker I just fixed. This is reasoned from the code, not reproduced; I'd rather not touch the tree while the gate is running, so I'll test it when that reports.

**The brand is compile-time only.** It makes bypass a type error in production code, but `packages/server/tsconfig.json` excludes `__tests__`, so tests can still write unbranded — and one does.

**No actor, no cross-row rules.** Deliberate. Each row is judged independently, so "no more than 5 open invoices per customer" isn't expressible, and "only finance can post" belongs to the gate, not here.

**Nothing renders it.** `rules_source` is stored and never displayed. No preview endpoint either — which is the dry-run idea from earlier, and cheap given the evaluator is already pure and batch-shaped.

**Changing a rule doesn't revalidate existing rows.** Tighten a rule and rows already violating it stay violating until someone writes to them. There's no backfill or report.

**The CLI path has never actually run.** Types and unit tests only — no real `lobu apply` with a `rulesFromFile` config against a live server. That's the lowest-confidence surface in the PR.

**Confidence: 88 on the runtime description** — I read every site cited above rather than recalling it, and the write path is covered by 185 passing authz tests. **60 on the crashed-rule gap** — reasoned from code, not reproduced. **65 on the CLI** — unchanged, untested end to end.

**Next:** when the Depot gate reports, (1) write the crashed-rule test and either close it or document it, (2) do the real `lobu apply`, (3) decide whether merge/unmerge gets an explicit documented exemption in this PR or a tracked follow-up — right now it's silent, which is the part I'd least want to discover later.
