---

PR #2842. `onEscalate: "defer" | "approved"` no longer exists anywhere.

## Why the mode flag was wrong

`if (onEscalate === "approved") continue` waived **every** escalate. Its own
comment claimed "a human already said yes to this exact proposal" — the code did
not check that. If the rule was redeployed or the row moved between propose and
apply, a brand-new escalation over a field nobody reviewed was silently blessed.
A comment asserting a property the code lacks is worse than no comment.

## The shape now

- `validateEntityRowPatch` / `validateEntityRowInsert` take
  `approvedFields?: readonly string[]`.
- An escalate is waived only when `verdict.fields.every(f => approvedFields.includes(f))`.
  A new escalation still needs its own card. A `deny` throws regardless.
- The grant rides on the proposal: **`escalated_fields` in `runs.action_input`**,
  which already persists. **No new table, no migration.**

I first designed a branded `ApprovalGrant` type for this and dropped it — the
proposal row already IS the un-fabricatable record. Reading fields off it is
equivalent to a brand with none of the machinery.

## What this does NOT fix

A brand makes bypass a compile error (`ValidatedEntityRowPatch`). `approvedFields`
is optional, so a careless apply path can still call the validator without it and
silently get defer semantics — which is exactly how site 2 of
[[reference_approval_verdict_class_has_five_sites]] happened. Closing that needs
a required parameter on the apply functions plus a scoped `no-restricted-imports`
so the approval module cannot reach the ungranted validator. Not built.

## Also landed

A rule denial previously left **no trace at all** — no event, no audit row. There
is now one structured `logger.info` on the deny path (`module: "entity-rules"`).
A real audit row needs a table and sign-off; see
[[reference_entity_audit_trail_is_inverted]].

Related: [[reference_entity_write_validation_seam_state]]

---
name: reference_approval_verdict_class_has_five_sites
description: "Every place a rule verdict meets an approval is the SAME bug class — five instances found one at a time; use the residual x full-proposal matrix, not a grep"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: d4dd595f-7813-471b-8289-6923b28b89fa
  modified: 2026-08-18T00:04:51.047Z
---

PR #2842, 2026-08-17/18. I declared this class closed **four times** and was
wrong each time. Two of the five were found by an independent reviewer, in code
I had already reviewed twice.

## The class

A rule's `escalate` becomes an approval card. Applying that card **re-runs the
rule**. So every site where a verdict meets an approval must say "this was
already approved" — and must say it about the *right* fields. Miss it and the
card can never clear: approving re-escalates, the write throws, forever.

The five sites:

1. `applyEntityFieldChangeProposal` metadata branch (`mergeEntityFields`)
2. `applyEntityFieldChangeProposal` attribute branch (`validateEntityRowPatch`)
3. `applyEntityChangeProposal` create branch (`createEntity`)
4. `updateEntity` defer branch — deferred without checking the FULL proposal, so
   an illegal proposal + a held field minted an unclearable card
5. `updateEntity` escalate branch — same gap as 4, one branch over

## Grepping does not find these

Sites 1-3 are greppable (`onEscalate` call sites). **4 and 5 are not** — they are
decisions about whether to create a card at all, in a `catch` block. What finds
them is enumerating the state space:

| residual verdict | full-proposal verdict | correct behavior |
|---|---|---|
| deny | allow | defer — the split rescue |
| deny | deny | throw, in the CALLER'S terms |
| deny | escalate | defer, record the **full** proposal's fields |
| escalate | deny | throw |
| escalate | allow | defer; the replay allows anyway |
| escalate | escalate | defer, prefer the **full** proposal's fields |

The residual is what remains after a permission hold strips human-owned fields.
The card replays the **full** proposal, so the full proposal's verdict is what
governs — taking fields from the caught (residual) error was instance 5.

## How to apply

- **Enumerate the matrix before claiming a class is closed.** "I grepped every
  call site" is not the same claim and was false here twice.
- A `catch` block that decides between throw and defer is part of the class even
  though it contains no call to the thing you grepped for.
- State coverage as a checkable claim ("6 cells, 4 tested, 2 traced"), never as
  "the class is closed."

Related: [[reference_entity_approval_grant_is_scoped_to_reviewed_fields]],
[[reference_entity_write_validation_seam_state]],
[[feedback_generalize_fix_then_grep_class]]

# Lobu — scope brief for the #2842 / write-rules session

You are building the per-write rule layer. One scope decision to hold throughout:

## What you are building (and why it is not the policy authority)
This is the **physics backstop**, not the place orgs express transitions or
authorization ("who may post", "which moves exist"). That lives in a separate
operations layer (Automations declare a guarded `transition`, `who`, `approval`).
Your rules validate the resulting STATE at the write seam, for agents AND bulk.

Keep: create-path closure, `onEscalate` scoped to the reviewed fields (a NEW
escalation at apply time is not waved through), deny observability, cost bounds,
branded `ValidatedEntityRowPatch`. All of that stays.

## Demote / stop, so it can ship as backstop not authority
- Transition tables and "who may X" are NOT your job. A rule may say "`posted`
  requires `einvoice_uuid`" (state), but not own "only accountant posts" (that is
  the operation's `who`, enforced at the op, and an actor check, not a rule bundle).
- Do not let the rule bundle grow into the org's policy DSL. That was killed once
  (`x-transitions`) — a second mechanism doing the same enforcement job is the drift.
- `delete` is absent from `op` deliberately. Merge/delete/link are exemptions the
  operations layer guards. Don't widen `op` to chase ERP here; note it and move on.

## Ship shape
Land clean and green (typecheck + regen first, then `pi-review` with
bug_free>=80 / 0 blockers — do not merge past a red reviewer like #2817).
Tests: approved field applies; a DIFFERENT field's escalation at apply time is
denied (mutation-test the security of this one); the create-path case.

## Call the scope in your summary
End with a one-line statement of the layer you own so it is never read back as
"the policy surface": *"rules validate state at the write seam; transitions and
who-may are operations-layer concerns."*

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

<!-- Per-repo agent rules loaded into every Claude Code session in this repo. Inlines AGENTS.md (shared project rules) first, then layers local-only notes below. User memory entries live under ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/. Don't add anything here unless it's only relevant to Claude agent specific. @AGENTS.md

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- `core` types/utils · `plugin-api` plugin contracts · `plugin-host` plugin composition · `server` gateway + embedded runtime · `agent-worker` agent execution · `connectors` built-in connectors · `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Read the nearest package `AGENTS.md` before editing that package; grep `docs/GOTCHAS.md` when something looks inexplicable.

## Unrecoverable — never do these
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout — other sessions share it. For a pure submodule-pointer bump, `make bump SUBMODULE=packages/owletto` is the lightweight isolated-worktree exception; it also posts the required statuses.
- **Stage by explicit path** (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`). A commit is a snapshot, so a stale file copy left by earlier work in the same worktree silently reverts merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal your intended file list; extras = stop.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone or supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are usually real signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI** — it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work. Rebase locally against `origin/main`; submodule-pointer branches `git merge` instead (`docs/GOTCHAS.md`).
- **Two writing agents must never share a worktree** — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work. Every subagent with Edit/Write/Bash gets its own through `make task-setup` (only task-setup does submodule pinning, `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation); only read-only agents share the parent.
- **Never add a table or change DB design, API surface, or SDK surface** without surfacing the proposal and receiving confirmation first.
- **Never auto-submit an interactive browser draft, in any package.** Drafts are page-activated: persist the operation, notify normally, and let the extension activate the run only when the user visits a pending URL in a user-owned tab. Only scrape-owned scratch tabs may be opened and closed automatically. Server, connector, and Owletto code all obey this (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`).

## Facts you cannot derive
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** A resync supersedes the row and mints a new id for the same source item, so cross-sync identity and dedupe must key on the connector's `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over `events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, … on a user-facing read path: history grows, the answer doesn't. Materialize at write time, read back by index, backfill in a migration. Bounded config tables (`connections`, `automations`, `agent_users`) are fine.
- **Shared state must be Postgres-mediated.** An in-memory Map or singleton is invisible to other replicas — correct in dev, broken in prod.
- **Workers never receive real credentials** — placeholders or proxied access only. The exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived leases (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one.
- **Automation is the product, API, and storage vocabulary.** Use it consistently in public contracts and internal identifiers; `make pre-pr-remote` rejects retired product and engine terminology.
- **`make review` is the semantic review gate, not CI.** It runs no typecheck, knip, or tests; a verdict or safe-class skip is not evidence CI will pass.
- **Depot serializes org-wide.** A newer dispatch silently cancels a peer session's running gate, and `gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch. Check `pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"` before dispatching.
- Default to static `import`; a new production dynamic import needs measured justification plus a call-site rationale comment. Tests may import dynamically after mocks; two Node-version gates are grandfathered (playbook).

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce red → fix → prove green, and paste both outputs in the PR. Cannot reproduce = report the dead end; never ship a speculative fix.
3. Iterate on focused tests: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. `make pre-pr-remote-fast` gives interim breadth and never substitutes for the final gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff, then re-read what it touched. Safe-class changes self-skip before selecting an LLM. Otherwise it runs BEFORE the first `make review` — never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop, since each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
5. Stage by explicit path, then `make pre-pr-remote`; it fails closed on unstaged or untracked changes. Reviewed workflow/action changes need `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1`.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD; it posts the required `pi-review` status. Narrow path/content-gated safe classes skip the cross-harness review; this includes pure `packages/owletto` pointer bumps and exact `model:` literal swaps, but not mixed runtime and source changes. The submodule's own repo owns its content review.
9. `make ui-review`. Non-Owletto changes and complete, forward-only Owletto pointer diffs confined to `deploy/` pass as not applicable; other pointer changes need exact hosted proof (`ARTIFACT=<url>`; see the playbook).
10. `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin` once green — never `--admin` past a check that has not reported. Lobu's required `integration` fan-in is absent from `gh pr checks` until it starts, not pending, so diff against the branch-protection list (playbook).
11. Prod-visible surface? Verify live after rollout: gate on the **squash commit**, not your branch head, keeping the argument order `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"`. Record the result.

## How to work
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create; no new `*.md` unless asked.
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- **Evidence, not assertion.** Never report done off a green typecheck — boot it, exercise every branch you touched, and clean up test data; if "compiles" is all you ran, say so. Show `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`, including for a dispatched agent's work.
- **Absence needs `origin/main`:** `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main`. A working-tree grep proves nothing, and the fetch is load-bearing.
- Deleting code needs structural evidence — a dangling import, a completed migration, a superseded implementation. Low prod usage is not evidence, and docs and help text are load-bearing.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other occurrence and fix in one pass. A diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one.
- One branch = one concern. Never `git stash`; use WIP commits.
- Prefer `bun`, never npm/yarn/pnpm. Before adding an env var, grep for the one already read, and do not rename existing vars unasked.
- Block only on irreversible or destructive actions and decisions genuinely the user's; otherwise take the recommended option and flag it in your summary.
- Never poll in the foreground — run long waits in the background and act on the notification. Poll delegated CLIs at most once every 4.5 minutes unless they finish or request input.
- Prefer DOM reads over screenshots, the top context-bloat source. The paired Owletto extension drives the user's real logged-in browser; CDP is not required (`docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`).
- Slack link pasted → run `scripts/slack-thread-viewer.js "<link>"` first.
- `make dev-remote` runs the live app on remote compute (commit first; `make dev-remote-pause` when finished).

---
name: reference_pure_batch_rules_enable_a_speculative_dry_run
description: "Rules are PURE and the evaluator is BATCH-shaped, so 'what moves are legal from here' is answerable by dry-running candidates (~3ms/1000) — no static analysis, no separate transition table"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

I told the user "Lobu can't read the rules" (they are opaque JS, unlike the old
declarative `x-transitions`). That was an **overstatement** and it nearly cost us
a second declarative mechanism alongside the rules.

## Why the readback works

Two properties of the shipped design, together:

- **Rules are pure.** They get no SDK — no DB, no network, no fs, no clock. A
  rule cannot observe that it is being asked hypothetically, and running one has
  no side effects.
- **The evaluator is batch-shaped** (`MAX_RULE_BATCH`, one isolate per
  (type, batch), see [[reference_entity_rules_must_be_batch_shaped]]).

So to answer "which transitions are legal from this row", you don't parse the
rule — you **enumerate candidate next-states and run them all through one
isolate**, then keep the ones that don't `deny`. Measured cost is the batch
number: ~3.2ms for 1,000 candidates. A status enum has maybe six.

This is the same trick the write path already uses; nothing new is needed to
implement it beyond an endpoint. **Not built** — recorded because the argument
"we lost introspection when we deleted the DSL" keeps resurfacing and is wrong.

## What it does NOT give you

- The *reason* a move is unavailable only comes back if the rule denies with a
  message. Enumeration yields a legal set, not an explanation graph.
- It needs a candidate generator. For a bounded enum in `metadata_schema` that's
  free; for open-valued fields there is nothing to enumerate. So this answers
  "which state may I move to", not "what is this rule".
- A dry-run is not an authorization answer. `runMutationGate` (permission) is a
  separate seam from `validateEntityRowPatch` (validation); dry-running the
  latter says the STATE would be legal, not that this principal may write it.

Related: [[reference_entity_write_validation_seam_state]],
[[reference_run_script_recompiles_its_source]]

---
name: feedback_a_red_test_must_fail_for_the_reason_you_claim
description: "A red test proves nothing until you read WHY it failed — twice on #2842 my repro was red for an unrelated reason, so the 'fix' was never exercised"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

"Reproduce red → fix → prove green" is the repo rule. On PR #2842 I satisfied it
twice while testing nothing.

**Case 1 — red for the wrong reason.** My repro for the escalate branch used a
rule where the target state was also *frozen*. The residual hit the frozen
`deny` before it ever reached the escalate path. Red, then green after the fix —
but the fix was in a branch the test never entered. Caught only by mutation
testing (revert the fix; the test stayed green).

**Case 2 — the setup didn't set up.** The agent in my test proposed the same
`status` value the human already held, so no field was ever held back, so the
whole split-proposal scenario the test named never occurred. It failed on a
different assertion entirely.

**Why:** I was reading the pass/fail bit and not the failure message. Both
messages said plainly what had happened (`promise resolved "{ id: 5 }" instead
of rejecting`; a reason string naming the *other* rule).

**How to apply:**
- Read the failure TEXT of a new red test and state, in one sentence, that it
  matches the mechanism you are fixing. If it names a different rule, field, or
  error than your hypothesis, the repro is wrong — not close enough.
- Then mutation-test: revert the fix and confirm this specific test goes red
  again. That is the only proof it exercises the fix
  ([[feedback_mutation_test_new_tests]]).
- Design fixtures so exactly ONE mechanism can fire. A rule with two deny
  clauses cannot prove which one ran; I ended up needing a second, narrower rule
  (`ESCALATE_RESIDUAL_RULE`) whose only behavior was the branch under test.
- Same class as [[feedback_unit_fixtures_must_match_the_producer_shape]]: a test
  that never touches the seam is worse than no test, because it reports coverage.

Related: [[feedback_verify_the_surface_not_the_builder]]

---
name: feedback_approval_tests_must_read_the_persisted_card
description: "Approval-path tests that hand-build the proposal object pass even with the propose→persist→apply plumbing severed — assert against `runs.action_input` instead"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Every apply-path test in `packages/server` constructs the proposal inline and
passes it straight to `applyEntityChangeProposal`. That skips the half of the
flow that actually breaks: propose → persist onto the `runs` row → read back at
apply time. I could have deleted the code that writes `escalated_fields` onto
the proposal and the whole suite would have stayed green.

**How to apply:** when a test covers a two-phase (propose, then apply) flow,
at least one case must round-trip through storage:

```ts
const [queued] = await sql<{ action_input: unknown }[]>`
  SELECT action_input FROM runs
  WHERE organization_id = ${org.id} ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`;
const input = (typeof queued.action_input === "string"
  ? JSON.parse(queued.action_input) : queued.action_input) as { escalated_fields?: string[] };
expect(input.escalated_fields).toEqual(["amount"]);
```

Note the string-or-object dance: `action_input` comes back as either depending
on the driver, so the parse is load-bearing, not defensive noise.

**Why:** the bug class on #2842 lived precisely in the plumbing
([[reference_approval_verdict_class_has_five_sites]]) — what the card RECORDS
versus what the rule later re-derives. A hand-built fixture asserts my own
belief about the card's shape back to me.

Related: [[feedback_a_red_test_must_fail_for_the_reason_you_claim]],
[[feedback_verify_the_surface_not_the_builder]]

`updateEntity` now re-validates the **full proposal** (not just the residual)
whenever a permission hold held any field, via `fullProposalVerdict()` in
`packages/server/src/utils/entity-management.ts`. That one helper resolves all
three failure modes this memory described:

- legal-but-held → defers as one unit instead of denying
- illegal proposal → throws in the **caller's own terms**, not the residual's

- escalating proposal → the card records the FULL proposal's fields

file this memory cited was replaced by that suite.

**The mechanism still generalizes.** Any seam that validates a *reduced* version
of a write and reports the result as if it described the original will
misattribute. Merge/unmerge and soft-delete still do not go through this path —
see the KNOWN GAP note on `transitionEntityMergeRows`.
'''

Two claims in the body above are now stale:

1. **"escalate throws 'escalation is not wired yet'"** — gone. `escalate` is
   fully wired for **updates** (`updateEntity` catch → `deferEntityFieldChange`)
   AND for **creates** (`manage_entity.handleCreate` catch → `deferEntityCreate`).
   I had claimed creates could not escalate because "approval routing exists for
   updates only"; the user corrected me and the machinery
   (`buildCreateDeferral`, `proposeEntityCreate`, `applyEntityChangeProposal`'s
   create branch) already existed. A create that escalates leaves **zero rows**
   behind — there is no half-created state to reconcile.

2. **"merge writes raw SQL at entity-merge.ts:345,360"** — wrong; those lines
   write *relationship* rows. Entity writes during a merge go through
   `transitionEntityMergeRows`, one documented kernel. It is still unvalidated,
   but it is a single seam, not scattered SQL.

Also landed: the escalation grant is scoped
([[reference_entity_approval_grant_is_scoped_to_reviewed_fields]]),
denials log, and `MAX_RULE_BATCH = 1_000`.

Still bypassing the seam: **merge/unmerge and softDelete**. `op` deliberately

6:# turn -> connector -> automation -> client), THIS gate proves that EVERY `lobu`
7:# command/subcommand actually RUNS -- argv parses, the handler executes, and a
8:# representative invocation returns the documented success marker (or, for the

10:# crash/stack trace).
12:# It boots ONE local `lobu run` (embedded Postgres + a deterministic mock

name: reference_apply_breaks_on_underscore_entity_type_keys
description: "lobu apply is NOT idempotent for entity-type keys containing an underscore — the server slugifies _ to - on create but the CLI diffs on the raw key, so the second apply halts"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: f0b3eac6-8946-4c9e-bbf8-24d856a5592a
  modified: 2026-08-14T12:03:06.628Z
---

`manage_entity_schema.ts:460` normalizes on create:

```ts
const slug = args.slug.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9-]/g, '-');
```

`_` is not in `[a-z0-9-]`, so key `stock_movement` is **stored as `stock-movement`**.
But the CLI sends the key verbatim (`map-config.ts:485` → `slug: entity.key`) and
builds its remote-diff map on the stored slug (`apply-cmd.ts:363`). The desired
slug therefore never matches its own row.

**Consequence — the second `apply` of the same unchanged config fails:**

```
+ entity-type stock_movement          <- plans a CREATE for a row that exists
...
error: POST /api/local-install/manage_entity_schema failed:
       Entity type 'stock_movement' not found
error: Apply halted on first failure.
```

The error message is misleading: the row exists, under the hyphenated slug.
Relationship-type keys are NOT affected — `quote_customer` round-trips fine.
Only entity-type keys are slugified.

**Workaround:** write entity-type keys already hyphenated (`key: "stock-movement"`).
Then apply is idempotent (`0 create, 0 update, 39 noop`).

Once the mismatched rows exist, re-applying in the hyphen spelling is ALSO
blocked — the pre-existing rows read as undeclared drift and apply refuses.
Recovery is to delete the orphans through the API, then re-apply.

Related: [[reference_apply_never_deletes_removed_entity_types]],
[[project_prodma_erp_to_lobu_poc]]

# ---- Reporting --------------------------------------------------------------
PASSES=0; FAILS=0; SKIPS=0
pass() { echo "  [OK]   $*"; PASSES=$((PASSES + 1)); }
skip() { echo "  [SKIP] $*"; SKIPS=$((SKIPS + 1)); }
note() { echo ""; echo "== $* =="; }
softfail() {
  echo "  [FAIL] $*" >&2
  echo "         -- last 12 lines of output --" >&2
  tail -12 "$OUT" 2>/dev/null | sed 's/^/         /' >&2
  FAILS=$((FAILS + 1))
}
# Hard failure for setup prerequisites -- no point walking commands if the
# server never came up.
die() { echo "ABORT: CLI smoke -- $*" >&2; [ -f "$RUN_LOG" ] && { echo "--- last 40 lines of run.log ---" >&2; tail -40 "$RUN_LOG" >&2; }; exit 1; }

# Run `lobu <args>` in <cwd>, capture combined output to $OUT, set RC to the
# CLI's exit code. errexit is disabled; callers inspect RC explicitly.
RC=0
runlobu() {
  local cwd="$1"; shift
  ( cd "$cwd" && node "$LOBU_BIN" "$@" ) > "$OUT" 2>&1 </dev/null
  RC=$?
}

# expect_grep <desc> <marker> <cwd> <args...>  -> exit 0 AND <marker> present
expect_grep() {
  local desc="$1" marker="$2" cwd="$3"; shift 3
  runlobu "$cwd" "$@"
  if [ "$RC" -eq 0 ] && grep -qF -- "$marker" "$OUT"; then pass "$desc"
  else softfail "$desc (exit=$RC, missing marker: $marker) [lobu $*]"; fi
}

# expect_ok <desc> <cwd> <args...>  -> exit 0 (no marker)
expect_ok() {

content.rawContent:
<!-- Per-repo agent rules loaded into every Claude Code session in this repo. Inlines AGENTS.md (shared project rules) first, then layers local-only notes below. User memory entries live under ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/. Don't add anything here unless it's only relevant to Claude agent specific. If other harnesses like pi or codex need it, modify AGENTS.md -->

@AGENTS.md

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- `core` types/utils · `plugin-api` plugin contracts · `plugin-host` plugin composition · `server` gateway + embedded runtime · `agent-worker` agent execution · `connectors` built-in connectors · `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Read the nearest package `AGENTS.md` before editing that package; grep `docs/GOTCHAS.md` when something looks inexplicable.

## Unrecoverable — never do these
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout — other sessions share it. For a pure submodule-pointer bump, `make bump SUBMODULE=packages/owletto` is the lightweight isolated-worktree exception; it also posts the required statuses.
- **Stage by explicit path** (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`). A commit is a snapshot, so a stale file copy left by earlier work in the same worktree silently reverts merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal your intended file list; extras = stop.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone or supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are usually real signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI** — it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work. Rebase locally against `origin/main`; submodule-pointer branches `git merge` instead (`docs/GOTCHAS.md`).
- **Two writing agents must never share a worktree** — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work. Every subagent with Edit/Write/Bash gets its own through `make task-setup` (only task-setup does submodule pinning, `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation); only read-only agents share the parent.
- **Never add a table or change DB design, API surface, or SDK surface** without surfacing the proposal and receiving confirmation first.
- **Never auto-submit an interactive browser draft, in any package.** Drafts are page-activated: persist the operation, notify normally, and let the extension activate the run only when the user visits a pending URL in a user-owned tab. Only scrape-owned scratch tabs may be opened and closed automatically. Server, connector, and Owletto code all obey this (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`).

## Facts you cannot derive
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** A resync supersedes the row and mints a new id for the same source item, so cross-sync identity and dedupe must key on the connector's `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over `events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, … on a user-facing read path: history grows, the answer doesn't. Materialize at write time, read back by index, backfill in a migration. Bounded config tables (`connections`, `automations`, `agent_users`) are fine.
- **Shared state must be Postgres-mediated.** An in-memory Map or singleton is invisible to other replicas — correct in dev, broken in prod.
- **Workers never receive real credentials** — placeholders or proxied access only. The exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived leases (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one.
- **Automation is the product, API, and storage vocabulary.** Use it consistently in public contracts and internal identifiers; `make pre-pr-remote` rejects retired product and engine terminology.
- **`make review` is the semantic review gate, not CI.** It runs no typecheck, knip, or tests; a verdict or safe-class skip is not evidence CI will pass.
- **Depot serializes org-wide.** A newer dispatch silently cancels a peer session's running gate, and `gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch. Check `pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"` before dispatching.
- Default to static `import`; a new production dynamic import needs measured justification plus a call-site rationale comment. Tests may import dynamically after mocks; two Node-version gates are grandfathered (playbook).

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce red → fix → prove green, and paste both outputs in the PR. Cannot reproduce = report the dead end; never ship a speculative fix.
3. Iterate on focused tests: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. `make pre-pr-remote-fast` gives interim breadth and never substitutes for the final gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff, then re-read what it touched. Safe-class changes self-skip before selecting an LLM. Otherwise it runs BEFORE the first `make review` — never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop, since each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
5. Stage by explicit path, then `make pre-pr-remote`; it fails closed on unstaged or untracked changes. Reviewed workflow/action changes need `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1`.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD; it posts the required `pi-review` status. Narrow path/content-gated safe classes skip the cross-harness review; this includes pure `packages/owletto` pointer bumps and exact `model:` literal swaps, but not mixed runtime and source changes. The submodule's own repo owns its content review.
9. `make ui-review`. Non-Owletto changes and complete, forward-only Owletto pointer diffs confined to `deploy/` pass as not applicable; other pointer changes need exact hosted proof (`ARTIFACT=<url>`; see the playbook).
10. `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin` once green — never `--admin` past a check that has not reported. Lobu's required `integration` fan-in is absent from `gh pr checks` until it starts, not pending, so diff against the branch-protection list (playbook).
11. Prod-visible surface? Verify live after rollout: gate on the **squash commit**, not your branch head, keeping the argument order `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"`. Record the result.

## How to work
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create; no new `*.md` unless asked.
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- **Evidence, not assertion.** Never report done off a green typecheck — boot it, exercise every branch you touched, and clean up test data; if "compiles" is all you ran, say so. Show `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`, including for a dispatched agent's work.
- **Absence needs `origin/main`:** `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main`. A working-tree grep proves nothing, and the fetch is load-bearing.

Verified 2026-08-17. Supersedes the coverage half of
[[reference_entity_change_history_already_exists]].

| what happened | audited? |
|---|---|
| successful UPDATE | yes — field-level diff, `manage_entity.ts:585` |
| successful CREATE | **no** (`handleCreate` :271 never calls it) |
| delete / merge / link / unlink / update_link | **no** (:1365, :675, :1737) |
| **DENIED write** | **no — structurally** |
| the audit write itself failing | **dropped** |

`recordChangeEvent` (`insert-event.ts:756`) returns `void` — not awaited — and its
`.catch` at `:775` logs
`"change audit event DROPPED after retry — audit trail is missing this row"`.

## Denial invisibility is structural

A deny throws → the transaction rolls back → anything written inside it
disappears. And the audit is POST-COMMIT anyway, so it never runs. Same shape as
the lost approval card in
[[reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial]].

**So you get a diff when nothing went wrong, and nothing when it did.** Adding
write rules makes this materially worse: every `deny` becomes a silent failure,
while case 3 proves a denial can be WRONG and misattributed.

## How to apply

- **Auditing denials is a PREREQUISITE for shipping rules, not a follow-up.**
  Write the audit event after the rollback on a fresh connection — this is the one
  place `getDb()` outside the write tx is correct, because the tx has ended, so
  there is no #2818 risk.
- Record: rule, reason, actor, entity, attempted patch.
- Make the denial audit DURABLE. Fire-and-forget with a DROP log is fine for a
  convenience diff; it is not fine for the record of why a write was refused.
- Auditing creates belongs with whichever phase starts validating creates.

## One thing that already composes

`insertConnectionlessAuditEvent` enforces idempotency via
`metadata._lobu_idempotency_key` + a unique index, handling the unique violation
at `:713-725`. So an SSI **retry** re-running the transaction will not duplicate
audit rows — that integration problem is already solved.

content.text:
I'll let the build finish and run the smoke. Meanwhile, here's the state of the two remaining gaps.

## 3 — merge/unmerge and delete bypass the write seam

The seam is a branded type: `patchEntityRows`/`insertEntityRow` only accept a `ValidatedEntityRowPatch`, which has no public constructor. So "did you validate?" is a compile-time question, not a review question. There is exactly one escape hatch, and it's deliberately ugly:

```ts
export function unvalidatedEntityRowPatch(params: {
  patch: EntityRowPatch;
  reason: string;   // required — an exemption must justify itself in code
}): ValidatedEntityRowPatch
```

Grepping `unvalidatedEntityRow` across `packages/server/src` returns the complete list of bypasses — five, all with a stated reason: `canvas-events.ts:112`, `member-entity.ts:267`, `eval-cases.ts:476`, and `entity-management.ts:1802` (soft-delete). The first three are platform-owned types no tenant rule governs, and I'm not worried about them. The two that matter:

**Merge/unmerge.** All six merge writes funnel through one kernel, `transitionEntityMergeRows` (`entity-management.ts:568`), called from `entity-merge.ts` at lines 317, 418, 430, 785, 798, 896. A rule that freezes a posted invoice does not stop that invoice being merged away or restored. The reason it isn't just "call the validator here" is that the rule's row shape can't express it — a rule sees `{ committed, patch, next, op }` where `op` is `"create" | "update"`. A merge changes `merged_into`, tombstones a row, and revives another; there's no field edit to judge. Closing it needs a merge-shaped verdict (winner/loser identities, not a patch), which is a rule-API change, and the isolate would then run inside a lock-holding compound transaction.

**Soft delete.** `deleteEntity` is deliberately a single pool-level statement, not a transaction. Validating there means reading the row on one pool handle and writing on another, so a concurrent write can overtake the check between the two. That check would *look* like enforcement and not be one, which is worse than the honest exemption that's there now. Closing it means giving soft-delete a transaction boundary — a separate change with its own #2818 pool-starvation risk, since the entity-write pool is what deadlocked before. Hard delete has the same hole via `hardDeleteEntityRows`.

**Practical exposure:** a rule can lock a document's fields but cannot keep the document from disappearing. For the ERP case that's the difference between "you can't un-post this invoice" and "you can't make this invoice go away" — the second one is currently unenforced.

## 4 — the audit trail is inverted

Successful updates are audited with a field-level diff (one `recordChangeEvent` call, `manage_entity.ts:632`). Nothing else is:

| what happened | recorded? |
|---|---|
| successful update | yes — field diff |
| successful create | no |
| delete / merge / link / unlink | no |
| **denied write** | no — structurally |

Denial invisibility is structural, not an oversight. A `deny` throws, the transaction rolls back, and anything written inside it disappears with it. The audit path is post-commit, so it never runs at all. You get a record when nothing went wrong and nothing when it did — and rules make that worse, because every `deny` is now a silent failure by design.

What shipped in #2842 is a `logger.info({ module: "entity-rules", outcome: "deny", reason })` on the deny path. That is a log line, not a record: not queryable, not joinable to the entity, gone with log retention. Note the asymmetry — an `escalate` becomes a `runs` row you can query forever; a `deny` becomes a grep.

Closing it: write the denial event *after* the rollback on a fresh connection. This is the one place `getDb()` outside the write transaction is correct, because the transaction has already ended — no #2818 risk. Record rule, reason, actor, entity, attempted patch. It must be durable, unlike `recordChangeEvent`, which is fire-and-forget and logs `"change audit event DROPPED after retry"` when it loses one. Idempotency already composes: `insertConnectionlessAuditEvent` dedupes on `metadata._lobu_idempotency_key`, so a transaction retry won't double-write.

## Other gaps, since you asked

- **`approvedFields` is optional.** The brand makes skipping validation a compile error; the approval grant has no equivalent. An apply-path caller that forgets it silently gets defer semantics — which is exactly how two of the five bugs happened. Making it required on the apply functions would close the class properly.
- **No cross-row invariants.** Rules are per-type and per-batch with no DB access, so "order total equals the sum of its lines" isn't expressible. That's the deliberate cost of purity (and of the dry-run capability that purity buys).
- **No local authoring loop.** You can't test a rule before `apply` ships it — no `lobu` command dry-runs one against sample rows. Every iteration is a round trip through the server.
- **Rules are invisible in the UI.** Owletto doesn't render `rules_source`, so what's enforcing on a type is only knowable from the config file or the DB.

The first is the one I'd close next: it's small, it's the same bug class that already bit five times, and unlike the others it's a correctness hole rather than a missing feature.

that opted into it.** To audit the seam, grep the SQL verbs, not the helper.

mechanism finds the callers who used it, never the ones who went around it.

- **[Entity write VALIDATION seam — #2842 SHIPPED, review clean](reference_entity_write_validation_seam_state.md)** — branded creates+updates; `x-transitions` DELETED for per-type rules in `entity_types.rules_source/rules_compiled`; `escalate` wired to cards for BOTH ops; merge/unmerge + softDelete still bypass · **[the approval grant is SCOPED](reference_entity_approval_grant_is_scoped_to_reviewed_fields.md)** — `onEscalate` DELETED for `approvedFields` ← the card's `escalated_fields`, no new table · **[verdict-meets-approval = ONE class, FIVE sites](reference_approval_verdict_class_has_five_sites.md)** — grep finds 3; use the residual×full matrix · **[rules are PURE ⇒ dry-run answers "what's legal next"](reference_pure_batch_rules_enable_a_speculative_dry_run.md)** — ~3ms/1000 candidates, no second DSL · **[`entities` has exactly FOUR physical writers](reference_entities_table_has_exactly_four_physical_writers.md)** — 2 branded, 2 NOT (merge kernel + hard delete); grepping `unvalidatedEntityRow` lists only the DECLARED exemptions · **[`runScript` RECOMPILES its source](reference_run_script_recompiles_its_source.md)** — `*_compiled` must be IIFE + one ESM runner or it silently denies all · **[isolate cost MEASURED](reference_isolate_per_write_costs_4_5ms.md)** — 4.5ms via SDK, per-MODULE ⇒ one script per type · **[ontology models VERIFIED](reference_ontology_write_rule_models_verified.md)** — all bind per-type
- **[RULES MUST BE BATCH-SHAPED — measured](reference_entity_rules_must_be_batch_shaped.md)** — per-ROW = 21s for a 5k sync; per BATCH = 29.7ms (the 13.5ms in that file is WRONG) and cost is SUPER-linear ⇒ `MAX_RULE_BATCH` = 1000, not 2000 · **[`runScript` compiled on EVERY call](reference_runscript_compiles_on_every_call.md)** — now memoized by source hash; any new per-write caller must check the memo exists
- **[WRITE-POLICY design (spec finalized, NOT built)](reference_entity_write_concurrency_model.md)** — per-row isolate serialization is **already free** (lock precedes rule position), so same-row invariants need ZERO new machinery · **[approval-hold-vs-rule: FIXED in #2842](reference_approval_hold_turns_legal_write_into_denial.md)** — `fullProposalVerdict()` re-validates the FULL proposal; the mechanism (validate a REDUCED write, report it as the original) still generalizes. STILL OPEN: **[the audit trail is INVERTED](reference_entity_audit_trail_is_inverted.md)** — every DENIAL is structurally invisible (deny now logs, but a log is not a record) · **[approval authority = admin/owner ∪ field owner](reference_entity_approval_routing_and_authority.md)** — `owner_user_id` NULL for agent-written fields
- **[#2818 SHIPPED + PROD-VERIFIED: entity-write pool DEADLOCK](reference_2818_root_cause_is_entity_write_pool_starvation.md)** — never `getDb()` inside `withEntityWriteTransaction` · **[a local repro needs a BASELINE run](feedback_a_local_repro_needs_a_baseline_run.md)**
- **[VOCABULARY: Automation is canonical; `behavior` AND `watcher` are BANNED repo-wide](reference_automation_is_canonical_behavior_and_watcher_both_banned.md)** — #2784 renamed the tables; index lines below still say "Behavior"
- **[ACL work SHIPPED + prod-verified](project_acl_purpose_classification_a2_state.md)** — trigger ARMED, cli 15.0.0 on npm. **OPEN: Owletto shows dead 403 buttons on `member_of`** · [unmerge fence race](reference_unmerge_acl_fence_has_a_commit_visibility_race.md) — org `FOR UPDATE` first · [invalidators are FIVE sites](reference_acl_invalidators_are_five_sites.md) · [ship triggers INERT](reference_acl_trigger_must_ship_inert_before_classifying.md) · [arming breaks RAW edge fixtures](reference_arming_acl_trigger_breaks_raw_edge_test_fixtures.md)
- **[Authorization-purpose UI program — DONE server-side, prod-verified](project_authorization_purpose_ui_program_state.md)** — #2837/#2839/#2840/#2843 + owletto#881 shipped. **LEFT: Owletto doesn't CONSUME `acl_managed` yet** · **[`inverse_type_id` is DISPLAY-ONLY](reference_inverse_type_id_is_display_only_not_an_edge_write_path.md)** — a straddling ACL pair is a listing bug, not a bypass · **[ui-review needs a HOSTED before/after when the owletto range touches `src/`](reference_ui_review_artifact_requires_a_hosted_before_after.md)** — swap ONLY the submodule SHA; NEVER `screencapture`
- **[Release publish fires on the RELEASE event, not the push](reference_release_publish_fires_on_release_event_not_push.md)** — green prod proves nothing about npm · [`device-action-wait` is a REAL 80ms flake](reference_device_action_wait_test_is_flaky_80ms_margin.md) — DB latency, not CPU
- **[`make pre-pr-remote` bases on the REMOTE branch](reference_pre_pr_remote_bases_on_the_remote_branch.md)** — rebase without pushing ⇒ gates a STALE tree; `pkill` can kill a PEER gate · **[biome in owletto needs its own scope](reference_biome_in_owletto_needs_its_own_scope.md)** — `--write .` reformatted 370 files
- **[`git push -u origin <name>` pushes a LOCAL branch, not HEAD](reference_git_push_can_resolve_a_stale_local_branch.md)** — use `HEAD:<name>` · **[ui-review + generated-client: 2 false positives from a stale base](reference_two_pr_gate_false_positives_from_a_stale_base.md)** — rebase; `[client-regen-not-needed]` for comment-only route edits · **[the review verdict CACHE keys on the DIFF hash](reference_review_verdict_cache_keys_on_the_diff_hash.md)** — a blocker fixed in the commit MESSAGE replays forever
- **[EDGE policy module EXISTS but is UNADOPTED](reference_edge_write_funnel_does_not_exist.md)** — `relationship-validation.ts` has the checks; 2 of 7 writers call it. Do NOT build a new funnel · **[connector edges are an ACL hole](reference_connector_declared_edges_acl_hole.md)** · **[reuse `attributions`, NOT a second resolver](reference_connector_edges_reuse_attributions_not_a_new_resolver.md)** · **[$links gate = chokepoint](project_links_gate_vs_edge_provenance_open_decision.md)** · **[Edge Authority Model](project_edge_authority_model.md)** — 8 files / 14 sites; edges are OR

note "apply --only validation (no server)"
expect_exit "lobu apply --only bogus -> exit 2" 2 "$PROJ" apply --only bogus

# ============================================================================
# Boot the embedded stack (auto-applies the project -> registers `local` ctx)
# ============================================================================
note "boot: lobu run --port $GW_PORT"
{
  printf '\n'
  echo "MOCK_API_KEY=mock-key-smoke"
  echo "WORKER_ALLOWED_DOMAINS=127.0.0.1,localhost"
  echo "LOBU_DISABLE_SYSTEMD_RUN=1"
} >> "$PROJ/.env"

( cd "$PROJ" && node "$LOBU_BIN" run --port "$GW_PORT" > "$RUN_LOG" 2>&1 ) &
# Wait on the auto-apply markers only -- "api docs:" prints BEFORE the project
# auto-applies, so breaking on it would race the apply (see sdk-e2e.sh).
for _ in $(seq 1 120); do
  grep -qiE "Apply complete|auto-apply skipped|Apply halted" "$RUN_LOG" 2>/dev/null && break
  sleep 1
done
grep -qi "Apply complete" "$RUN_LOG" || die "lobu run did not auto-apply (skipped/halted?)"
pass "lobu run booted + auto-applied the project"

# The two compatibility aliases must reach the same run handler. Point them at
# the already-listening gateway port: a controlled "already in use" failure
# proves argv dispatch without booting two extra stacks.
expect_fail_grep "lobu dev alias -> run handler" "already in use" "$PROJ" dev --port "$GW_PORT"
expect_fail_grep "lobu start alias -> run handler" "already in use" "$PROJ" start --port "$GW_PORT"

# Trigger loopback auth (local-init) + resolve the bootstrap org slug.
runlobu "$PROJ" whoami -c local
ORG="$( ( cd "$PROJ" && node "$LOBU_BIN" org current -c local 2>/dev/null ) | grep -oE '[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*' | grep -vE '^local$|^org$|^for$|^context$|^current$|^no$|^active$|^set$' | tail -1 )"

content.text:
Here's where things stand while that resolves.

**Done:** the `rulesFromFile` smoke case is written (`scripts/cli-smoke.sh`, syntax-checked). It declares an `invoice` entity type carrying `rules: rulesFromFile("./rules/invoice.ts")` in the project the gate boots, so the boot auto-apply ships the rule the same way a user would, then asserts three things: an illegal create comes back with the rule's own reason, the legal create still succeeds (the contrast case — without it, a rule that denied everything would pass), and a re-apply of unchanged rule source renders as `= entity-type invoice`, the noop verb, which is the idempotence check that underscore-keyed types fail.

**Not yet proven:** the gate aborts before reaching my cases — `lobu run` boots but never calls `/api/local-init`, so `localContextReady` stays false and `shouldAutoApplyLocalProject` returns false. No apply, no `(auto-apply skipped: …)` line either, because that branch is never entered.

I ran the unmodified script from `HEAD` as a baseline and it is reaching the same wall: same boot, same two routes (`/api/health`, `/api/workers/poll`), no `local-init`. So this looks environmental rather than caused by my change — but I'm waiting for the baseline to actually print its ABORT before I claim that, because a baseline that hasn't finished isn't evidence.

If the baseline confirms, local end-to-end verification isn't available on this machine and the honest path is CI: `cli-command-smoke` runs this exact script, so `make pre-pr-remote` is the real check.

**Confidence**
- Smoke case as written — **60**. Basis: `bash -n` clean, `lobu validate` accepted the new config with `rulesFromFile` (so the marker resolves and the export exists in `dist`), and the assertions are built from formats I read in source (`= entity-type <slug>` from `VERB_PREFIX`/`renderRow`, the deny message shape `new invoice: <reason>` from `entity-row-validation.ts:376`). Not run end to end, and one assumption is unverified: that a rule denial surfaces its message through the REST layer to `lobu call` rather than being flattened into a generic error. If it flattens, my first assertion fails — and that would itself be a finding worth fixing.
- Gaps explanation (3 and 4) — **90**. Basis: read on `origin/main`, not recalled.

Two corrections to what I told you earlier, both from checking rather than remembering: there are **four** declared exemption call sites, not five; and grepping `unvalidatedEntityRow` does **not** enumerate the bypasses. `transitionEntityMergeRows` and `hardDeleteEntityRows` write their own SQL and never touch the branded helpers, so they're invisible to that grep. The real check is the SQL verbs — `entities` has exactly four write statements repo-wide, all in `entity-management.ts`: insert and patch are branded, merge and hard-delete are not. That makes gap 3 sharper than I put it: the bypasses that matter are precisely the ones the greppable convention doesn't cover. Saved as memory.

input.content:
Follow-up to #2842, which shipped per-entity-type write rules enforced at the entity write seam. The mechanism works and is reviewed clean, but four things are knowingly unfinished. Filing them together because they share one theme: the seam is sound where it applies, and the remaining risk is entirely in what it does *not* cover and what it does *not* record.

Everything below was verified against `origin/main` at 70e5abae1, not recalled.

## 1. Merge, unmerge and delete bypass the seam

The `entities` table has exactly four physical write statements repo-wide, all in `packages/server/src/utils/entity-management.ts`:

| line | function | validated? |
|---|---|---|
| 447 | `insertEntityRow` | yes — takes `ValidatedEntityRowInsert` |
| 533 | `patchEntityRows` | yes — takes `ValidatedEntityRowPatch` |
| 585 | `transitionEntityMergeRows` | **no** |
| 611 | `hardDeleteEntityRows` | **no** |

```
git grep -n "UPDATE entities\|INSERT INTO entities\|DELETE FROM entities" origin/main -- packages/server/src
```

Worth stating plainly, because it caught me: grepping `unvalidatedEntityRow` does **not** find these. That grep returns the four *declared* exemptions (`canvas-events.ts:112`, `member-entity.ts:267`, `eval-cases.ts:476`, `entity-management.ts:1802`), which route through the branded helpers with a required `reason`. The two kernels above write their own SQL and never touch those helpers, so the convention only documents the bypasses that opted into it. Audit the SQL verbs, not the helper.

Practical exposure: a rule can freeze a document's fields but cannot stop the document being merged away, restored, or deleted. For the ERP case that is the difference between "you can't un-post this invoice" and "you can't make this invoice go away" — the second is currently unenforced.

**Merge/unmerge** (`transitionEntityMergeRows`, called from `entity-merge.ts` at 317, 418, 430, 785, 798, 896). Not a missing call — the rule's row shape cannot express it. A rule sees `{ committed, patch, next, op }` with `op: "create" | "update"`; a merge changes `merged_into`, tombstones one row and revives another, and there is no field edit to judge. Closing it needs a merge-shaped verdict (winner/loser identities, not a patch), which is a rule-API change, and the isolate would then run inside a lock-holding compound transaction.

**Soft delete** (`deleteEntity`, the exemption at `entity-management.ts:1802`). Deliberately a single pool-level statement, not a transaction. Validating there means reading on one pool handle and writing on another, so a concurrent write can overtake the check. A check that looks like enforcement and isn't is worse than the honest exemption. Closing it means giving soft-delete a transaction boundary, which carries its own #2818 pool-starvation risk.

## 2. The audit trail is inverted

Successful updates are audited with a field-level diff (one `recordChangeEvent` call, `manage_entity.ts:632`). Nothing else is:

| what happened | recorded? |
|---|---|
| successful update | yes — field diff |
| successful create | no |
| delete / merge / link / unlink | no |
| **denied write** | no — structurally |

Denial invisibility is structural, not an oversight. A `deny` throws, the transaction rolls back, and anything written inside it goes with it; the audit path is post-commit, so it never runs. You get a record when nothing went wrong and nothing when it did — and rules make that worse, since every `deny` is now a silent failure by design.

#2842 added `logger.info({ module: "entity-rules", outcome: "deny", reason })`. That is a log line, not a record: not queryable, not joinable to the entity, gone with retention. Note the asymmetry — an `escalate` becomes a `runs` row you can query forever; a `deny` becomes a grep.

Fix: write the denial event *after* the rollback on a fresh connection. This is the one place `getDb()` outside the write transaction is correct, because the transaction has already ended, so there is no #2818 risk. Record rule, reason, actor, entity, attempted patch. It has to be durable, unlike `recordChangeEvent`, which is fire-and-forget and logs `"change audit event DROPPED after retry"` when it loses one. Idempotency already composes: `insertConnectionlessAuditEvent` dedupes on `metadata._lobu_idempotency_key`, so a transaction retry won't double-write.

## 3. `approvedFields` is optional, so the approval grant has no compile-time floor

The brand makes skipping *validation* a compile error. The approval grant has no equivalent: `approvedFields?: readonly string[]` is optional on `validateEntityRowPatch` / `validateEntityRowInsert`, so an apply-path caller that forgets it silently gets defer semantics instead of failing to build.

That is not hypothetical — it is exactly how two of the five instances of this bug class happened during #2842. Each one was found individually; the class is only closed structurally.

Fix: make the parameter required on the apply functions, plus a scoped `no-restricted-imports` so the approval module cannot reach the ungranted validator.

This is the smallest of the four and the only one that is a correctness hole rather than a missing capability, so it is the one I would do first.

## 4. CLI smoke coverage for `rulesFromFile` — written, unverified

Branch `feat/cli-smoke-rules` (commit 3d0fe835c), pushed, no PR yet.

Nothing exercised the CLI write-rules path against a booted server. Unit tests cover each half — the CLI resolving the marker, the server executing a compiled rule — but nothing proved the halves agree on the wire. The branch declares an `invoice` type carrying rules in the project the gate boots, so the boot auto-apply ships it the way a user would, then asserts the rule's own reason comes back on an illegal create, the legal create still succeeds, and a re-apply of unchanged source renders as `= entity-type invoice`.

It is unverified end to end. The gate aborts before reaching those cases on my machine: `lobu run` boots but never calls `/api/local-init`, so `localContextReady` stays false and `shouldAutoApplyLocalProject` returns false — no apply, and no `(auto-apply skipped: …)` line either, because that branch is never entered. Reproduced identically on unmodified `HEAD`, so it is environmental rather than caused by the change. Verification belongs to the `cli-command-smoke` CI job, which runs this script.

One assumption in the branch is unchecked: that a rule denial surfaces its message through the REST layer to `lobu call` rather than being flattened into a generic error. If it flattens, the first assertion fails — and that is itself worth fixing, since a rule denial reaching a user as an opaque 500 is bad behaviour.

Worth deciding separately: whether the local `/api/local-init` failure is a real regression in `lobu run` or specific to my machine. It makes the whole smoke gate unrunnable locally, which is its own problem.

## Not in scope, recorded so they aren't rediscovered

- **No cross-row invariants.** Rules are per-type and per-batch with no DB access, so "order total equals the sum of its lines" is not expressible. That is the deliberate cost of purity — and purity is what buys the speculative dry-run (enumerate candidate next-states through one isolate, ~3ms per 1000 candidates, no static analysis needed).
- **No local authoring loop.** No way to test a rule before `apply` ships it; every iteration is a server round trip.
- **Rules are invisible in the UI.** Owletto does not render `rules_source`, so what is enforcing on a type is only knowable from the config file or the DB.

content.text:
Mixed — and the numbers change my answer on one of them.

**Item 3 (`approvedFields`) — I'd downgrade this from "smallest" to "needs a design call first."** There are 17 validator call sites; only 3 pass `approvedFields`, all in `entity-field-approval.ts`. So doing literally what the issue says — make the parameter required — forces 14 innocent callers to type `[]`. That's not a safety improvement: passing `[]` and passing the wrong list are equally easy, and now every ordinary write carries approval vocabulary it has nothing to do with. The shape that actually closes the hole is different: either a separate entry point that approval-path callers must use, or a discriminated `grant: {kind: "none"} | {kind: "approved", fields}` so "I didn't think about it" stops being spellable. That's a judgment call, and a weaker model following the issue text verbatim would produce the version that compiles, passes review, and fixes nothing. My issue wording is partly to blame; I wrote the naive prescription.

**Item 2 (denial audit) — medium code, bad failure mode.** The write itself is small. The trap is that the obvious implementation — record the denial where the denial happens — is inside the transaction that's about to roll back, so it silently writes nothing. It looks right, it passes a test that asserts "no exception," and it produces an empty audit table in prod. You'd also be adding a durable write, which under AGENTS.md needs your sign-off before anyone starts. Delegatable only with the ordering spelled out (after rollback, fresh connection, and a test that asserts the row exists *after* a denial, not that the code ran).

**Item 1 (merge/delete) — not a delegation target at all.** It needs a new rule-API verb, which is public SDK surface and needs your approval before code exists. Then it runs an isolate inside a lock-holding compound transaction, and soft-delete needs a new transaction boundary in the exact area that deadlocked in #2818. This is design work with a concurrency hazard attached.

**Item 4 — genuinely easy, and the only thing I'd hand off as-is.** Open the PR on `feat/cli-smoke-rules`, read `cli-command-smoke`, fix what it says. Mechanical. The `/api/local-init` diagnosis bundled with it is open-ended debugging and is a separate, harder job.

The general pattern: none of these are large diffs. What makes them hard is that the wrong version type-checks, reads sensibly, and passes a plausible test — which is exactly the failure mode a weaker model produces most reliably. Three of the five bugs in #2842 were that shape, and two of them survived my own review twice.

Where the repo helps: `make review` and mutation testing catch some of this, and the branded types make one whole class into a compile error. Where it doesn't: nothing catches "recorded the denial inside the doomed transaction," because there's no failure to observe.

My recommendation: hand item 4 to a cheaper model now. For 2 and 3, the expensive part is the spec, not the code — if you want, I'll write both specs precisely enough that a weaker model can execute them, including the test that would catch the silent-failure version. Item 1 stays with you until the rule-API shape is decided.

Want me to write those two specs and attach them to #2865?

message.content: what are these design calls

content.text:
Three clusters. Here they are concretely.

## Item 3 — how do you make "I forgot the grant" unspellable?

The invariant is: *only the apply path may waive an escalation.* Four ways to express it:

**(a) Required param everywhere.** 17 sites, 14 of which type `grant: []`. Rejected — `[]` and the wrong list are equally easy to type, so it buys nothing.

**(b) Required discriminated union**, `grant: {kind:"none"} | {kind:"approved", fields}`. Still touches all 17, but the noise now *means* something: every caller states whether an approval is in play. Forgetting becomes impossible; being wrong stays possible.

**(c) Two entry points** — `validateEntityRowPatch` (no grant) and a granting variant only the approval module may import, enforced by a scoped `no-restricted-imports`. Zero changes to the 14 innocent sites, and it puts the restriction exactly where the invariant lives: a module boundary.

**(d) Don't pass fields at all** — thread the proposal into the apply functions and let them derive it. Nothing to forget because nothing is supplied. But it couples the validator to a proposal shape, which is bad layering.

I'd take (c). The decision you actually have to make is what enforces it, because TypeScript has no module-private: lint is the realistic ceiling, and lint can be disabled.

One thing worth flagging, since it's a trap I already fell into once: a brand doesn't help here. I built and dropped an `ApprovalGrant` brand during #2842 because the proposal row is already un-forgeable. That reasoning was about *forgery*. This problem is *forgetting*, and a brand on a value nobody passes protects nothing.

## Item 2 — five calls, and one of them is the whole scope

1. **Where does it live?** `events` is append-only and already has idempotency via `insertConnectionlessAuditEvent`, so it composes for free. The counter-argument: a denial isn't something that *happened* to the entity, and putting it in the timeline makes the entity's history include writes that never occurred. A separate table is cleaner semantically but needs your sign-off per AGENTS.md.
